Residency is the legal right to live in a country, which can be temporary, while citizenship is full membership with the right to vote and hold a passport.

examples.everyday: We're applying for citizenship next year, so we have to study for the civics test.
examples.professional: Our global HR team needs to check each candidate's citizenship status before the relocation paperwork is filed.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that citizenship is more than legal status; it also involves a shared commitment to public life.

nuance.analogy: It is like a passport that does more than allow travel: it gives you a voice, a vote, and a place in the community.
nuance.etymology: From citizen plus the suffix -ship, meaning "status or condition."
common_mistakes: Confusing "citizenship" with "residency" when someone has a green card but is not a citizen yet.
Stressing the last syllable as "ship" with a long vowel instead of a short i.

senses.definition: A loud, ringing sound, like that made by free-hanging metal objects striking each other; usually, one considered more jarring than melodious.
senses.example: The loud clang of the dumpster lid woke the whole street.

senses.definition: Quality of tone. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The old church bell had a deep, mellow clang that carried for miles.

senses.definition: The cry of some birds, including the crane and the goose.
senses.example: Overhead, a flock of geese let out a harsh clang as they flew south.

senses.definition: A word or phrase linked only by sound and not by meaning, characteristic of some mental disorders.
senses.example: The psychiatrist noted the patient's clang in her speech, rhyming words without meaning.

senses.definition: To strike (objects) together so as to produce a clang.
senses.example: Please don't clang the pots together while the baby is sleeping.

senses.definition: To give out a clang; to resound.
senses.example: The iron gate clanged shut behind us, echoing through the empty courtyard.

senses.definition: To utter a word or phrase linked only by sound and not by meaning, characteristic of some mental disorders.
senses.example: During the episode, she began to clang, stringing together rhymes that made no sense.

senses.definition: Imitative of a loud metallic ringing sound.
senses.example: Clang! went the pipe as the wrench slipped off the valve.

senses.definition: Said after someone has name-dropped (mentioned a famous person with whom they are acquainted).
senses.example: Clang! I had dinner with the mayor last week, you know.

core.definition: A loud, harsh, ringing metallic sound, such as a bell, a gate, or pans striking something hard.

pronunciation.tip: Clang has one syllable with a short a, as in 'cat', not a long a like 'clay'. Say the ng as one nasal sound and do not add a g or k after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it often suggests a harsh or unpleasant noise. In vivid description it can be expressive rather than negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'clang' for loud metal sounds: a gate closing, a bell, a trash can lid, or a dropped pan. It is an everyday word in ordinary speech and writing, and the verb is also common, as in 'the bell clanged all morning'. The bird-call sense is rare in everyday American use. The interjection 'clang!' is a jokey remark said after someone name-drops a famous acquaintance, and it appears mainly in informal speech.

distinctions.note: Clank is a shorter, duller sound of heavy metal, like chains or pipes; clang is longer and more ringing.
Ring suggests a clear, often musical tone that can be pleasant; clang is harsher and less musical.
Clatter describes many quick, rattling sounds, like dishes or hooves; clang is a single loud, ringing metal sound.

collocations: the clang of pots and pans

examples.everyday: The screen door gave a loud clang every time the kids ran out to the backyard.
examples.professional: The alarm on the loading dock makes a clang that carries across the whole warehouse, so we switched it to a quieter tone.
examples.analytical: Epic poets often imitate the clang of battle through harsh consonants, so that the sound itself becomes part of the fight.

nuance.analogy: Like a dropped skillet on a tile floor, a clang announces itself at once and then fades out.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of a loud metallic ringing sound.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long a, like 'clayng'; the vowel is short, as in 'bang'.
Confusing clang with clank; clang rings longer and sharper, while clank is a shorter, heavier sound.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Corinthians 13:1 Paul uses the Greek phrase 'kymbalon alalazon', a clashing or clanging cymbal, and 'chalkos echōn', sounding bronze. He says that eloquent speech without love is no better than a clanging cymbal, meaning noisy and empty. Psalm 150:5 calls for praise with loud cymbals, showing that the same sound can serve worship when joined to devotion.

senses.definition: A group of people hired to attend a performance and to either applaud or boo.
senses.example: The opera house had hired a claque to applaud loudly at the end of the aria.

senses.definition: A group of fawning admirers.
senses.example: The young actor surrounded himself with a claque of fawning admirers who followed him everywhere.

senses.definition: A group of people who pre-arrange among themselves to express strong support for an idea, so as to give the false impression of a wider consensus.
senses.example: Critics accused the company of paying a claque to flood the comment section with praise for the product.

core.definition: A group of people paid or organized to applaud, boo, or praise someone, creating a false impression of popular support.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short a as in cat and a hard k at the end. The French origin does not change the American pronunciation, so do not add a French nasal or an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that the support is staged, paid, or manipulative rather than genuine.
nuance.usage_note: Claque is mainly used in writing about theater, politics, media, and reviews. Americans rarely use it in casual speech, where they would say a planted crowd or paid fans. Use it when you want to suggest that applause or praise was arranged in advance.

distinctions.note: A fan base is made of genuine supporters, while a claque is organized to look like support whether or not people actually agree.
An entourage follows a celebrity for social or practical reasons, while a claque is specifically there to applaud or boo on cue.

collocations: to pack the room with a claque

examples.everyday: The guy in the front row is clearly part of a claque, because he starts clapping every time the singer hits a high note.
examples.professional: Our product launch felt staged, as if the vendor had brought in a claque to cheer every demo.
examples.analytical: The praise for the novel was partly the work of a claque hired by the publisher, which distorted the critical reception.

nuance.analogy: A claque is like a laugh track on a sitcom, supplying applause on cue so the room seems more enthusiastic than it really is.
nuance.etymology: From French claque, a slap or clap, from claquer, to clap; the word is imitative in origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as clake or with a long a.
Using claque for any group of fans, when it specifically implies paid or staged enthusiasm.

senses.definition: Fees which are paid at the conclusion or closing of a real estate transaction.

core.definition: Fees paid by the buyer and seller to finish a real estate purchase, such as loan charges, title insurance, and taxes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on closing, the first word, and costs is weaker. The final s in costs is a plain s, and the vowel in costs is the same as in cot in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since they are extra expenses that surprise many buyers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use closing costs whenever they talk about buying a house, and it is common in mortgage discussions. People often say we had to pay the closing costs or the closing costs were higher than we expected. In the UK people might say completion costs or conveyancing fees, but Americans normally say closing costs.

distinctions.note: A down payment is the upfront share of the price; closing costs are separate fees paid when the sale is finalized.
A mortgage payment repeats monthly; closing costs are a one-time set of charges at the closing.

collocations: roll closing costs into the loan

examples.everyday: The closing costs were way more than we expected, so we had to bring extra cash to the title office.
examples.professional: Our loan officer sent a breakdown of the closing costs before we sign the final documents.
examples.analytical: Closing costs shift part of the price of ownership onto the buyer, which complicates any simple comparison of mortgage rates.

nuance.analogy: Closing costs are like the service charges on a plane ticket: the base price looks clear, but the final total includes several fees.
nuance.etymology: Closing from the verb close, from Latin claudere, meaning to shut; costs from Old French cost, meaning expense.
common_mistakes: Saying closing cost in the singular when speaking about the usual set of fees
Using the British term completion costs or conveyancing fees instead of the American closing costs

senses.definition: A fabric, usually made of woven, knitted, or felted fibres or filaments, such as used in dressing, decorating, cleaning or other practical use. Sometimes, woven fabric specifically.
senses.example: She bought a soft cotton cloth to wipe the kitchen counters after dinner.

senses.definition: Specifically, a tablecloth, especially as spread before a meal or removed afterwards.
senses.example: Grandma spread a white cloth over the table before the holiday guests arrived.

senses.definition: A piece of cloth used for a particular purpose.
Substance or essence; the whole of something complex.
senses.example: Ethics is the cloth of human life, woven through every decision we make.

senses.definition: Appearance; seeming.
senses.example: Under the cloth of politeness, the negotiators were clearly furious with each other.

senses.definition: A form of attire that represents a particular profession or status.
senses.example: The young priest finally received the black cloth after years of seminary study.

senses.definition: The priesthood.
senses.example: He is a respected man of the cloth.

core.definition: A woven or knitted fabric, or a piece of fabric used for a practical purpose such as cleaning or covering.

pronunciation.tip: The final th is voiceless, with the tongue between the teeth and no voice, so it sounds like a soft breath. Do not voice it into the sound in clothe.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is practical and everyday, though the sense of fine fabric can sound more formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cloth for a piece of fabric to wipe something, as in grab a cloth, or for the material itself, as in cotton cloth. For clothing in general, Americans use clothes or clothing, not cloth. For a tablecloth, Americans usually say tablecloth or table linen in formal settings.

distinctions.note: Fabric is the general term for woven or knitted material, often used in technical or retail contexts; cloth often suggests a specific piece.
A rag is a worn or torn piece of cloth used for cleaning, often seen as less valuable; a cloth may be new and neat.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a cloth? The counter is sticky after dinner.
examples.professional: The shop sells natural cloth by the yard, which we are testing for the prototype sample.
examples.analytical: The cloth in the ancient story is less an object than a symbol of mourning and of hidden identity.

nuance.analogy: Cloth is the raw material, like flour before bread; clothes are what the cloth becomes when it is cut and sewn.
nuance.etymology: From Old English clāþ, meaning cloth or garment, from a Germanic root.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final th as a voiced sound, which makes it sound like clothe
Using cloth to mean all clothing in general, which sounds odd to Americans

cloth.etymology: From Middle English *cloth*, *clath*, from Old English *clāþ* (“cloth, clothes, covering, sail”), from **klaiþ*, from Proto-Germanic **klaiþą* (“garment”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European **gleyt-* (“to cling to, cleave, stick”), a form of **gleh₁y-* (“to…

senses.definition: The fact of a thing occurring simultaneously with something else; correlation.
senses.example: Researchers found a strong co-occurrence between high blood pressure and poor sleep in the study population.

senses.definition: An instance of a thing occurring simultaneously with something else; coexistence or coincidence.
senses.example: The co-occurrence of thunderstorms and power outages on our street happened twice this summer.

core.definition: The fact of two or more things happening or appearing together, more often than chance alone would predict.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KUR and the secondary stress on KOH. The second part reduces to uh-KUR-uns, and the double c is just a k sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a pattern without implying cause or meaning, so it is used carefully in research.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use co-occurrence mainly in statistics, linguistics, data science and academic writing. In everyday talk, people say things happen together or show up at the same time. The term does not imply that one thing causes the other.

distinctions.note: Correlation is a measured statistical relationship, often with a direction and strength. Co-occurrence only says things appear together.
Coincidence implies a surprising or chance match. Co-occurrence is neutral and can be a systematic pattern.
Association suggests a link or mental connection between things. Co-occurrence is the observed fact that they appear together.

examples.everyday: Rain and traffic jams seem to have a pretty clear co-occurrence on Friday afternoons.
examples.professional: The model flags pairs of products with high co-occurrence in past baskets, so we can recommend them together.
examples.analytical: Her critique argues that co-occurrence alone cannot establish meaning without a theory of context.

nuance.analogy: Like two friends who always show up at the same parties, without either one causing the other to come.
nuance.etymology: From co- (together) and occurrence, from Latin occurrere, to run into or meet.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the primary stress is on KUR, not KOH.
Treating co-occurrence as proof of cause; it shows things happen together, not that one produces the other.

senses.definition: An instance of colliding.
senses.example: He has retired due to the collision.

senses.definition: Clipping of naming collision.
senses.example: We fixed the collision in the config file before deploying the service.

senses.definition: Clipping of collision detection; tangibility.
senses.example: The game engine's collision code kept the character from walking through walls.

senses.definition: Any event in which two or more bodies exert forces on each other in a relatively short time. In a collision, physical contact of two bodies is not necessary.
senses.example: In the lab, the two billiard balls transferred momentum during the collision.

core.definition: A violent crash between two moving objects, such as vehicles, or a sharp clash between conflicting interests or ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIZH, and the final syllable is a quick, weak 'un' with no clear vowel. Learners often say 'kuh-LIZH-ee-un' with an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it usually suggests harm, damage or an unwanted conflict.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'collision' for car accidents, especially in insurance and police contexts, where it is more formal than 'crash' or 'wreck'. In everyday talk, people more often say 'fender bender' for a minor car collision. In business or technology, 'collision' can also mean two things clashing, such as interests or data records.

distinctions.note: Crash is the everyday word for a sudden impact, while collision is more formal and often used in insurance, law or technical writing.
Accident is any unintended event, while collision specifically means two things striking each other.

examples.everyday: There was a minor collision in the parking lot, but nobody got hurt and the insurance will cover it.
examples.professional: Our hash table produces a collision when two different keys map to the same bucket, so we need a resolution method.
examples.analytical: A collision between two moral principles does not automatically prove that one of them is false, only that both cannot be fully honored in this case.

nuance.analogy: A collision is like two people walking straight at each other in a narrow hallway: neither can pass without one of them stopping or giving way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin collisio, 'a striking together', from collidere, 'to strike together'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it with a hard s, like 'kuh-LIS-un', instead of the 'zh' sound.
Using collision for a near miss; a collision requires actual contact.

collision.etymology: From Middle French *collision*, from Latin *collīsiō* (“clash, concussion, collision”) (whence *-ion*), from *collīsus* (“clashed together, conflicted, contended”), past participle of *collīdō* (“to clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together”) (whence…

senses.definition: A vertical line of entries in a table, usually read from top to bottom.
A body of troops or army vehicles, usually strung out along a road.
senses.example: The enemy column stretched for miles along the dusty road toward the river crossing.

senses.definition: A body of text meant to be read line by line, especially in printed material that has multiple adjacent such on a single page.
senses.example: It was too hard to read the text across the whole page, so I split it into two columns.

senses.definition: A unit of width, especially of advertisements, in a periodical, equivalent to the width of a usual column of text.
senses.example: Each column inch costs $300 a week; this ad is four columns by three inches, so will run $3600 a week.

senses.definition: A recurring feature in a periodical, especially an opinion piece, especially by a single author or small rotating group of authors, or on a single theme.
senses.example: His initial foray into print media was as the author of a weekly column in his elementary-school newspaper.

senses.definition: Something having similar vertical form or structure to the things mentioned above, such as a spinal column.
senses.example: The surgeon explained that the injury had damaged two vertebrae in his spinal column.

senses.definition: A solid upright structure designed usually to support a larger structure above it, such as a roof or horizontal beam, but sometimes for decoration.
senses.example: The marble columns at the front of the courthouse hold up a heavy stone portico.

senses.definition: The gynostemium.
senses.example: The orchid's column holds both the pollen masses and the stigma in a single fused structure.

senses.definition: An instrument used to separate the different components of a liquid or to purify chemical compounds.
senses.example: The chemist packed the glass column with silica gel before running the mixture through it.

core.definition: A vertical arrangement of entries in a table or spreadsheet, read from top to bottom.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak vowel plus a syllabic m, so say 'KAH-lum', not 'KAH-luh-mn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices and data work, column refers to a vertical set of cells in a spreadsheet or database, usually with a header, and its horizontal counterpart is a row. Americans also use column for a newspaper or magazine feature and for a military formation on the march. Context usually makes the meaning clear, so ask 'Which column?' if you need to be sure.

distinctions.note: A row runs horizontally across a table, while a column runs vertically.
In databases, column and field often name the same thing, but field is more common in forms and software interfaces.

examples.everyday: The prices are in the right-hand column, right next to the menu items, so you can compare them quickly.
examples.professional: Please rename the customer_id column before you merge the two tables, or the join will fail.
examples.analytical: Each column in the dataset represents a variable, and each row represents a single observation.

nuance.analogy: A column is like a vertical lane of cars in a parking garage: it runs straight up and down, while rows run across.
nuance.etymology: From Latin columna, meaning a pillar.
common_mistakes: Saying 'co-lum-n' with an extra vowel in the last syllable
Calling a horizontal set of cells a column instead of a row

column.etymology: From Middle English *columne*, *columpne*, *columpe*, borrowed from Old French *columne*, from Latin *columna* (“a column, pillar, post”), originally a collateral form of *columen*, contraction *culmen* (“a pillar, top, crown, summit”).

senses.definition: In a commensurate manner; so as to be equal or proportionate.
senses.example: Her salary rose commensurately with her responsibilities after the promotion.

senses.definition: With equal measure or extent.
senses.example: Both teams were funded commensurately, so neither side could claim an unfair advantage.

core.definition: In a way that matches in size, degree, or amount; in proportion to something else.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on MEN. The -ately ending is weak: the middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'ur-ut' and the last syllable is 'lee.' Learners often stress the -ate syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds precise and formal, so it works well in careful writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say this in casual conversation. It appears in reports, contracts, and policy writing, such as 'rewarded commensurately.' In speech, 'proportionally' or 'to match' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Proportionally is common in everyday and technical speech. Commensurately is more formal and emphasizes matching a measure.
Equally means the same amount for everyone. Commensurately means the amount changes to match something else.

examples.everyday: If your hours go up, your pay should go up commensurately, right?
examples.professional: Budget and headcount will be adjusted commensurately once the new scope is approved.
examples.analytical: Her moral claim grows commensurately with the harm she has suffered and the duty owed to her.

nuance.analogy: Like adding water to a recipe in the same ratio as the flour: when one changes, the other changes to keep the balance.
nuance.etymology: From commensurate plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -ate syllable: 'kuh-men-suh-RATE-lee.'
Using it in casual speech where 'proportionally' would sound more natural.
Confusing it with 'commiserately,' which is a different word.

senses.definition: The act of commiserating; sorrow for the hardships or afflictions of another; pity; compassion.
senses.example: Her quiet commiseration after the layoff meant more to me than any job-search advice.

core.definition: Sympathy or shared sadness for someone's troubles, often expressed by sharing a similar experience or offering comfort.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on RAY, the '-ation' syllable, and the first syllable is weak. Learners often stress MIZ, which is wrong for this noun. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes warm, shared sympathy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use commiseration in written or formal speech, such as a note, speech, or thoughtful message. In casual talk, people more often say 'I feel for you' or 'That sucks.' A natural reply to a friend's sympathy is 'Thanks for listening.'

distinctions.note: Sympathy is the general feeling of care for another's pain. Commiseration suggests sharing the sorrow or complaining together.
Compassion is an active care that wants to relieve suffering. Commiseration is a shared feeling of sadness.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the commiseration. I needed to vent about my landlord after that terrible day.
examples.professional: Her message to the affected engineers offered commiseration but gave no clear next steps.
examples.analytical: Moral philosophers debate whether mere commiseration differs from genuine concern for another's welfare.

nuance.analogy: Like sitting on the same porch step after a storm, sharing the sadness without fixing anything.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin commiseratio 'pity,' from commiserari 'to pity.'
common_mistakes: Stressing MIZ instead of RAY, as in 'KUH-miz-uh-ray-shun.'
Using 'commiseration' as a verb; the verb is 'commiserate.'
Confusing it with 'commiseration' sounds like 'commission' or 'commissary' in speech.

senses.definition: In AI: The text a language model generates to continue a prompt.
The act or state of being or making something complete; conclusion, accomplishment.
senses.example: The fundraising campaign was successfully stewarded to completion on time.

senses.definition: The conclusion of an act of conveyancing concerning the sale of a property.
senses.example: The completion of the house sale is scheduled for Friday at the title company's office.

senses.definition: A forward pass that is successfully caught by the intended receiver.
senses.example: His completion in the fourth quarter set up the game-winning field goal.

senses.definition: The act of making a metric space complete by adding points.
senses.example: The proof of the theorem relies on the completion of the rational numbers under the metric.

senses.definition: The space resulting from such an act.
senses.example: The completion of the rationals is the real numbers, which are complete under the usual metric.

senses.definition: Synonym of autocomplete.
senses.example: tab completion

senses.definition: Orgasm.

core.definition: The act of finishing something; in AI, the text a language model generates to continue a given prompt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLEE, the second syllable, and the -tion ending is a quick 'shun' with a reduced vowel. Don't stress the first syllable; say kum-PLEE-shun, not KOM-plee-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday use it means finishing something; in AI it is a technical term with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English people usually say finish, done, or 'when it's done' rather than completion, which sounds formal or official, as in paperwork, a project milestone, or a course. In AI, a completion is the model's generated continuation of a prompt, and the term is common in API documentation, where a completion request returns text. Engineers say things like 'the completion came back empty' in chat. Use the technical sense only with people who work with models.

distinctions.note: Finish is the everyday verb and noun for ending something; completion is more formal and emphasizes the state of being done.
A conclusion is the end of an argument, event, or document; completion is the act of making something whole and finished.

examples.everyday: I'm waiting for the completion of the bathroom remodel, so the house is a mess right now.
examples.professional: The completion rate for the onboarding survey went up after we shortened it to five questions.
examples.analytical: A model's completion is only a probable continuation, so its fluency should not be taken as proof of understanding.

nuance.analogy: Like an improv partner who finishes your sentence with the most likely next words.
nuance.etymology: From Latin completio, from complere, to fill up or finish.
common_mistakes: Using completion for everyday 'finish' in casual speech, which sounds stiff; say 'when we finish' instead.
Stressing the first syllable: say kum-PLEE-shun, not KOM-plee-shun.
Confusing the noun with the verb: say 'the completion of the form', not 'I completion the form'.

conversation.text: The completion stopped mid-sentence because it hit the max tokens limit.
Older completion endpoints took raw text, while chat endpoints take a list of messages.
Project completion is scheduled for the end of the quarter.

senses.definition: The property of being computable by purely mechanical means.
senses.example: The paper examines the computability of certain functions, showing which ones no algorithm can solve.

core.definition: The property of a problem or function that can be solved or calculated by a mechanical procedure, such as an algorithm running on a machine.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress shifts to BIL, the fourth syllable, even though the adjective 'computable' is stressed on PYOO. The final -ity is a short 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use computability almost exclusively in mathematics, logic and computer science, especially in the phrase computability theory. In ordinary conversation they would say a problem 'can be solved by computer' or ask whether it is 'computable'. Using the noun outside technical contexts sounds odd.

distinctions.note: Computable describes a single problem or function that can be calculated; computability is the general property, or the field that studies it.
Decidability asks whether a yes-or-no answer can be found by a procedure; computability is the wider concept of producing any output by a procedure.

examples.everyday: My friend in the math department said some puzzles are beyond computability, so no machine could ever solve them.
examples.professional: Before we build the tool, we should check the computability of the model's output, since some targets cannot be calculated in finite time.
examples.analytical: Gödel's and Turing's results show that computability is a real limit on formal systems, not merely a limit of current hardware.

nuance.analogy: Computability is like a map of which destinations a car can reach by road: some places are reachable, and some are not on any road at all.
nuance.etymology: From computable, from compute, from Latin computare, to reckon together, plus the suffix -ability.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on COM, as in KOM-pyoo-tuh-bil-ih-tee; the main stress is on BIL.
Confusing computability with computation: computability is a property of problems, while computation is the act of calculating.

senses.definition: The act or process of computing; calculation; reckoning.
The result of computation; the amount computed.

core.definition: The process of calculating a result, often through a sequence of mathematical or logical steps carried out by a computer.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on TAY, and the 'pyoo' syllable is reduced to 'pyuh'. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, objective word with no emotional charge, though it can sound heavy in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use computation in science, engineering and computing contexts, and it often suggests a multistep process rather than a quick sum. In casual speech people say 'math' or 'the calculation'. In a work meeting, saying 'the computation takes about an hour' is natural, and a common reply is 'Can we speed it up?'

distinctions.note: Calculation is the general word for working out a number, while computation often implies a longer, systematic or automated process.
Computing is the broader field or activity of using computers, while computation is a specific calculation or the act of performing one.

examples.everyday: My phone takes a while to finish the computation when I run that photo filter.
examples.professional: The nightly model refresh is slow because the feature computation runs on a single machine.
examples.analytical: Every physical process can be described as a computation, but whether the universe itself computes is a contested question.

nuance.analogy: Think of computation as a long kitchen recipe that a machine follows step by step, while calculation is one quick mental sum.
nuance.etymology: From Latin computatio, 'a reckoning together', from computare.
common_mistakes: Using computation for a simple everyday sum, where calculation is more natural.
Confusing computation with computing, which refers to the field or activity in general.

computation.etymology: From late Middle English *computacioun*, from Middle French *computation*, from Latin *computatiō*, from *computare* (“sum up, reckon, compute”); see compute.

senses.definition: To convert a manual function or system into a computer system.
To equip with a computer or a computer system.
To enter data into such a system.
senses.example: The county finally decided to computerize its paper land records, entering decades of data into the system.

senses.definition: To become computerlike.

core.definition: To convert a manual task or system so that a computer performs or runs it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PYOO, the second syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced American 'ur' sound. The final -ize is pronounced 'ighz', like 'eyes', not 'eez'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it describes a practical change. It can sound negative when it implies losing a human touch, as in 'computerized customer service' that feels impersonal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word often in offices, schools, banks and government, for example 'We are computerizing our records this year.' It is standard in business and IT. Americans say 'digitize' when converting paper or photos into digital files, which is narrower, while 'computerize' means having a whole process run on computers.

distinctions.note: Digitize means converting analog information such as paper documents or photos into digital form; computerize means making an entire process or system run on computers.
Automate means making a process run with little or no human input; computerize only means moving work onto computers, which may still need people.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's pharmacy finally computerized its prescription records, so refills take much less time now.
examples.professional: We plan to computerize the approval workflow next quarter so managers can track requests in one dashboard.
examples.analytical: To computerize a practice is not merely to store its records electronically; it reorganizes the procedure around rules that can be executed and audited.

nuance.analogy: Like moving a filing cabinet into a spreadsheet that can search, sort and calculate for you.
nuance.etymology: From computer plus the verb-forming suffix -ize, meaning to make into or treat in a certain way.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'com-PYOO-ter-ize' with a full, strong middle vowel instead of a reduced one.
Using it for simple typing, such as 'I computerize my essay'; Americans would say 'I type' or 'I write' in that case.
Confusing it with 'computing', which is the noun for the use of computers.

senses.definition: Of or relating to conception.
Relating to a concept, idea, or thought. (More often, conceptual.)
senses.example: Her conceptional framework for the thesis was clearer than the empirical results.

core.definition: Relating to conception, meaning the beginning of pregnancy or the start of a thing. For ideas, Americans say conceptual.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SEP, and the ti is pronounced sh as in 'shun'. Do not say it like conceptual, which has a 'choo' sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise medical or technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'conceptional' and mostly use 'gestational age' in medical settings. For ideas, use 'conceptual'. 'Conceptional' is most likely to appear in medical or formal writing about the time of conception.

distinctions.note: Conceptional relates to conception, the beginning of a pregnancy or of a thing; conceptual relates to ideas and concepts, and is the word Americans use for ideas.
Conception is the noun for the act of conceiving or the starting moment; conceptional is the adjective that modifies it.

examples.everyday: The nurse said the baby's conceptional age is about six weeks, so we're still early in the pregnancy.
examples.professional: Our neonatal report lists both gestational and conceptional age for each patient, which helps with the timing of care.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers debated the conceptional moment at which the soul enters the body, and their answers shaped later doctrine.

nuance.analogy: Conceptional timing is like the start date on a project plan: it marks when the process began, not what the project is about.
nuance.etymology: From conception, from Latin conceptio, from concipere 'to take in', with the suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using conceptional for ideas, as in 'a conceptional framework'; say 'conceptual framework' instead.
Saying kon-SEP-choo-nul, mixing it up with conceptual; the middle sound is sh.

senses.definition: A piece of music for one or more solo instruments and orchestra.

core.definition: A large musical work for one or more solo instruments accompanied by an orchestra, usually in several movements.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the 'ch' is pronounced like the 'ch' in 'church'. The final syllable is a clear 'toh' with a long o, not 'tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term from classical music and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'violin concerto' or 'piano concerto' and name the composer, as in 'Mozart's piano concerto.' In everyday talk, people may say 'concert' for a live event, which is different from a concerto. The plural is usually 'concertos', though musicians sometimes use the Italian 'concerti'.

distinctions.note: A symphony is an orchestral work without a featured soloist, while a concerto features one or more soloists.
A sonata is usually written for a solo instrument or a small duo, with no orchestra.

examples.everyday: My daughter is playing a violin concerto at her school recital this Thursday.
examples.professional: The orchestra's new season opens with a cello concerto, so we need to confirm the soloist's travel plans.
examples.analytical: In the concerto, the soloist's virtuosity is both set against the orchestra and absorbed into its texture.

nuance.analogy: A concerto is like a conversation between one lead singer and a full choir, where each takes turns leading.
nuance.etymology: From Italian concerto, meaning 'agreement' or 'harmony', from Latin concertare, 'to strive together'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'CON-cer-toh'.
Using 'concerti' in everyday speech; 'concertos' is the common American plural.

senses.definition: To end; to come to an end.
senses.example: The story concluded with a moral.

senses.definition: To bring to an end; to close; to finish.
senses.example: The judge concluded the hearing at noon and sent everyone home.

senses.definition: To bring about as a result; to effect; to make.
senses.example: to conclude a bargain

senses.definition: To come to a conclusion, to a final decision.
senses.example: From the evidence, I conclude that this man was murdered.

senses.definition: To shut off; to restrain; to limit; to estop; to bar.
senses.example: The defendant is concluded by his own plea.

senses.definition: To deduce, to infer (develop a causal relation)
senses.example: From the bank records, the auditor concluded that the funds had been moved deliberately.

core.definition: To end something, or to reach a decision or judgment after considering evidence, facts or discussion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, klood, and the first syllable is very short and reduced to kun. The final d is a clear voiced sound, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds more formal and deliberate than finish or end.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conclude in both speech and writing, though in casual talk they more often say wrap up or finish. In meetings, 'Let's conclude' signals the end of the agenda, and in writing 'I conclude that' is common. A natural reply to 'So what do you conclude?' is a brief summary such as 'I think the data points to a small but real effect.'

distinctions.note: Finish is everyday and general, while conclude suggests an orderly, formal or planned ending.
Decide means choosing an option, while conclude means reaching a judgment after reasoning about evidence.

examples.everyday: The movie concluded with a huge car chase, which I did not love.
examples.professional: Let's conclude the meeting by assigning an owner to each action item.
examples.analytical: From these results we can conclude that the effect is real but small, though the sample is limited.

nuance.analogy: Like closing a file folder after the last page has been signed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concludere, meaning to shut up or enclose, from con- 'together' and claudere 'to close'.
common_mistakes: Using conclude for a physical ending, as in 'the store concluded at nine'; say closed or ended instead.
Using conclude to with a noun or infinitive; use conclude that or conclude from.

conclude.etymology: From Middle English *concluden*, borrowed from Latin *conclūdō* (“to shut up, close, end”).

senses.definition: To puzzle, perplex, baffle, bewilder (somebody).
senses.example: The complicated tax forms completely confused my father, so he called an accountant for help.

senses.definition: To mix up, muddle up (one thing with another); to mistake (one thing for another).
senses.example: Please don't confuse the two cold medicines; their boxes look almost identical on the pharmacy shelf.

senses.definition: To mix thoroughly; to confound; to disorder.
senses.example: The gusty wind confused the papers on my desk and scattered them across the entire office floor.

senses.definition: To make uneasy and ashamed; to embarrass.
senses.example: His teasing remarks about my clumsy dancing at the wedding confused me in front of my whole family.

senses.definition: To rout; discomfit.
senses.example: The cavalry charged the enemy line and confused the troops before they could regroup and form ranks.

senses.definition: To be confused.
senses.example: When the instructions changed halfway through the exam, most students began to confuse and panic.

senses.definition: (of a person) unable to think clearly or understand.
(of a person or animal) disoriented.
senses.example: The elderly patient felt confused after waking from anesthesia in a strange room with unfamiliar faces.

senses.definition: Chaotic, jumbled or muddled.
senses.example: The confused pile of invoices on the desk made it nearly impossible to find last month's payment record.

senses.definition: Making no sense; illogical.
senses.example: Her explanation of the budget was so confused that nobody in the meeting understood a single number.

senses.definition: Embarrassed.
senses.example: He turned red and looked confused when the teacher mentioned his embarrassing mistake in front of everyone.

core.definition: Unable to think clearly or understand something; not sure what is happening, what to think, or what to do.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FYOOZD, and pronounce the final -ed as a /d/ sound because it follows a voiced z sound. Many learners add an extra syllable or say 'kon-FYOOST', which sounds wrong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It describes a state of mind, and saying 'I'm confused' is an everyday, polite way to ask for clarification.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm confused' or 'I'm a little confused' in meetings and conversation to ask for explanation without sounding rude. It is more natural than 'I don't understand' in some settings because it sounds less like blaming the speaker. For a more sympathetic tone, say 'I'm a bit confused about...'.

distinctions.note: 'Confused' describes a person's state of mind, while 'confusing' describes the thing that causes confusion, such as 'a confusing instruction'.
'Puzzled' is milder and suggests a short moment of not understanding, while 'confused' often lasts longer or involves more disorientation.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm a little confused, did you say the meeting is at two or at three?
examples.professional: I'm confused about the ownership of this dashboard, so can we clarify who maintains it before we merge?
examples.analytical: A confused reader may be distinguished from a confident one, because the first lacks the conceptual frame needed to assign meaning to the argument.

nuance.analogy: Being confused is like walking into a dark room with no light: you know something is there, but you cannot see where things are or how to move.
nuance.etymology: From confuse, from Latin confusus, past participle of confundere, 'to pour together, mix up'.
common_mistakes: Using 'confusing' when describing a person, as in 'I am confusing', which means the thing is confusing rather than that you feel confused.
Pronouncing the final -ed as 't', as in 'kon-FYOOST'.
Confusing 'confused' with 'confusing' in written reports.

confused.etymology: Originally from Middle English *confused* (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman *confus* + Middle English *-ed*, from Latin *cōnfūsus*, past participle of *cōnfundō*; now equivalent to *confuse* *ed*.

conversation.text: I'm confused. Are we meeting at six or seven?
The directions were so confusing that we all got confused.
Sorry, you lost me. I'm a little confused.

senses.definition: Viscid, coagulated; jelly-like, unusually thick (of a liquid).
senses.example: The congealed gravy on the stovetop had turned thick and jelly-like overnight.

core.definition: Thickened and stiff, usually after cooling, into a jelly-like or clotted state, as with gravy, fat or blood.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JEELD, which has a long 'ee' vowel. The ending is a final 'd' sound, not a short 't', and learners often shorten the vowel to 'jell-d'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, since it usually describes unappetizing food, but can be neutral when describing blood or physical processes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it most often for food, such as 'congealed gravy' or 'congealed fat on the plate', and for blood in medical or crime-scene descriptions. It is rarely used for pleasant things. In casual speech, people might say 'it's gone cold and thick' or 'it's all gooey'.

distinctions.note: Solidified means turned into a solid, often from a liquid, while congealed suggests thickening into a jelly-like or clotted state.
Coagulated is a technical term, especially for blood, while congealed is more everyday and often used for food.
Thickened is a neutral kitchen word for becoming denser, sometimes on purpose, while congealed implies it has gone cold and stiff.

examples.everyday: Don't eat that gravy; it's been sitting out and it's all congealed.
examples.professional: The lab tech said the sample had congealed during transport, so we need to rerun the test.
examples.analytical: The writer's image of a congealed silence suggests a family that has stopped speaking for years, the feeling hardened into habit.

nuance.analogy: Like gravy setting as it cools, a feeling left alone too long stiffens until it is hard to move.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congelare, 'to freeze together' (con- 'together' + gelare 'to freeze').
common_mistakes: Shortening the vowel to a 'jell' sound instead of using a long 'ee' in kuhn-JEELD.
Using 'congealed' for liquids that are only cold; it suggests a thick, gel-like or clotted texture.

senses.definition: Clipping of congratulations.
senses.example: You were cast in the show? Congrats!

senses.definition: Clipping of congratulations.
senses.example: Accept our congrats for all your hard work!

core.definition: A casual short way to say congratulations when someone has good news or has achieved something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, GRATS, and the first vowel is a reduced uh sound. Do not say KON-grats with a strong o.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It is warm but casual, so it fits friends and coworkers better than formal situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Congrats!' casually to friends, coworkers, or on social media after a promotion, engagement, or new baby. Avoid it in formal letters or with someone you do not know well; use 'Congratulations' instead. A natural reply is 'Thanks!' or 'Thank you, I'm so excited.'

distinctions.note: Congratulations is the full, polite form for any situation. Congrats is casual and friendly.
Well done praises a specific effort or result. Congrats celebrates an event, such as a wedding or a job offer.

examples.everyday: Congrats on the new house! When do you move in?
examples.professional: Congrats on shipping the Q3 release, the whole team worked really hard on it.
examples.analytical: A quick congrats in a department email is ritual, but it still signals warmth and recognition of the work.

nuance.analogy: Like a quick high five in words: warm, short, and casual.
nuance.etymology: Clipping of congratulations, from Latin congratulari, 'to rejoice with'.
common_mistakes: Using congrats in formal writing or to a senior person you do not know well.
Saying kon-GRATS with a long o instead of the reduced uh sound in the first syllable.

conversation.text: Congrats on the new job! When do you start?
I heard you got engaged. Congrats!
"We bought a house!" "Congrats, you guys! That's so exciting."

senses.definition: In a conical manner.
senses.example: conically-shaped

core.definition: In the shape of a cone, tapering evenly from a broad base to a point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAH, with the vowel of 'cot,' not the 'aw' vowel of 'caught.' Keep the final syllable short and light, like 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a shape and is used precisely in description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use conically in conversation. It appears mostly in technical or descriptive writing, such as a manual or a design specification. In everyday speech people say 'shaped like a cone' or 'tapers to a point.'

distinctions.note: Tapering is a general word for narrowing gradually, while conically specifies that the narrowing follows the shape of a cone.
Cylindrically describes a shape with straight, parallel sides, while conically describes a shape that narrows to a point.

examples.everyday: The roof of the old barn rises conically, like a witch's hat.
examples.professional: The nozzle is machined to taper conically, which keeps the spray pattern even.
examples.analytical: A surface that narrows conically from a base to a single apex is determined by one generating line.

nuance.analogy: Something that narrows conically is like a sharpened pencil, wide at one end and tapering evenly to a point.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the adjective conical with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable with the 'aw' vowel of caught, as in 'KAWN-ik-lee,' which is less common in American speech.
Confusing conically with conically's near-homophone conic, which is an adjective.

senses.definition: Either term of a conjunction.
An adjunct that supplements a sentence with information, connecting the sentence with previous parts of the discourse. Not considered to be an essential part of the propositional content.
senses.example: In the sentence, however is a conjunct connecting it to the previous paragraph.

senses.definition: (rare) Either term of a conjunctive conjunction.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Conjoined.
senses.example: Set A is conjunct with set B.

senses.definition: Acting together; collaborative.
senses.example: The two departments took a conjunct approach to the budget, sharing data and decisions.

core.definition: In logic, either of the statements joined by 'and' in a conjunction, such as p and q in 'p ∧ q'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a short 'uh' vowel in the second syllable. As an adjective meaning 'joined together', the stress often moves to the second syllable: kun-JUNKT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in logic and grammar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'conjunct' almost only in logic, philosophy, and computer science. In everyday speech, people say 'part' or 'condition', as in 'both conditions must be met'. You may also see it in linguistics, where it means a sentence adjunct joined to other material.

distinctions.note: 'Conjunction' is the whole combined statement or the connecting word. 'Conjunct' is one of the parts being joined.
A disjunct is joined by 'or' in logic. A conjunct is joined by 'and'.

examples.everyday: If someone says 'I want pizza and I want it cheap,' each half is a conjunct of that wish.
examples.professional: The filter requires both conjuncts to be true, so we should check the age and region conditions separately.
examples.analytical: In 'p and q,' the whole is true only if each conjunct is true, which is why Boolean filters split into independent conditions.

nuance.analogy: It's like a two-key safe: each conjunct is a key, and both must turn before the door opens.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conjunctus, the past participle of conjungere, 'to join together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'conjunct' with 'conjunction', which refers to the operation or the connecting word.
Using 'conjunct' in everyday speech, where 'part' or 'condition' sounds more natural.

conjunct.etymology: From Latin *conjunctus*, the perfect past participle of *conjungō*.

senses.definition: An agreement on some data value that is needed during computation.
senses.example: The distributed nodes must reach consensus on the latest block before committing it.

senses.definition: A process of decision-making that seeks widespread agreement among group members.
senses.example: Our book club makes decisions by consensus, so no single member can overrule the rest.

senses.definition: General agreement among the members of a given group or community, each member of which exercises some discretion in decision-making and follow-up action.
senses.example: reach consensus

senses.definition: Average projected value.
senses.example: a financial consensus forecast

senses.definition: To seek consensus; to hold discussions with the aim of reaching mutual agreement.
senses.example: The team spent an hour trying to consensus on the new API naming conventions.

core.definition: A general agreement among the members of a group, reached after discussion and with the support of most or all of them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN, the second syllable. The first syllable is a reduced kuhn, and the final -sus is a soft uhs, not a long ee or oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fairness, shared understanding, and cooperation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use consensus often in workplace meetings, politics, and news, such as 'we reached a consensus' or 'there is a broad consensus that...' In casual talk people say 'everyone agreed' or 'we're all on the same page.' Avoid saying 'consensus' when only two people agree; it suggests a group decision.

distinctions.note: Agreement can be between two people or a group. Consensus specifically refers to a broad group opinion reached through discussion.
A majority is a larger number of votes for one option. Consensus means most people accept the outcome, even if some still disagree.

examples.everyday: Our neighbors finally reached a consensus about where to put the new playground.
examples.professional: Let's get consensus on the API design before we start writing the tickets.
examples.analytical: Habermas treats consensus not as a given but as the outcome of rational public discourse among free participants.

nuance.analogy: Consensus is like a group of friends agreeing on a restaurant after everyone has said what they want: no one is fully happy, but everyone can live with it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consensus 'agreement, harmony,' from consentire 'to feel together, agree.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'a consensus with him' when one person agrees; in American usage it usually refers to a group, so say 'agreement with him.'
Using 'consensus' as a verb in formal writing; say 'reach consensus' or 'build consensus' instead, although it is used informally.

consensus.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *cōnsēnsus* (“agreement, accordance, unanimity”), from *cōnsentiō* (“feel together; agree”); see *consent*.

conversation.text: We didn't reach a consensus, so we'll vote next week.
The consensus is that we should launch in the fall.
Let's try to build consensus before we present this to leadership.

senses.definition: A hypothesis alleging that the members of a coordinated group are, and/or were, secretly working together to commit illegal or wrongful actions including attempting to hide the existence of the group and its activities.
senses.example: Many of my students believe a conspiracy theory about the moon landing being staged.

senses.definition: Hypothetical speculation that is commonly considered untrue or outlandish.
senses.example: Your claim that aliens run the stock market is pure conspiracy theory, honestly.

core.definition: A belief that a group is secretly working together to do something harmful or illegal, often without good evidence.

pronunciation.tip: Theory is stressed on its first syllable, THEER, and is never 'THEE-or-ee'. In the first word the stress is secondary, so do not over-stress the first syllable, and link the two words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dismissive, especially when used about a belief the speaker considers false. Calling someone a conspiracy theorist is usually an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conspiracy theory for beliefs about hidden plots, such as claims about secret government operations or staged events. It is often used with a skeptical tone. Saying 'that's just a conspiracy theory' ends a discussion, so use it carefully with friends or colleagues. For a real, proven plot, say 'conspiracy' instead.

distinctions.note: A conspiracy is an actual secret agreement; a conspiracy theory is a claim or belief that one exists, which may be true or false.
A hypothesis is a testable proposal in science; a conspiracy theory is usually untestable and resistant to contrary evidence.

examples.everyday: My uncle keeps sending me videos about some wild conspiracy theory on the moon landing.
examples.professional: We can't put that conspiracy theory in the incident report unless we have log evidence to support it.
examples.analytical: A conspiracy theory explains events by positing hidden coordination, and its resistance to disconfirming evidence is often what makes it persuasive to believers.

nuance.analogy: A conspiracy theory is like a detective story in which every clue, even the contradictory ones, is read as proof of the same hidden hand.
nuance.etymology: Conspiracy from Latin conspirare, 'to breathe together'; theory from Greek theoria, 'contemplation, a view'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing theory as 'THEE-or-ee'; the American form is THEER-ee.
Using conspiracy theory for a proven plot; once a plot is proven, it is simply a conspiracy.
Treating conspiracy theorist as neutral; it is usually an insult.

senses.definition: Relating to or causing construction.
senses.example: The crew's constructive phase of the bridge project began in early March after the permits cleared.

senses.definition: Carefully considered and meant to be helpful.
senses.example: Her constructive feedback on my code review helped me fix the bugs quickly.

senses.definition: Serving a useful purpose.
senses.example: Our weekly meetings were constructive, since we finally agreed on the budget for next year.

senses.definition: Deemed after the fact to exist or to have occurred, despite the formal process not having been followed; often when there was no intention to do so at the time.
senses.example: constructive dismissal

senses.definition: Not direct or expressed, but inferred.
senses.example: Because he had visited the property, the court treated him as having constructive knowledge of the lien.

core.definition: Meant to help improve something; useful and positive, as in feedback, criticism, or suggestions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STRUK. The vowel in the first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -tive is 'tiv', not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Calling feedback constructive signals that it is intended to help, not to attack.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'constructive feedback' or 'constructive criticism' in workplaces, schools, and meetings to soften a critique. It is polite and professional. Saying 'That wasn't very constructive' can sound like a sharp complaint that the idea was unhelpful.

distinctions.note: 'Critical' can mean harshly negative, while 'constructive' means negative points offered in order to help.
'Helpful' is general and casual; 'constructive' implies careful thought and an aim to improve a plan or work.

examples.everyday: Your advice about the recipe was constructive, so I'll try a little less salt next time.
examples.professional: Thanks for the constructive comments on the draft; I've revised the section on sampling bias.
examples.analytical: Constructive criticism presupposes a shared goal, without which critique becomes mere opposition.

nuance.analogy: Constructive feedback is like a good map: it points out the road you missed and helps you get there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin constructivus, from construere, 'to build, pile together'.
common_mistakes: Using 'constructive' to mean 'constructed' or 'built'; in a general sense, 'constructive' means helpful.
Confusing it with 'destructive', its opposite.

senses.definition: The surroundings, circumstances, environment, background or settings that determine, specify, or clarify the meaning of an event or other occurrence.
senses.example: —In what context did your attack on him happen? —We had a pretty tense relationship at the time, and when he insulted me I snapped.

senses.definition: The text in which a word or passage appears and which helps ascertain its meaning.
senses.example: Without context, I can't tell if dish refers to a plate, or to the food served thereon.

senses.definition: The surroundings and environment in which an artifact is found and which may provide important clues about the artifact's function and/or cultural meaning.
senses.example: The excavation report stressed that the pottery's context within the buried layer mattered more than its style.

senses.definition: The trama or flesh of a mushroom.
senses.example: The mycologist sliced the cap and examined the context beneath the gills.

senses.definition: For a formula: a finite set of variables, which set contains all the free variables in the given formula.
senses.example: For this formula, the context must include x and y, since both occur free.

senses.definition: The data (register contents, program counter value, etc.) needed to switch to another thread of execution.
senses.example: The scheduler saves each thread's context before switching to another process.

core.definition: The circumstances or background information that help explain the meaning or importance of a word, event or statement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN, with a short 'ah' as in cot. The ending is 'tekst', with a sharp k and t, and no extra vowel before the t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a tool for interpretation, but in arguments it can sound defensive, as in you're taking that out of context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use context constantly in ordinary speech, in phrases like in context, out of context, and when explaining why something matters. Saying you're taking it out of context is a common reply when someone repeats your words unfairly. In business and academic writing, context also means the background of a project, as in give some context for the numbers.

distinctions.note: Background is the history or general situation behind something, while context is the specific surrounding information that changes how a word or event should be understood.
Content is what something contains or says, while context is the setting that tells you how to interpret that content.

examples.everyday: If you read her text without the context, you'd think she was angry, but she was just joking.
examples.professional: Can you give me some context on why the churn rate spiked last quarter before I present it?
examples.analytical: A claim about justice cannot be understood apart from the historical context in which it was made.

nuance.analogy: Context is like the setting of a photo: the same face looks different on a beach than in a hospital.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contextus, a joining together or connection, from contexere, to weave together.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying con-TEXT; the first syllable is the strong one.
Saying in context of without the; the usual phrase is in the context of.

senses.definition: A meeting or gathering.
senses.example: The convention was held in Geneva.

senses.definition: A formal deliberative assembly of mandated delegates.
senses.example: The EU installed an inter-institutional Convention to draft a European constitution.

senses.definition: The convening of a formal meeting.
senses.example: The national convention drew delegates from every state to the arena in Chicago.

senses.definition: A formal agreement, contract, rule, or pact.
senses.example: Under the Geneva convention, prisoners of war must be treated humanely and given medical care.

senses.definition: A practice or procedure widely observed in a group, especially to facilitate social interaction; a custom.
senses.example: Table seatings are generally determined by tacit convention, not binding formal protocol.

senses.definition: A treaty or supplement to such.
senses.example: The Vienna convention at the Vienna Congress (1814-15) standardized most of diplomatic conduct for generations.

core.definition: A large, organized gathering of people with a shared profession or interest, usually lasting a few days.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VEN, and pronounce the final '-tion' as 'shun.' Do not add an extra syllable or stress the first one.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes an event that is usually exciting for people who attend.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'convention' for large trade shows, fan events and professional gatherings, such as a comic convention or a data science convention. In casual talk, people often say 'I'm going to the convention downtown.' The word also means an accepted custom, so context matters. In formal or political settings, 'convention' can mean a national party meeting.

distinctions.note: A conference is usually more focused on talks and academic or professional presentations, while a convention is often bigger and includes exhibits and fan or hobby activities.
Convening is the act of calling people together, while a convention is the gathering itself.

examples.everyday: We went to the comic convention downtown, and the line for the cosplay contest went around the block.
examples.professional: I'm presenting at the data science convention in Boston next month, so I need the slides by Friday.
examples.analytical: Ritual conventions of the assembly, such as the opening prayer and roll call, signal that the gathering is legitimate.

nuance.analogy: A convention is like a giant family reunion for one profession or hobby, where thousands of people gather in one place for a few days.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conventio, 'a coming together, agreement,' from convenire 'to come together.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'convention' with 'convening' or 'conventional' when describing the event.
Using 'convention' for a small meeting, where 'conference' or 'meeting' is more natural.

convention.etymology: Recorded since about 1440, borrowed from Middle French *convention*, from Latin *conventiō* (“meeting, assembling; agreement, convention”), from *conveniō* (“come, gather or meet together, assemble”), from *con-* (“with, together”) + *veniō* (“come”).

senses.definition: A woman who flirts or plays with people's affections.
Any hummingbird in the genus Lophornis.
senses.example: On the reserve's trail, we spotted a tiny coquette hovering over the red flowers.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a feminine style of clothing involving ribbons, frills, and bows.
senses.example: Her grandmother's closet held a coquette blouse covered in ribbons, frills, and tiny bows.

core.definition: A woman who flirts with people, playing with their affections without serious intent.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final t is a crisp, unaspirated stop. Do not say the final syllable as 'ket' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly disapproving. It suggests a woman who uses charm to attract admiration, often without sincerity, and it can sound old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, literature, or commentary about a person's flirtatious behavior. In casual speech they usually say flirt or tease. Calling someone a coquette is a judgment, so it can offend.

distinctions.note: A flirt is the everyday, neutral word for someone playing with attraction; coquette is more literary and carries a sense of calculated, self-centered teasing.
Tease describes playful provoking in general, while coquette specifically describes a woman's cultivated charm for attracting admirers.

examples.everyday: My sister says her new coworker is a bit of a coquette, but I think he is just friendly.
examples.professional: In the meeting notes, the reviewer described the marketing pitch as coquettish, meaning it teased the client without making any real commitment.
examples.analytical: Austen's heroines often resist the coquette's manipulation, since the coquette treats affection as a game rather than a moral commitment.

nuance.analogy: A coquette is like a lamp that draws moths: bright and inviting, but the light is meant to attract attention rather than to warm anyone.
nuance.etymology: From French coquette, the feminine of coquet, meaning flirtatious, from coq, rooster.
common_mistakes: Using coquette as a general adjective for any flirtatious act; the adjective is coquettish.
Confusing the noun with the hummingbird sense, which is rare in everyday American talk.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: Any of many species of marine invertebrates in the class Anthozoa, most of which build hard calcium carbonate skeletons and form colonies, or a colony belonging to one of those species.
senses.example: We snorkeled over a reef where bright coral clung to the rocks below.

senses.definition: A hard substance made of the skeletons of these organisms.
senses.example: The necklace's beads were carved from red coral and strung on silk.

senses.definition: A somewhat yellowish orange-pink color; the color of red coral (Corallium rubrum) of the Mediterranean Sea, commonly used as an ornament or gem.
senses.example: coral:

senses.definition: The ovaries of a cooked lobster; so called from their color.
senses.example: At the seafood restaurant, the lobster's coral was considered the tastiest part.

senses.definition: (historical) A piece of coral, usually fitted with small bells and other appurtenances, used by children as a plaything.
senses.example: Grandmother kept an antique coral with tiny silver bells for her infant.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Made of coral.
senses.example: She admired the coral beads on the antique bracelet.

senses.definition: Having the orange-pink color of coral.
senses.example: She painted the front door a warm coral that matched the sunset.

core.definition: A hard, colorful skeleton formed by tiny sea animals, or the animals that build it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second syllable as a reduced schwa with a light l. Do not pronounce it as two full syllables, 'kor-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It can also suggest beauty, warmth, or tropical settings in everyday use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coral in everyday talk for the color, for ocean reefs, and for jewelry. The color sense is very common in clothing and paint descriptions. In technical biology the animal sense is also used, especially in marine science.

distinctions.note: A coral reef is a structure built by coral colonies; coral alone can refer to the animal, skeleton, or color.
Salmon is a fish color that can look similar; coral is a more pinkish or orange-pink shade often used for paint and fashion.

examples.everyday: We went snorkeling last summer and saw bright fish swimming around the coral.
examples.professional: The design team picked a coral accent color for the app's buttons because it felt warm and friendly.
examples.analytical: Coral is a living organism and a mineral-like structure, which makes it a useful example of how biological processes produce geological features.

nuance.analogy: Coral is like a city built one brick at a time by tiny workers, with each new layer resting on the skeletons of the last.
nuance.etymology: From Latin corallium, from Greek korallion, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with two full syllables, 'kor-al'.
Confusing coral the color with the color of the Mediterranean red coral sense.
Using coral as a verb in everyday English, which is not standard.
nuance.biblical_note: In Job 28:18 coral is mentioned as a precious item that cannot compare with wisdom. The Hebrew word here is ra'moth, usually rendered as coral in translations, and the verse uses it to say that wisdom is worth more than valuable materials.

coral.etymology: From Old French *coral*, from Latin *corallium*, from Ancient Greek *κοράλλιον* (“coral”).

senses.definition: Asking someone to speak up because you can't hear well.

core.definition: A polite request asking someone to talk at a higher volume because you cannot hear them well.

pronunciation.respelling: kood yoo speek uh LIT-uhl LOW-der
pronunciation.tip: Little has its primary stress on the first syllable (LIT-tl), and louder ends in an r-colored schwa (LOW-der). The a in a is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it is a helpful request that people accept without offense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this on the phone, in noisy restaurants, or when someone speaks softly in a meeting. It is courteous, and you can soften it further with 'Sorry, could you speak a little louder?' A typical reply is 'Oh, sure, is this better?'

distinctions.vs: speak a little louder vs. speak up
distinctions.note: Speak up is shorter and more casual; speak a little louder is more polite and specific.
Louder is the standard comparative of loud; more loudly is grammatically possible but less natural.

examples.everyday: The TV is really loud in here. Could you speak a little louder?
examples.professional: Could you speak a little louder? The people on the video call can't hear the back of the room.
examples.analytical: Could you speak a little louder? I want to hear the full reasoning of the argument before I respond.

nuance.analogy: Like turning up the volume on a radio that is playing too softly for the room.
nuance.etymology: Speak comes from Old English specan; louder comes from Old English hlūd, loud, with the comparative suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Speak more louder' with a double comparative.
Pronouncing louder with a clear second syllable (LOW-der) instead of a reduced r-colored ending.

conversation.text: Could you speak a little louder? I'm on a busy street.
"Could you speak a little louder?" "Sure. Is this better?"

senses.definition: Any bird of the family Gruidae, large birds with long legs and a long neck which is extended during flight.
senses.example: A pair of sandhill cranes stood in the shallow marsh, necks stretched toward the sky.

senses.definition: Ardea herodias, the great blue heron.
senses.example: Along the creek, a crane waded patiently through the reeds, hunting small fish.

senses.definition: A mechanical lifting machine or device, often used for lifting heavy loads for industrial or construction purposes.
senses.example: The construction crew used a tower crane to lift steel beams onto the fifth floor.

senses.definition: An iron arm with horizontal motion, attached to the side or back of a fireplace for supporting kettles etc. over the fire.
senses.example: The cook swung the iron crane over the hearth so the stew pot hung above the flames.

senses.definition: A siphon, or bent pipe, for drawing liquors out of a cask.
senses.example: He used a crane to draw the wine out of the barrel without disturbing the sediment.

senses.definition: A forked post or projecting bracket to support spars, etc. generally used in pairs.
senses.example: Two wooden cranes held the long boom above the deck of the old schooner.

senses.definition: To extend (one's neck).
senses.example: The goose cranes its neck to look over the tall grass before it steps out.

senses.definition: To raise or lower with, or as if with, a crane.
senses.example: The crew cranes the heavy generator onto the roof before the storm season starts.

senses.definition: To pull up before a jump.
senses.example: The rider cranes her horse back before the fence, avoiding a dangerous fall.

core.definition: A tall, long-legged bird with a long neck, or a large machine with a long arm used to lift heavy loads at construction sites.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and make the diphthong glide smoothly from 'ay' to 'n'. Be sure to pronounce the r clearly at the start, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The bird sense is descriptive, and the machine sense is practical and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use crane for the construction machine, especially when they see a tower crane over a building site. The bird sense appears in nature writing and in Bible translations. The verb 'to crane your neck' is a common everyday expression meaning to stretch your neck to see something.

distinctions.note: A heron is a long-legged wading bird, often with a short neck pulled into an S-shape in flight; a crane has a longer, straighter neck that extends forward in flight.
A hoist is any device for lifting, often a simple winch; a crane is a larger machine with a movable arm or boom.

examples.everyday: Everyone on the sidewalk was craning their necks to see the parade float.
examples.professional: The site manager said the tower crane will be moved before the steel delivery arrives on Monday.
examples.analytical: In Isaiah the crane is used as an image of mourning, a bird whose cry expresses grief and lament.

nuance.analogy: A construction crane is like a giant arm with a hand at the end, lifting weight that a human arm could never move.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cran, the bird, related to Greek geranos, crane; the machine sense developed later from the bird's long neck and arm-like shape.
common_mistakes: Confusing crane (bird or machine) with crank, which is a handle or a grouchy person.
