senses.example: Victorian dyers prized grenadine for brightening wool, though its crimson faded in sunlight.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A sweet, red syrup, traditionally made from pomegranates, used to flavor and color cocktails and sodas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced 'uh'. The final syllable is often said as 'deen' in casual speech, though 'din' is also common.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, everyday word for a bar or kitchen ingredient with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear grenadine in bars and at restaurants, where it is a standard ingredient in drinks like the Shirley Temple and the Tequila Sunrise. Many commercial grenadines contain little or no pomegranate, so the word now often names a sweet red syrup flavored with fruit or artificial flavoring. If you want a fresh, unsweetened version, ask for pomegranate juice.

distinctions.note: Pomegranate juice is unsweetened fruit juice, while grenadine is a sweetened syrup used in small amounts for flavor and color.
Simple syrup is plain sugar dissolved in water, while grenadine is sweet, red, and fruit-flavored.

examples.everyday: Could you add a splash of grenadine to my Shirley Temple? I like it sweeter.
examples.professional: The bar menu lists a house-made grenadine for the new mocktail program, so we need to order more pomegranate juice.
examples.analytical: The name grenadine comes from the French word for pomegranate, although many commercial versions today contain no fruit at all.

nuance.analogy: Think of grenadine as the sugar-and-color bottle behind the bar, like the red food coloring that makes a cake look festive.
nuance.etymology: From French grenadine, from grenade, meaning pomegranate, from Latin granatum.
common_mistakes: Confusing grenadine (a syrup) with grenade (an explosive weapon), since the two words look and sound similar.
Assuming grenadine is always made from pomegranates when many American bottles are artificially flavored.

grenadine.etymology: Borrowed from French *grenadine*, from Middle French *grenade* (“pomegranate”).

senses.definition: Initialism of graduate student instructor.
Initialism of get(ting) someone in (“home improvements or maintenance performed by a third party, as opposed to DIY/do it yourself”).
senses.example: Our deck repair was a GSI job, so the contractor handled everything while we were away.

core.definition: Graduate student instructor, a graduate student who teaches discussion sections or labs for undergraduate courses under a professor.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters G, S and I with the stress on the final I, which sounds like EYE. Do not say it as a word; it is spelled out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a formal institutional title, but everyday use among students is casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use GSI mainly at universities such as UC Berkeley and the University of Michigan, where it is the official title for a graduate student who teaches sections. Other schools more often use TA or teaching assistant. Students may say I'm a GSI this semester, and a natural reply is 'Oh, which class?'

distinctions.note: TA is the broader and more common title across American universities; GSI is a local or school-specific title used in some institutions.
A professor leads the course and sets its content; a GSI leads sections or labs and usually grades under the professor's direction.

examples.everyday: My roommate is a GSI this semester, so she's stressed about grading the midterms.
examples.professional: Each GSI will run two discussion sections and hold office hours before the exam, according to the course syllabus.
examples.analytical: The GSI model shapes how undergraduate learning is organized, since much of the close reading happens in sections rather than in the lecture hall.

nuance.analogy: A GSI is like a coach on a team: the professor writes the playbook, but the GSI runs the practices where players learn the moves.
nuance.etymology: An initialism from graduate student instructor, using the first letters of the three words.
common_mistakes: Saying the letters as a word, like jeez; say each letter separately.
Using GSI for every teaching assistant abroad; GSI is mostly used at certain American universities, so TA is safer.

senses.definition: A person who spends an unusually large amount of time at a gym.

core.definition: A person who spends an unusually large amount of time at the gym, often as a serious habit or devoted hobby.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GYM, which is the more prominent word, and keep the rat lightly stressed. The 'r' in rat is American rhotic and the vowel is short, like 'rat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'gym rat' affectionately or neutrally about someone who is always at the gym, including athletes who practice constantly. In basketball, 'gym rat' is praise for a player who loves to practice and shoot. It can be mildly teasing when applied to someone who seems obsessed.

distinctions.note: A 'gym rat' is usually focused on training or sport, while a 'gym bunny' is more often focused on appearance.
A 'fitness enthusiast' is a neutral, broad term; 'gym rat' emphasizes the sheer time spent at the gym.

examples.everyday: Ask Dave about the machines; he's a total gym rat and knows everything there.
examples.professional: Our VP is a gym rat, so the team's Friday workouts start at six in the morning.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'gym rat' suggests a compulsive, habit-driven relation to exercise rather than a goal-driven one.

nuance.analogy: A gym rat is like a regular at a coffee shop: always there, knows the staff, and nobody is surprised to see them.
nuance.etymology: 'Gym' comes from gymnasium; 'rat' in the sense of a devoted frequenter, as in 'basketball rat', is informal American slang of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'gym rat' for a person who is simply fit; it refers to the time spent, not the physique.
Pronouncing 'rat' with a long vowel, which makes it sound like 'rate'.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a habit; established as a habit; performed over and over again; recurrent, recurring.
senses.example: Her habitual lying was the reason for my mistrust.

senses.definition: Regular or usual.
senses.example: Professor Franklein took his habitual seat at the conference table.

senses.definition: Of a person or thing: engaging in some behavior as a habit or regularly.
senses.example: He’s a habitual chain-smoker.

senses.definition: Pertaining to an action performed customarily, ordinarily, or usually.
One who does something habitually, such as a serial criminal offender.
A construction representing something done habitually.

core.definition: Done regularly as a habit, or happening again and again; usual or customary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'BIT'. The 'tch' sound is like 'ch' in 'church', and the final syllables are reduced and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'habitual' in writing, speech about behavior, and some professional contexts, but often choose 'usual', 'regular', or 'constant' in casual talk. It can sound slightly formal. Use it neutrally, or add a negative sense only when describing bad habits, such as 'habitual lateness'.

distinctions.note: 'Usual' simply means normal or typical; 'habitual' emphasizes that the action is repeated as a settled habit.
'Chronic' usually describes a long-lasting problem or illness; 'habitual' describes repeated behavior, which can be good or bad.

examples.everyday: My friend is a habitual early bird, so she's always the first one at the coffee shop.
examples.professional: Our reports showed a habitual pattern of late deliveries from one vendor, so we renegotiated the contract.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguished virtue as a habitual disposition that is formed through repeated right action.

nuance.analogy: A habitual action is like a path worn into grass by many steps, so the next walk follows it almost automatically.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin habitualis, from habitus, condition or habit.
common_mistakes: Using 'habitual' for something done only once or occasionally.
Pronouncing the 'tch' as 'ch' in 'chin' with an extra vowel, like 'huh-BIT-chew-al' with too many syllables.

habitual.etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English *habitual* (“of one's inherent disposition”), from Medieval Latin *habituālis* (“customary; habitual”), from Latin *habitus* (“character; disposition; habit; physical or emotional condition; attire, dress”)…

senses.definition: A piece of cloth, usually square and often fine and elegant, carried for wiping the face, eyes, nose or hands.
senses.example: He sneezed into his handkerchief during the meeting.

senses.definition: A piece of cloth shaped like a handkerchief to be worn about the neck; a neckerchief or neckcloth.
senses.example: The cowboy tied a red handkerchief around his neck before riding into the dusty wind.

core.definition: A small square piece of cloth used for wiping the nose, face or eyes, often carried in a pocket.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'HANG', and the 'd' is silent, so do not say 'hand-ker'. The ending 'chif' is pronounced 'chif', not 'chee-eff' or 'chef'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday object, though in a casual context Americans may say 'tissue' instead.
nuance.usage_note: In modern American speech, many people say 'tissue' or 'Kleenex' for disposable paper, but 'handkerchief' is used for cloth ones, especially for formal or traditional settings. A man might carry one in a suit pocket for a wedding or funeral. A natural reply to someone offering one is 'Thanks, I've got it.'

distinctions.note: A 'tissue' is usually disposable paper; a 'handkerchief' is usually reusable cloth.
A 'bandana' is a colorful cloth often worn around the neck or head; a 'handkerchief' is mainly for wiping.
A 'napkin' is used at the table for wiping the mouth and hands; a 'handkerchief' is carried for personal use.

collocations: wipe your eyes with a handkerchief

examples.everyday: Here, take my handkerchief, you're crying a little too much at that movie.
examples.professional: Bring a handkerchief or tissues to the outdoor conference, since the reception will be in the heat.
examples.analytical: The handkerchief in the novel functions as a symbol of inherited class, carrying both intimacy and status.

nuance.analogy: Like a small portable towel for the face, always ready to be pulled from a pocket.
nuance.etymology: From 'hand' plus 'kerchief', from Old French 'couvrechief', meaning a head covering.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'd' as in 'handkerchief' with a hard 'd' sound, when it is silent.
Saying 'hand-ker-chef' with a final 'ef' sound, when the ending is 'chif'.
nuance.biblical_note: The handkerchief appears in the New Testament as a cloth carried from the body of Paul to heal the sick and drive out evil spirits; the Greek is soudarion, meaning a sweat cloth or face cloth, and in John 11:44 (RSV) it refers to the cloth bound over Lazarus's face. Acts 19:12 (RSV) describes handkerchiefs or aprons taken from Paul being used for healing, showing God's power working through an apostle's ordinary items. John 20:7 (RSV) mentions the cloth that had been over Jesus's head, lying apart from the linen clothes, as a detail of the empty tomb. These passages use the word for a cloth related to burial or personal use rather than a modern pocket handkerchief.

senses.definition: To spend time with somebody; to regularly meet with somebody.
senses.example: After the film, do you want to go hang out?

senses.definition: To lodge or reside; to exist.
senses.example: For the whole summer, the interns hung out with a family friend near the lake while they worked downtown.

senses.definition: To crave or desperately want (something).
senses.example: After that long shift, I could hang out with a hot shower and a nap right now.

senses.definition: To endure or delay.
senses.example: We had to hang out with the traffic jam for two hours before we finally reached the airport.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hang,‎ out.
senses.example: When a dog pants, its tongue often hangs out of its mouth.

senses.definition: (dated) To be unyielding; to hold out.
senses.example: The juryman hangs out against an agreement.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To spend time socially with a particular person in a relaxed, informal way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on OUT, and 'with' is weak, so it sounds like 'with' with a short, reduced vowel. Say the phrase smoothly as 'hang-OWT-with'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; the choice of companions can carry a judgment, as in 'Who has she been hanging out with?'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hang out with for friends, family, coworkers, or classmates in relaxed settings. The phrase often appears in questions about companions, and a parent might ask it with concern. The sense 'crave' from some dictionaries is rare, so avoid it.

distinctions.note: Spend time with is neutral and can describe any time together; hang out with is more relaxed and informal.
Hang around with is similar but can sound more negative, suggesting idle or questionable company.

collocations: hang out with the team after work

examples.everyday: I hang out with my cousins every Sunday, and we usually watch the game.
examples.professional: I hang out with the data engineers at lunch, so I hear about pipeline problems early.
examples.analytical: Sociologists study whom people hang out with, since peer networks shape habits and opportunities.

nuance.analogy: Like sharing a booth at a diner, where the conversation matters more than the plan.
nuance.etymology: From hang (Old English hangian), out, and with (Old English wiþ).
common_mistakes: Using hang out with to mean 'crave' or 'desperately want', which is rare and sounds unnatural.
Dropping with and saying 'I hang out my friends'.

conversation.text: I'm hanging out with some friends from work tonight.
Who's your son hanging out with these days?
I love hanging out with my grandkids on Sundays.

inflections: hung out with, hanged out with

senses.definition: A small, light axe with a short handle; a tomahawk.
Belligerence, animosity; harsh criticism.
senses.example: to bury the hatchet

senses.definition: To cut with a hatchet.
senses.example: He hatcheted the dead oak into kindling before the first frost arrived.

core.definition: A small axe with a short handle, held and swung with one hand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HATCH, with a sharp 'ch' like 'catch'. The final syllable is a reduced 'it', not the word 'eat' or 'ate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when literal; negative in 'hatchet job', and positive in 'bury the hatchet' for making peace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hatchet for a small, one-handed tool, often for camping, kindling, or woodworking, while ax is the general word for larger tools. Figuratively, 'bury the hatchet' means to make peace after a quarrel, and a natural way to say it is 'We finally buried the hatchet.' Hatchet also works as a verb meaning to chop with one.

distinctions.note: An ax is a larger tool with a long handle, usually held with two hands for chopping logs; a hatchet is smaller and one-handed.
Tomahawk is a term for a hatchet, mostly used in historical or Native American contexts; in everyday American speech, hatchet is the normal word.
A machete is a long, flat blade for clearing brush; a hatchet is a short, heavy chopping tool.

examples.everyday: Can you hand me the camping hatchet? I want to split some kindling for tonight.
examples.professional: Our crew keeps a hatchet in every truck for quick cuts on the job site.
examples.analytical: Medieval chronicles often mention the hatchet as an ordinary weapon, showing how everyday tools became instruments of violence.

nuance.analogy: A hatchet is the short-handled cousin of an axe: small enough for one hand, quick enough for kindling.
nuance.etymology: From Old French hachette, a diminutive of hache, axe.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'hatchette' with an extra e at the end.
Saying 'hatchet the tree' for a casual chop; the verb is rare, and 'chop' is the everyday word.

hatchet.etymology: From Middle English *hachet*, a borrowing from Old French *hachete*, diminutive of *hache* (“axe”), from Vulgar Latin **happia*, from **happjā*, from Proto-Germanic **hapjǭ*, **habjǭ* (“knife”), from Proto-Indo-European **kop-* (“to strike, to beat”).

senses.definition: Synonym of eat-in.
senses.example: Our coffee shop charges more for have here seating, but takeout is cheaper.

core.definition: Eaten on the premises instead of taken out; the standard American phrase is 'for here.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'here,' which is a long 'ee' followed by a clear American r. The 'h' in 'have' is light, and the vowel in 'have' is the short 'a' of 'cat.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a casual, functional phrase used only in ordering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say 'have here.' At a restaurant or coffee shop, the staff normally ask 'For here or to go?' and the customer answers 'For here' or 'To go.' Some people say 'eat in' or 'dine in' instead. 'Have here' is therefore best understood as a non-standard form that you should recognize but usually replace with 'for here.'

distinctions.note: 'For here' is the standard American phrase used in ordering at counters and drive-throughs.
'Eat in' is a verb phrase and is common when describing where you plan to eat, while 'for here' is the set phrase used by staff.
'Dine in' sounds more formal and suggests a sit-down meal rather than a quick counter order.

examples.everyday: At the counter, the cashier asks, 'For here or to go?' and I say, 'For here, please.'
examples.professional: Can you note on the ticket that the two sandwiches are for here, not to go?
examples.analytical: The difference between for here and to go marks how a restaurant organizes its space, its labor and its packaging.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note on a food order that tells the kitchen where the meal will be eaten.
nuance.etymology: Have from Old English habban (to hold, possess); here from Old English her.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Have here?' at a counter, when the standard question is 'For here or to go?'
Writing 'eat-in' as a noun or adjective in everyday ordering, when 'eat in' as a verb phrase is more natural.

senses.definition: Risky; dangerous; with the nature of a hazard.
(rare) Of or involving chance.
senses.example: Hazardous games such as dice depend on chance rather than skill.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Dangerous or risky, especially because something could cause harm, injury, or illness if not handled carefully.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'er' sound (/ɚ/), and the ending is a quiet 'us' (/əs/), not 'dis'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it signals a real danger that needs caution, often in warnings, safety rules, or reports. It is stronger and more official than 'risky'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hazardous' mostly on signs, in safety regulations, and in news reports about chemicals, weather, or roads, as in 'hazardous materials' or 'hazardous driving conditions'. In casual talk people usually say 'dangerous' or 'unsafe' instead. A natural reply to a warning is simply 'Good to know, thanks.'

distinctions.note: 'Dangerous' describes something that can hurt people in general; 'hazardous' often points to a specific source of risk, such as a substance or condition.
'Risky' is more casual and often describes a choice a person takes on, like a risky investment, while 'hazardous' describes a situation or material.

examples.everyday: Don't walk on that ice; the sidewalk is hazardous this morning.
examples.professional: We need to label these solvents as hazardous before they go to the warehouse.
examples.analytical: Whether a technology is hazardous depends not only on its failure rate but on who bears the consequences of that failure.

nuance.analogy: A hazardous situation is like a loose wire in a wall: the danger is built into the thing itself.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman hasard, a game of dice, through the idea of chance and risk.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable or pronouncing the ending as 'dis' instead of 'dus'.
Using 'hazardous' for a person ('a hazardous man') instead of a situation or substance.

core.definition: A place in the wilderness where Israel camped during the Exodus journey, and where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'th' is voiceless, as in 'math'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a biblical place name used in religious study and teaching.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name mainly in Bible study, sermons, and academic discussion of the Pentateuch. It is rarely used in everyday conversation. Readers often find it in maps of the Sinai wilderness.

distinctions.note: Hazeroth is a camp in the desert of the Exodus, while Hazor is a major Canaanite city in northern Israel.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group is reading about Israel's stop at Hazeroth in Numbers this week.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Hazeroth marks the point where the complaints against Moses begin to escalate.
examples.analytical: The Numbers account places the Miriam and Aaron episode at Hazeroth, linking leadership dispute with the theme of divine judgment.

nuance.analogy: Hazeroth is like a rest stop on a long road trip where something important happened, which you remember by the place name.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Hazeroth, meaning enclosures or settlements.
common_mistakes: Confusing Hazeroth with Hazor, which is a different place in a different part of the Bible.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Hazeroth is a camp of Israel during the wilderness wanderings, named in Hebrew as Hazeroth, meaning enclosures or settlements. Numbers 11:35 says the people set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth. Numbers 12:1-16 describes Miriam and Aaron speaking against Moses, and Miriam being struck with leprosy and shut out of the camp for seven days; the people set out again only after she was brought back. Deuteronomy 1:1 lists Hazeroth among places in the wilderness east of the Jordan.

senses.definition: The person in charge of an organization, clan, tribe, or other group.
senses.example: The village head man met the surveyors at the gate and asked why they had come.

senses.definition: The leader of a village.

core.definition: The leader or chief who is in charge of a village, tribe, or local community.

pronunciation.tip: The word is usually written as one word, 'headman', with the stress on HEAD and a reduced final syllable 'muhn'. Do not give 'man' a full vowel as in 'man' or 'mane'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a descriptive term used in history, anthropology, or travel writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in discussions of village or tribal leadership, often in anthropology, colonial history, or travel writing about Africa, South Asia, or the Pacific. In everyday talk, Americans would say 'village chief' or 'village leader'. As two words, 'head man' can sound like a boss in a workplace, so the one-word form is safer.

distinctions.note: 'Chief' is a broader term for a leader of a tribe or group, while 'headman' usually means a lower-level village leader.
A foreman is a workplace supervisor, while a headman leads a village or local community.

examples.everyday: Our guide told us we had to meet the village headman before we set up camp.
examples.professional: The consultant's report described the local headman as the main link between the company and the community.
examples.analytical: Colonial administrators often relied on a headman whose authority was partly invented by the system that appointed him.

nuance.analogy: Like an unofficial mayor of a small town who is trusted by the people but has no formal government powers.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'head' and 'man', meaning the chief man of a community.
common_mistakes: Writing 'head man' as two words when the standard form is 'headman'.
Using 'headman' for a workplace boss, which sounds odd in American English.

head-man.etymology: From Middle English *heed man*, from Old English *hēafodmann* (“leader; captain, head of a group”), from **haubidamann*, equivalent to *head* + *man*.

senses.definition: Emotional distress or pain, often caused by a loved one or their absence.

core.definition: Deep emotional pain, often caused by a loss, a broken relationship or missing someone you love.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HEART. 'Ache' rhymes with 'make', not 'each' or 'ak'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes sadness and loss, though songs and stories often use it intensely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heartache for emotional pain, especially after a breakup, a death or a family conflict. It is not used for physical pain, where people say headache or chest pain. For minor disappointments, 'bummer' or 'that's too bad' is more natural. A natural reply is 'I'm sorry, that sounds really hard.'

distinctions.note: Heartbreak often describes a sharp, sudden grief, while heartache is a longer lasting emotional ache.
Sadness is a general feeling, while heartache specifically refers to pain connected to love or loss.
Headache is physical pain in the head; heartache is emotional, so the two are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: After the divorce she carried a lot of heartache, but she's doing much better now.
examples.professional: Our team has been through a lot of heartache since the layoffs, so let's check in on each other this week.
examples.analytical: The novel traces how inherited heartache shapes three generations of a Southern family without offering easy resolution.

nuance.analogy: Like a bruise on the inside: you cannot point to the exact spot, but you feel it whenever you touch the memory.
nuance.etymology: From heart (Old English heorte) plus ache (Old English æce).
common_mistakes: Using heartache for minor disappointments; a missed bus or a bad meal is not heartache.
Confusing it with headache when describing emotional pain, which is a common slip for learners.

heartache.etymology: From Middle English *heorteece*, *heorte-ece*, from Old English *heorteċe*, equivalent to *heart* + *ache*.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or operating throughout a hemisphere.
senses.example: Officials announced a hemispheric effort to track the spread of avian flu across the Western Hemisphere.

senses.definition: (uncommon) Having the shape of half a sphere.
senses.example: The hemispheric dome of the observatory opens to reveal the night sky.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: Of or affecting a whole hemisphere of the Earth, or one half of the brain.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -SPHER-, with a light secondary stress on HEM. The final '-ic' is short and unstressed: 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hemispheric in political and climate discussions, such as 'hemispheric cooperation' or 'hemispheric trade'. In neuroscience it describes the brain's halves, for example 'hemispheric lateralization'. In casual speech people more often say 'across the whole hemisphere' or use 'regional'.

distinctions.note: Hemispheric relates to a hemisphere as a region or half of the Earth or brain; hemispherical describes the shape of half a sphere.
Regional covers any area; hemispheric is specifically about a half of the globe, so it covers a much larger zone.

examples.everyday: The wildfire smoke affected air quality across the whole hemispheric region, not just our city.
examples.professional: We need a hemispheric view of the data, so we'll combine the Northern and Southern sensor networks.
examples.analytical: Scholars argue that hemispheric integration requires shared institutions as well as shared economic interests.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather map that covers half the globe, a hemispheric problem spreads far beyond one town.
nuance.etymology: From hemisphere, from Greek hemisphairion, meaning half of a sphere.
common_mistakes: Using 'hemispheric' for the shape of a dome; use 'hemispherical' for shape.
Stressing the first syllable (HEM-uh-sfer-ik) instead of the -SPHER- syllable.

senses.definition: A female hero.
A female lead character.
(rare) Characteristic of a heroine; heroic.
senses.example: Her heroine response to the flood earned her a county medal.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A woman admired for her courage or achievements, or the female main character of a story, book, film or play.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel sounds like 'air'. The word is a homophone of 'heroin', so context matters and the spelling differs only at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing a brave or admirable woman. As a story term, it is neutral. Some Americans now prefer 'hero' for women to avoid gender labels, but 'heroine' is still standard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'heroine' for the female lead of a novel or movie, and for a woman who does something brave, such as a local heroine who saved people from a flood. Many people now call a brave woman a 'hero' instead, so both forms are acceptable. The word 'protagonist' is the gender-neutral term for a main character.

distinctions.note: Protagonist is gender-neutral and means the main character of a story, whereas heroine implies a woman who is also admirable or brave.
Heroin is an illegal opioid drug, and the two words sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.

examples.everyday: My sister's a local heroine since she pulled that kid out of the pool last summer.
examples.professional: In the leadership seminar, the speaker told the story of a nurse who became the heroine of our hospital's crisis response.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the classic heroine of nineteenth-century fiction is often defined by her suffering, which limits her agency as a moral figure.

nuance.analogy: A heroine is like the lead singer in a band: she is the person the whole story is built around.
nuance.etymology: From Latin heroina, from Greek hērōinē, the feminine form of hērōs, 'hero'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'HER-oh-een' or 'hih-ROH-in' instead of HAIR-oh-in.
Confusing it with 'heroin', the drug, in writing or speech.

heroine.etymology: From Latin *hērōīna*, from late Ancient Greek *ἡρωΐνη* (2nd century), a feminine equivalent of *ἥρως* (“hero, demigod”), equivalent to *hero* + *ine*.

senses.definition: Something possessing a value or beauty that is not immediately apparent, and which therefore has received far less recognition than it deserves.
senses.example: This tiny taqueria downtown is a hidden gem that locals rarely mention online.

core.definition: A place, product, or person of great value that few people know about yet and that deserves more recognition.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on gem, and hidden is quick and reduced to HID-n. Do not put equal stress on both words or say the word hidden with a full second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a discovery, though it is sometimes overused in marketing and reviews.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hidden gem for restaurants, bars, shops, trails, and albums, especially in conversations about travel or food. It is informal, and it can sound cliched when used for something famous. A natural reply is 'Oh, I'll have to check it out.'

distinctions.note: Undiscovered means nobody has found it yet, while a hidden gem is known to some people but not widely.
A hole in the wall is a small, plain place, and it may or may not be a hidden gem depending on its quality.

collocations: a hidden gem in the neighborhood

examples.everyday: That little Thai place off Fifth Street is a hidden gem, so get the curry.
examples.professional: The analytics tool is a hidden gem, and few of our teams know it exists, but it cut our reporting time in half.
examples.analytical: The paper's central finding is a hidden gem: a simple estimator that outperforms more complex models under the stated assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone on a riverbed that looks ordinary until the water is clear and the light hits it.
nuance.etymology: Gem comes from Latin gemma, 'bud, jewel'; hidden comes from Old English hydan, 'to hide'.
common_mistakes: Using hidden gem for something famous and widely known, which contradicts the meaning.
Stressing both words equally, so the phrase sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Intellectually stimulating, highly cultured, sophisticated.
senses.example: highbrow entertainment

senses.definition: A cultured or learned person or thing.
senses.example: Critics called him a highbrow, but he simply loved opera and rare first editions.

core.definition: Intellectual, cultured, and serious in taste, often in a way that suggests a more refined or elite audience than mass culture.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HY, and brow rhymes with 'cow', not 'row'. Make the final vowel a clear 'ow' diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use highbrow for art, books, films, and music that aim at intellectual or cultural sophistication, often with a slight teasing tone. Calling someone a highbrow can sound a bit snobbish if said with contempt. Its opposite, lowbrow, is also common and sometimes affectionate.

distinctions.note: Intellectual describes a person or mind that thinks deeply; highbrow describes taste in culture and often carries a slight suggestion of pretension.
Sophisticated means worldly and refined in manners or taste; highbrow focuses on serious, learned, artistic culture.

examples.everyday: My sister loves highbrow documentaries, but I usually just want a funny show after work.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants the campaign to feel highbrow, so we should pick a more serious tone and fewer jokes.
examples.analytical: The distinction between highbrow and popular culture has been criticized as a class marker that treats taste as a measure of worth.

nuance.analogy: A highbrow taste is like a set menu at a formal restaurant: refined, carefully prepared, and not for everyone.
nuance.etymology: From high + brow, with brow used figuratively for forehead and intellect, dating to the early 20th century in American English.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing brow as 'brow' to rhyme with 'row' instead of 'cow'.
Using highbrow as a noun for a person without the 'person' context; the noun is usually used as 'a highbrow' meaning a cultured person.

highbrow.etymology: A compound of the words *high* + *brow*, first recorded usage in 1875.

senses.definition: The land immediately next to, and inland from, a coast.
The rural territory surrounding an urban area, especially a port.
senses.example: Farms in the hinterland supply fresh produce to the port city every morning.

senses.definition: A remote or undeveloped area.
senses.example: Few roads reached the hinterland, so the survey team traveled mostly by mule.

senses.definition: That which is unknown or unexplored about someone.
senses.example: Her quiet manner hid an emotional hinterland that few friends had ever explored.

senses.definition: An area of land far from the sea.
Anything vague or ill-defined, especially something that is ill understood.
senses.example: Much of the theory remains a hinterland of half-formed ideas and speculation.

core.definition: The rural land lying behind and inland from a coast, port or city, often seen as supporting it economically.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HIN, and the middle syllable is a weak, rhotic 'er' sound, not 'ee' or 'ah'. Many learners stress the second syllable or turn the middle vowel into a full 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing geography or economics; it can carry a faintly distant or undeveloped sense when used for remote areas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hinterland mostly in news, business and geography contexts, for example the hinterland of a port city. In casual speech people more often say 'out in the sticks' or 'way out in the country'. It is a little literary, so use it in writing or formal talk rather than as everyday small talk.

distinctions.note: A suburb is a residential area on the edge of a city; a hinterland is broader, more rural, and defined by its relationship to a city or port.
A frontier is the edge of settled territory, often used for the moving boundary of development; hinterland describes the surrounding land itself, not a boundary.

examples.everyday: We drove out to the hinterland last weekend to see the farms and the old barns.
examples.professional: Our logistics model depends on the trucking routes that serve the hinterland of each port.
examples.analytical: The city's wealth rested on its hinterland, whose farms and forests supplied the port with goods for export.

nuance.analogy: Think of a city as a stage and its hinterland as the backstage that supplies everything the performance needs.
nuance.etymology: From German Hinterland, from hinter ('behind') and Land ('land').
common_mistakes: Saying 'hinterlands' for a single area; the singular 'hinterland' is normal.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a clear 'ah' instead of a light rhotic 'er'.

hinterland.etymology: Borrowed from German *Hinterland*, from *hinter* + *Land*, cognate to + *land*.

senses.definition: That produces or is accompanied with a hiss.
senses.example: The hissing radiator kept us awake half the night in the old apartment.

senses.definition: The sound of a hiss.
senses.example: A sharp hissing came from the pressure cooker when I opened the lid.

core.definition: Making a sharp, sustained 's' sound, like steam, a snake or a crowd showing disapproval.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ing ending is a soft nasal 'ng', so say it as in 'sing', not as 'in' followed by a separate 'g'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing steam, kettles or snakes; negative when describing a crowd or speech showing disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hissing for sounds like a kettle, a radiator, a leaking tire or a cat's warning. It also describes a crowd booing or a whispered angry remark, as in 'hissing at someone.' It is an everyday word, so you can use it freely.

distinctions.note: Whistling is a clear tone made by air through the lips or a device; hissing is a noisy 'sss' sound without a clear pitch.
Booing uses a vocal sound of disapproval, while hissing is a sharp 's' sound; both express displeasure in a crowd.

examples.everyday: The kettle is hissing, so can you turn off the burner?
examples.professional: The compressor was hissing when we tested the line, which points to a pressure leak.
examples.analytical: The essay describes the hissing crowd as a single collective voice that turns the speaker's authority into shame.

nuance.analogy: A hissing sound is like a leaking tire: steady, continuous and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of the sound; the verb hiss comes from Middle English hissen.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'hissin' in writing.
Using it for a clear whistling tone rather than a noisy 'sss' sound.

senses.definition: A writer of history.
One who studies or researches history.
senses.example: The local historian spent years digging through county records for the mill's history.

senses.definition: One who recounts their own medical history.
senses.example: At the clinic, she's a real historian about her own surgeries and allergies.

core.definition: A scholar who studies and writes about the past, using documents, records, and other evidence.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STOR, and the final -ian is a weak, unstressed syllable that sounds like 'un'. Don't stress HIS or give the last syllable a full 'ahn' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is a respected professional title that describes what someone does, not how they feel about the past.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use historian for anyone who researches and writes about the past, from university professors to public-history writers and museum staff. In casual talk, an enthusiast is a history buff, not a historian. Someone who teaches history in school is usually called a history teacher.

distinctions.note: A history buff is a casual enthusiast with no training, while a historian is usually a trained professional who researches and publishes.
A historiographer studies how history has been written, while a historian researches and writes history itself.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a retired historian, and she knows every story about our town.
examples.professional: Our project needs an economic historian to review the archival records from the 1930s.
examples.analytical: A careful historian must weigh the testimony of contemporary witnesses against claims made in later memoirs.

nuance.analogy: A historian is like a detective for the past, piecing together clues from documents because nobody alive saw the crime.
nuance.etymology: From Latin historia, from Greek historia, meaning inquiry or knowledge gained by investigation.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as HIS-tor-ee-an; the stress belongs on STOR.
Assuming a historian must be a teacher; many historians research and write without teaching in a school.

historian.etymology: From Middle English *historian*, *historien*, from Old French *historien*, from Latin *historia* (“story, history”), equivalent to *history* + *-ian*.

senses.definition: A methodological approach to the study of society, economics, and history, looking for the causes of developments and changes in human society in the means by which humans collectively produce the necessities of life.
senses.example: Marx's historical materialism explains social change through the evolution of the means of production.

core.definition: Marx and Engels' theory that economic conditions and methods of production shape society, politics, and history.

pronunciation.tip: Stress STOR in the first word and TIHR in materialism, with the -ial ending reduced to 'ee-uh'. Don't say it as 'ma-TAY-ree-al', which shifts the vowel and stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic writing, but politically charged in everyday talk, since listeners may hear it as a Marxist claim and argue about it.
nuance.usage_note: In American universities, historical materialism is a standard term in history, sociology, and political economy, especially in courses on Marx. In conversation, Americans often say Marxist approach to history, which is clearer to most listeners and less likely to start a debate. In academic writing, use the full term and define it at first mention.

distinctions.note: Dialectical materialism is the broader Marxist philosophy of nature and change, while historical materialism applies it specifically to human society and history.
In everyday American talk, materialism often means greed or love of possessions; historical materialism is a theory about economic causes of social change.

collocations: an account based on historical materialism

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law loves talking about historical materialism at dinner, and everyone rolls their eyes.
examples.professional: Our policy team uses a historical materialist framework to explain why labor strikes cluster during economic downturns.
examples.analytical: Historical materialism holds that changes in the means of production, rather than ideas alone, drive the major transformations of society.

nuance.analogy: Historical materialism is like tracing a river's course back to the shape of the land: the economy is the terrain that determines where the water flows.
nuance.etymology: From historical and materialism; the theory was developed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the mid-1800s.
common_mistakes: Using materialism in its everyday sense of loving possessions when discussing this theory.
Reducing the final syllables to 'muh-TEER-ee-ul-iz-um' instead of the clear 'uh-liz-uhm' ending.

senses.definition: Up to this place.
senses.example: Hitherto, the team had relied on paper forms, but now they would use the new app.

senses.definition: In speech or writing: up to this point; thus far.
Synonym of hereto (“regarding this subject; to achieve this result; to this end”).
senses.example: The council adopted the ordinance, and all departments were directed hitherto to follow its terms.

senses.definition: Up to this or that time.

core.definition: Until now; up to this point in time. It is common in formal writing and speech.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HITH, and give a lighter secondary stress to the final 'too'. The middle syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, so do not pronounce three full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal. It sounds precise and somewhat elevated, and it works best in writing or prepared speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hitherto' in formal writing, reports, academic papers, legal documents, and speeches, usually to say something was true until a new point in time. In casual conversation, people say 'until now' or 'so far' instead. Using 'hitherto' in relaxed talk can sound stiff or showy.

distinctions.note: Until now is the plain, everyday equivalent that works in both speech and writing.
So far is conversational and often suggests that things may still change, while hitherto sounds more formal and historical.
Previously means before some point, not necessarily up to the present, so it does not carry the same sense of continuing until now.

examples.everyday: At the wedding toast, my uncle said, 'Hitherto we have known him as a quiet friend, but today we welcome him as family.'
examples.professional: Hitherto, the team has relied on manual reviews, but starting next sprint we will automate those checks.
examples.analytical: Hitherto, theologians have treated grace as a single category, but the new reading distinguishes its prevenient and sanctifying aspects.

nuance.analogy: Like a bookmark that shows how far you have read so far, without telling you what comes next.
nuance.etymology: From 'hither' plus 'to', meaning up to this place, later applied to time.
common_mistakes: Using 'hitherto' in casual speech where 'until now' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'hither', which refers to place, not time.

hitherto.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *hiderto* (“to the present time, until now; up to this point”), from *hider* (“in this direction, to or toward this place; up to the present time, until now”) (from Old English *hider* (“to here, hither”)) + *to* (“in the…

senses.definition: A person who is interested in an activity or a subject as a hobby.
senses.example: This computer magazine is targeted at both professionals and hobbyists.

senses.definition: A client in a girlfriend experience.

core.definition: A person who pursues an activity or subject for pleasure in their free time rather than for pay.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HOB. The middle syllable is a reduced 'bee,' and the ending -ist sounds like 'ist,' not 'eest.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it shows enthusiasm and skill developed outside of paid work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hobbyist to describe someone who builds model trains, does ham radio, woodworking, or photography for fun. It is respectful and everyday, and it often appears in clubs, magazines, and online forums. Saying 'he's a hobbyist' implies he is skilled but not professional. It can sound slightly dismissive if the person's work is actually excellent.

distinctions.note: Amateur focuses on lacking payment or professional status, and it can imply lower skill; hobbyist focuses on the activity being a personal pastime.
Enthusiast emphasizes passion and excitement, while hobbyist emphasizes that the activity is a regular pastime.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a hobbyist who restores old motorcycles in his garage on weekends.
examples.professional: Our hobbyist community of Raspberry Pi builders gave us useful feedback on the prototype.
examples.analytical: The distinction between hobbyist and professional mathematicians has become blurry as open problems are attacked by motivated outsiders.

nuance.analogy: Like a cook who makes amazing dinners for friends every Sunday but never opens a restaurant.
nuance.etymology: From hobby (noun, originally a small horse) plus the suffix -ist, meaning one who practices an activity.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable and saying 'hob-BY-ist.'
Using hobbyist to mean a professional who earns money from the activity.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being holy.

core.definition: The quality of being holy: set apart for God, morally pure, and sacred; also a title for certain religious leaders, as in 'His Holiness.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a long 'oh' as in 'go'. The ending '-ness' is weak, pronounced 'nus', and the 'l' is clear before 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent, implying purity and awe. It can sound pious or stiff in casual talk, and 'holier-than-thou' is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use holiness mostly in religious settings: sermons, hymns, and Bible study. 'His Holiness' is the form of address for the Pope and the Dalai Lama. 'Holiness' also names a Protestant movement (the Holiness movement) stressing sanctification.

distinctions.note: Sanctity is more formal and often means the inviolable or sacred character of something, like the sanctity of life.
Righteousness emphasizes right conduct and standing before God, while holiness emphasizes being set apart and pure.
Piety is human devotion to God, while holiness is a quality, primarily of God and secondarily of persons or things dedicated to him.

examples.everyday: Our pastor spoke this morning about what it means to live a life of holiness at work.
examples.professional: In today's lecture I'll examine how the Old Testament links holiness to both ritual purity and ethics.
examples.analytical: Otto's idea of the numinous argues that holiness is not merely moral goodness but an encounter with the wholly other.

nuance.analogy: Holiness is like a room set aside for one purpose only: not merely clean, but dedicated.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hālignes, from hālig 'holy', related to 'whole' and 'hale'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'holyness' instead of 'holiness'.
Mispronouncing it as 'HAW-lee-ness' or stressing the middle syllable.
Using it for ordinary cleanliness; it is a religious or moral term.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew qodesh (holiness, set-apartness) and Greek hagiosyne or hagiasmos describe God's unique otherness and the consecration of his people. Leviticus 19:2 commands Israel to be holy because the Lord is holy. Isaiah 6:3 shows the seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy.' Hebrews 12:14 urges pursuing holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.

traditions.view: Holiness is participation in God's own life, theosis, through the sacraments and ascetic struggle. The saints show it, though God alone is holy by nature.
Holiness is the fullness of charity, received through sanctifying grace and the sacraments. The Second Vatican Council taught a universal call to holiness for all the baptized.

Most Protestants hold that believers are declared holy in Christ and grow in sanctification by the Spirit. Wesleyan and Holiness traditions stress entire sanctification, while Reformed groups stress progressive growth that is never perfect in this life.

holiness.etymology: From Middle English *holynesse*, *holinesse*, *halinesse*, from Old English *hāliġnes* (“holiness, a holy thing, rites”), from **hailagnassī*, equivalent to *holy* + *-ness*.

senses.definition: A state or condition or being honorable.

core.definition: The quality of being honorable; a reputation for good character, integrity and trustworthiness.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -BIL-, so say ahn-er-uh-BIL-ih-tee. Do not stress the -ar- or the final -ty syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a serious, respected quality of character and is usually used in formal or evaluative contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use honorability mostly in formal writing, legal or institutional contexts, and discussions of character. In everyday speech they would more often say that someone is honorable or has integrity. Use it for a quality or reputation rather than for a title.

distinctions.note: Honesty refers specifically to telling the truth, while honorability is a broader reputation for integrity and noble conduct.
Integrity is a consistent commitment to moral principles, while honorability is the respected reputation that results from such conduct.

examples.everyday: Nobody doubts her honorability, even after that awkward scandal at work.
examples.professional: The board reviewed the candidate's honorability and reputation before approving the appointment.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats honorability as a settled state of character, not as a single noble act performed under pressure.

nuance.analogy: Honorability is like a bank's reputation: built slowly through many trustworthy transactions and lost in a single betrayal.
nuance.etymology: From honorable plus -ity; honorable comes from Latin honorabilis, meaning worthy of honor.
common_mistakes: Using honorability for a person; say an honorable person instead.
Confusing honorability with the formal title The Honorable, which is used for judges and some officials.

senses.definition: The back of a horse.
senses.example: They came on horseback across the plains.

senses.definition: A ridge of sand, gravel, and boulders.
senses.example: The hikers followed the horseback across the frozen lake toward the glacial valley.

senses.definition: On the back of a horse.

core.definition: On the back of a horse; while riding a horse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on the second. The r is clearly pronounced, and the final 'back' has the short 'a' of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a way of traveling or riding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use on horseback in everyday talk about riding, trail tours, ranch life or historical travel. It is the normal phrase, and you would not say on the horse's back in ordinary speech. It is also used for horseback riding as an activity.

distinctions.note: On horseback describes the position of riding, while horseback riding is the activity itself.

examples.everyday: We spent the afternoon exploring the canyon on horseback, and my legs were sore for days.
examples.professional: The national park offers a half-day guided tour on horseback for groups of up to eight people.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the early settlers' mobility on horseback shaped how they understood distance and territory.

nuance.analogy: Horseback is like riding in a car but with a living animal beneath you, so the travel feels slower and more personal.
nuance.etymology: From horse and back.
common_mistakes: Saying on a horseback instead of on horseback, since the phrase has no article.
Using horseback as a noun in the sense of a horse's back when on horseback is the usual phrase.

senses.definition: (archaic) The act of exhorting, inciting, or giving advice; exhortation.
senses.example: His hortation to the troops rallied them before the dawn assault on the fortress.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Earnest encouragement or urging to do something good, usually given in a speech or writing; an exhortation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the 'tay' syllable, and the ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'. Many learners put the stress on the first syllable, so keep it on the middle.

nuance.connotation: Positive and earnest, but it can sound preachy or old-fashioned if the speaker lectures too much.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'hortation' today; it appears mostly in religious, literary, or historical writing. In ordinary speech Americans say 'a pep talk,' 'a call to action,' or 'an exhortation.' If you hear it, it usually signals a formal sermon, a letter, or a stirring toast.

distinctions.note: Exhortation is the standard modern word for the same thing and is much more common in American English.
An admonition is a warning or reproof, usually firmer and more negative than encouragement.

examples.everyday: At my cousin's wedding, Uncle Ray gave a hortation to the couple to keep laughing together through every hard year.
examples.professional: In her closing remarks at the all-hands meeting, the director gave a hortation to the team to finish the migration before the holiday freeze.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters combine doctrinal argument with hortation, urging believers to live out in conduct what they have received in faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach's halftime speech: it aims to renew effort and courage rather than to give new information.
nuance.etymology: From Latin hortatio, from hortari, 'to urge or encourage'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'hortation' with 'horticulture' because the words look alike.
Using it in everyday conversation, where 'pep talk' or 'exhortation' sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, the Greek word paraklesis, meaning exhortation, encouragement, or comfort, is the idea behind hortation. Romans 12:8 describes the gift of exhortation as a service given to build up the church. Acts 13:15 shows synagogue leaders inviting visitors to offer a word of exhortation to the people, and Hebrews 13:22 calls the letter itself a word of exhortation.

hortation.etymology: From Latin *hortatio*, from *hortari* (“to incite, exhort”), from *hori* (“to urge”).

senses.definition: Becoming very vocal or even violent when angered or frustrated.
senses.example: The hot-tempered coach threw his clipboard after the referee's bad call.

core.definition: Quick to become angry, loud, or aggressive when provoked or frustrated.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on tem, in the second part of the compound, with a lighter stress on hot. The final syllable is a reduced ər sound, so it sounds like erd, not temp-ed with a separate ed.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a person's readiness to anger, which can be seen as a flaw.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hot-tempered to describe someone who gets angry quickly, often in a light or critical way. It is common in everyday talk about family, sports, or bosses, and it is less harsh than violent. A natural reply might be Yeah, he does lose his temper fast.

distinctions.note: Short-tempered and hot-tempered are close in meaning, but short-tempered often describes a brief, easily irritated mood, while hot-tempered suggests a more fiery temperament.
Quick-tempered is almost identical, and it is a common alternative in American speech.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a good guy, but he's pretty hot-tempered when the Yankees lose.
examples.professional: Our manager is hot-tempered in reviews, so it helps to bring facts rather than emotion to the meeting.
examples.analytical: Proverbs 15:18 contrasts the hot-tempered man, who stirs up strife, with the patient person, and the contrast is a central piece of wisdom ethics.

nuance.analogy: A hot-tempered person is like a kettle with a loose lid: a little heat and it boils over.
nuance.etymology: Hot is from Old English hāt; tempered is from Latin temperare, to mix in due proportion.
common_mistakes: Using angry for a permanent trait, when hot-tempered describes a habit or personality.
Pronouncing the last syllable as a full ed sound instead of a reduced ərd.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the hot-tempered person is often contrasted with the wise person who is slow to anger. Proverbs 15:18 says a hot-tempered man stirs up strife, while the patient person calms a quarrel. The Hebrew idea behind anger is often connected to heat, ḥēmāh (wrath), which Proverbs uses to describe destructive emotion.

senses.definition: (dated) Theory and practice involving the skills and specialized knowledge in performing the domestic tasks required to care for the home and its occupants.
senses.example: Her grandmother taught household arts at the girls' school before the Second World War.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Skills for managing a home, such as cooking, sewing, cleaning and budgeting, taught in older school courses.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'arts', and 'household' keeps a lighter first stress. The r in 'arts' is clear, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly old-fashioned; it sounds historical rather than everyday.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say 'household arts' today. They say 'home economics' for the school subject, now often called family and consumer sciences, or 'domestic skills' or 'housekeeping' for everyday work. You will mostly see the term in older books, school histories and historical writing.

distinctions.note: Home economics is the modern US school subject name, while household arts is older and more historical.
Housekeeping is the everyday work of cleaning and organizing, while household arts is broader and includes cooking and sewing.

examples.everyday: My grandmother learned household arts like canning and mending at a country school.
examples.professional: The district dropped its household arts program in favor of family and consumer sciences.
examples.analytical: Historians of education show how household arts trained women for domestic roles before home economics replaced them.

nuance.analogy: Household arts are the craft of the home, just as carpentry is the craft of building.
nuance.etymology: Household comes from house and hold; art comes from Latin ars, meaning skill or craft.
common_mistakes: Using 'household arts' for everyday housework, where 'chores' or 'housework' is natural.
Putting equal stress on both words, which makes the phrase sound flat.
nuance.biblical_note: Proverbs 31:27 (RSV) praises a capable wife who 'looks well to the ways of her household,' describing household management as a serious skill. The Hebrew underlying household is bayit, meaning house or household.

senses.definition: Everyday things for the home, like cleaning supplies and paper towels.
senses.example: Before the move, we bought household items like paper towels, dish soap, and trash bags.

core.definition: Everyday things used in a home, such as cleaning supplies, paper towels, soap and light bulbs.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'household' has primary stress on its first syllable, and 'items' has primary stress on its first syllable as well. The final 'ms' of 'items' is a single unvoiced cluster, so do not add a vowel between 'm' and 'z'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term, often used on store signs and shopping lists.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase on store signs, in shopping lists or when describing a purchase, as in 'The household items are in aisle nine.' It is more general than naming specific products, so it works well for a broad category. In everyday conversation, people more often say 'stuff for the house' or name the item directly.

distinctions.note: Household goods is more formal and often used for moving companies or legal and insurance contexts, while household items is the everyday shopping term.
Groceries refers to food and drink, while household items refers to non-food products for the home.

examples.everyday: Could you grab some household items on the way home, like paper towels and dish soap?
examples.professional: Procurement needs to finalize the vendor contract for the household items used in the office break rooms.
examples.analytical: The category 'household items' groups together products whose function is domestic rather than food-related, which makes it a useful bucket in retail data.

nuance.analogy: Like a junk drawer, it is a practical catch-all for things every home needs.
nuance.etymology: 'Household' combines 'house' and 'hold' (a household is a family unit or home), and 'item' comes from Latin 'item', meaning 'likewise'.
common_mistakes: Using 'household article' or 'house items', which sound unnatural to Americans.
Mispronouncing 'items' as 'eye-tems' with a stressed first vowel shift; the first vowel is a diphthong ai and the second syllable is reduced.

conversation.text: Paper towels and other household items are on the left side of the store.
We spend a lot on household items like trash bags and soap.
The dollar store is great for basic household items.

senses.definition: (rare) To prepare for a journey.
senses.example: Before dawn, the pilgrims began to housel their mules and pack provisions for the long road.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To give Communion to a dying person as a final sacrament; an archaic term used in older English religious writing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HOW, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel, like 'uhl.' The 'z' is voiced, like the 'z' in 'houses' as a verb.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It belongs to religious or historical writing and is not used in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use 'housel' today. You would find it in older English poetry, historical novels or theological history. In modern American religious life people say 'administer the last rites' or 'give the Eucharist to someone who is dying,' and Catholics use 'viaticum' for final Communion.

distinctions.note: Viaticum is the technical Catholic term for Communion given to someone near death, while housel is an older English word for the same practice.
Last rites is a broader term for prayers, anointing and Communion for the dying, while housel refers only to the Communion.

examples.everyday: My grandmother asked the priest to housel her before she passed, which was an old custom in our family.
examples.professional: In the medieval manuscript, the chaplain is instructed to housel the sick before the morning bell.
examples.analytical: Older English devotional writing treated the act of housel as a sacred preparation for death, linking the sacrament to the soul's final journey.

nuance.analogy: To housel someone is like giving a traveler a final meal and blessing before a long journey: the sacrament is the last provision for the road ahead.
nuance.etymology: From Old English húsl, meaning the Eucharist or sacrament of the altar.
common_mistakes: Using 'housel' for a general journey or travel preparation; the word has only a religious meaning.
Confusing 'housel' with 'housewife' or 'house' because the spelling looks similar.

traditions.view: Communion is given to the dying as part of the Mystery of the Eucharist, usually through the reserved Holy Gifts, and it is understood as spiritual nourishment for the passage to death.
Final Communion, called viaticum, is given to dying Catholics as a sacrament for the journey from this life, and it is part of the anointing and last rites.
Many Protestants do not reserve the sacrament for the dying, though some Anglican and Lutheran churches offer Communion to the sick and dying, and practices vary widely.

housel.etymology: From Middle English *housel*, from Old English *hūsl* (“housel, Eucharist, the Host, a sacrifice”), from Proto-Germanic **hunslą* (“sacrifice”), from Proto-Indo-European **ḱwen-* (“holy”).

senses.definition: To become enraged in an imposing or intimidating manner.
senses.example: When the referee made a bad call, the coach started to hulk out, shouting and stomping across the field.

senses.definition: To gain significant muscle mass from exercise.
senses.example: After a year of heavy lifting, he began to hulk out and his shirts no longer fit.

core.definition: To suddenly become furious and physically intimidating, often in an exaggerated, comic way, as if transforming into a giant.

pronunciation.tip: In phrasal verbs Americans usually stress the particle, so 'out' carries the main stress. 'Hulk' has a short u, like 'hull', ending in a clear k.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous. It describes someone losing their temper in a loud, looming way, and it is usually said with amusement or mild criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this slang mostly in casual talk, often with a nod to the Incredible Hulk, the green giant from Marvel comics. You hulk out at someone or on something, for example at a referee or a slow printer. For muscle gain, the same phrase sometimes appears in fitness talk, but 'bulk up' is the more standard choice there. Avoid it in formal writing or when reporting serious conflict.

distinctions.note: Blow up is common and general for losing your temper, while hulk out adds a sense of physical, looming intimidation.
Bulk up is standard for gaining muscle; hulk out for muscle gain is informal and playful.

collocations: hulk out after a bad call

examples.everyday: Don't hulk out at the cashier; they're just trying to get the line moving.
examples.professional: When the vendor missed the deadline, our director hulked out in the meeting, which didn't help anyone fix the problem.
examples.analytical: Outbursts like these, when people hulk out under pressure, reveal less about strength than about how fragile self-control can be.

nuance.analogy: Like a cartoon character whose anger makes him grow three sizes in a few seconds.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb from the noun hulk, a large, bulky person, with a popular echo of the Incredible Hulk, a Marvel comic character from the 1960s.
common_mistakes: Using it in formal writing or serious reports, where it sounds too casual.
Stressing 'hulk' heavily and saying the particle quietly, when Americans stress 'out' in this phrasal verb.

hulk-out.etymology: From *Hulk*, a fictional character, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby for the Marvel Comics Universe, who gains superhuman strength when he becomes angry.

i-have-a-hard-stop-at-three.phonetic: /aɪ hæv ə ˌhɑɹd ˌstɑp æt ˈθɹi/

senses.definition: Saying you must leave at exactly 3 o'clock.

core.definition: Saying you must leave a meeting at exactly 3 o'clock and cannot stay any longer.

pronunciation.respelling: eye hav uh hahrd stahp at THREE
pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on THREE, and 'a' and 'at' are weak. 'Hard stop' has its own stress on HARD, with an r sound in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and businesslike. It sets a boundary politely, but sounds more direct than 'I need to leave by three'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in workplace meetings to warn others that you must leave at a fixed time because you have another commitment. It is common in tech and corporate settings. A natural reply is 'Got it, let's prioritize the main points' or 'Thanks for letting us know.'

distinctions.vs: I have to leave at three
distinctions.note: I have to leave at three is neutral and clear, while a hard stop sounds more professional and business-like.
Drop off means leaving a call early, while hard stop means you cannot stay past a set time in a meeting.

examples.everyday: I have a hard stop at three, so I can't stay for the whole party.
examples.professional: I have a hard stop at three, so let's go over the roadmap first.
examples.analytical: A hard stop at three means the team must decide which items are essential before the discussion expires.

nuance.analogy: Like a theater curtain that falls at a fixed time: the scene ends whether or not the story is finished.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hard stop at 3' with the wrong stress, putting stress on 'stop' instead of 'three'.
Using 'stop' alone to mean leave, which sounds unclear.

conversation.text: Just a heads-up, I have a hard stop at three.
Sorry, I have a hard stop at three, so I'll need to drop off.

senses.definition: I understand.

core.definition: A short phrase that means you understand what someone has just said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'see,' which is a long vowel. Do not shorten it to 'sih.' In casual speech, the two words may run together into 'eye-SEE.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I see' to acknowledge information, often during a conversation or a phone call. It can sound cold if said flatly, so add a nod or a follow-up question. It is equally common in casual and professional settings.

distinctions.note: 'I understand' sounds more formal and explicit, while 'I see' is brief and conversational, and can also mean 'I see what you mean' or 'I get it.'

examples.everyday: I see, so the store closes early on Sundays.
examples.professional: I see, so the vendor needs our signed contract before they can start the migration.
examples.analytical: I see the argument, but the author's premise about causation still needs independent support.

nuance.analogy: Like turning on a light in a dark room so you can see the layout.
common_mistakes: Using 'I see' to mean 'I agree,' which is a different meaning
Saying it flatly, which can sound dismissive

conversation.text: "You press this button first, then that one." "Oh, I see."
I see what you mean. That makes more sense now.
"I'm not coming tonight." "I see. Is everything okay?"

senses.definition: Choosing the dish of the day; "go with" means choose.

core.definition: I'll choose the dish of the day that the restaurant is offering as its special, instead of something from the regular menu.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPEH in special, and go is only lightly stressed. Non-native speakers often say the vowel of special as 'spay-shul'; in American speech the first vowel is short, as in 'speck'. In fast speech, 'I'll go' links into one smooth sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It is a normal, polite way to order at a casual or sit-down restaurant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a server asks what you would like and you want the daily special. The server will usually describe it, and you can add 'sounds good' or 'that sounds great.' Saying 'I'll go with the special' is the same as ordering it, so you do not need to add 'please' to make it polite, though a smile helps.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning. 'Go with' sounds a bit more conversational and suggests you are choosing it over other options.
A question asking what the special is, not a choice. Use it before you decide.

antonyms: I'll get something off the menu
collocations: go with what the server recommends

examples.everyday: The waiter said the special was grilled chicken, so I'll go with the special.
examples.professional: We're having lunch at the deli, and I'll go with the special so I don't spend too long choosing.
examples.analytical: When faced with a menu of many options, I'll go with the special, since it reduces the decision to a single choice made by the kitchen.

nuance.analogy: Like taking the chef's pick at a concert, you accept the recommendation the house is already offering.
nuance.etymology: 'Go with' comes from the sense of agreeing with or accepting something, dating to the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I go with the special' without the 'I'll', which sounds like a habit rather than a decision in the moment.
Pronouncing special as 'SPAY-shul' with a long a sound.

conversation.text: That sounds great. I'll go with the special.
I can't decide, so I'll go with the special, please.
I'll go with the special and a glass of the house red.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of identity card.
senses.example: I left my ID card at home, so the clerk wouldn't let me pick up the package.

core.definition: A small card, usually with your name and photo, that officially shows who you are, such as a work badge or student card.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters eye-dee, stressing the first word, then card with a strong rhotic r. Learners often say the first word like the word id, but it is the letters I and D.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an everyday document with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say ID card for employee, student or state IDs, and everyday speech often shortens it to just ID. The British term identity card is not normal in American usage, so say ID card or simply ID. For driving, Americans say driver's license instead of ID card.

distinctions.note: A driver's license allows you to drive and often serves as ID, while an ID card is a separate document that has no driving function.
A badge is usually worn for a workplace or event, while an ID card can be used for official checks, purchases or building access.

examples.everyday: Do you know if the gym takes a student ID card, or do I need my driver's license?
examples.professional: Please swipe your ID card at the lobby turnstile so the badge system logs your visit.
examples.analytical: A national ID card scheme raises hard questions about who has the authority to certify a person's identity and what happens when the system makes errors.

nuance.analogy: An ID card is like a passport for a building or organization, granting access to a specific place rather than a whole country.
nuance.etymology: ID is short for identification, and card comes from Latin charta through Greek and French, meaning a piece of paper or card.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing ID as the word id, with a short i sound.
Using identity card, which is common in Britain but sounds foreign to Americans.

senses.definition: Synonym of hypochondriasis.
senses.example: After months of worrying about every ache, he was diagnosed with illness anxiety disorder.

core.definition: A condition in which a person has a persistent, excessive fear of having a serious illness, even with few or no symptoms.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress in anxiety falls on ZY, and disorder stresses SOR. The t in anxiety is often a soft flap, and the final -er in disorder is a reduced sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; a clinical label that can feel stigmatizing if used casually.
nuance.usage_note: This is the current DSM-5 name, which replaced hypochondriasis in clinical practice. Americans use it with doctors and in medical writing, and many people dislike the word hypochondriac, so the newer term is preferred. In casual talk people say they worry about every symptom, and it is unkind to use the label to tease someone.

distinctions.note: An older name for the same condition, now replaced by illness anxiety disorder in DSM-5.
Here the main problem is distressing physical symptoms themselves, while illness anxiety disorder centers on fear of having a disease even when symptoms are mild or absent.

collocations: cognitive behavioral therapy for illness anxiety disorder

examples.everyday: My brother says he has illness anxiety disorder, so he tries not to search every ache online.
examples.professional: The clinical team referred her for therapy after assessing her for illness anxiety disorder.
examples.analytical: Illness anxiety disorder raises a philosophical question about where bodily sensation ends and interpretation begins.

nuance.analogy: It is like a smoke detector that goes off every time someone makes toast: the alarm works, but it is set far too sensitively.
nuance.etymology: Illness from ill plus -ness; anxiety from Latin anxietas, distress, from anxius, troubled.
common_mistakes: Flattening the stress and missing the main stress on ZY in anxiety.
Using the term for ordinary worry about a real diagnosis; it refers to a persistent, excessive pattern of fear.
