senses.example: Grandma still remembers doing the slop at her high school dance in 1964.

senses.definition: (dated) Human urine or excrement.
senses.example: The old nurse emptied the slop pail beside the sickbed every morning.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (uncommon) A policeman.
senses.example: Watch out, the slop is coming round the corner, the thief hissed.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: Being or relating to slops (cheap or ready-made clothing).
senses.example: He bought a cheap slop jacket at the dockside shop.

senses.definition: To spill or dump liquid upon; to soil with a spilled liquid.
senses.example: I slopped water all over my shirt.

senses.definition: In a game of pool or snooker, to pocket a ball by accident; in billiards, to make an ill-considered shot.
senses.example: He slopped the cue ball into the side pocket on his final shot.

senses.definition: To feed pigs.
senses.example: Every morning my uncle slops the hogs before he eats breakfast.

senses.definition: To make one's way through soggy terrain.
senses.example: We slopped through the flooded field in our rain boots all afternoon.

core.definition: Watery, messy food waste, or liquid that has been carelessly spilled on a surface.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short, open vowel of cot and end with a clean p; do not stretch it into sloap or slope.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests mess, waste or low quality.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, slop is watery leftover food or any liquid spilled messily, as in Careful, you're spilling slop everywhere. In recent years it has also named low-quality, mass-produced AI content, a sense you will see in tech news. It is informal, so define it in a formal report before using it.

distinctions.note: Slush is partly melted snow or ice, while slop is any watery mess, including food and spilled drinks.
Mush is soft, thick, pulpy food, while slop is more liquid and suggests carelessness.

examples.everyday: Careful, you're going to slop coffee all over the carpet.
examples.professional: The AI-generated drafts were full of slop, so we added a human review step before anything went to customers.
examples.analytical: Critics use the word slop for mass-produced, low-quality AI content that crowds out careful work and buries real insight.

nuance.analogy: Slop is like cheap cafeteria food: filling in bulk, but nobody chose it for quality.
common_mistakes: Confusing slop with slope; slope is a hill or incline, not a mess.
Using slop for a neat dish or a carefully poured drink; slop always implies mess or poor quality.

slop.etymology: From Middle English *slop*, *sloppe*, *slope*, from Old English **slop* (found in *oferslop* (“an outergarment, surplice”)).

senses.definition: Likely to snap or bite.
senses.example: A snappish cur

senses.definition: Exhibiting irritation or impatience; curt; irascible.

core.definition: Quick to speak sharply or irritably, sounding short-tempered and curt, often because of impatience or annoyance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SNAP, and make the last syllable a short 'ish,' like the end of 'finish.' Don't pronounce the final sh like 'sh-ee.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes irritable, unfriendly speech or behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use snappish to describe someone who replies sharply or irritably, often when tired, stressed or impatient. It is a descriptive word for everyday conversation, and it sounds softer than rude. A natural comment is 'You sound snappish today, is everything okay?'

distinctions.note: Snappy can mean quick and lively or irritable, but snappish only means irritable or sharp in speech.
Curt describes brief, cold speech, while snappish adds impatience or irritability.

examples.everyday: Don't be snappish with your brother; he didn't mean to forget the milk.
examples.professional: The manager sounded snappish during the call, so I kept my update short.
examples.analytical: Her snappish reply revealed irritation rather than a real argument.

nuance.analogy: A snappish reply is like a dog that barks before it knows who is at the door.
nuance.etymology: From snap, to speak sharply, with the adjective suffix -ish.
common_mistakes: Confusing snappish with snappy, which can mean stylish or quick.
Using snappish for a physical bite; it describes speech or temper more often.

senses.definition: Prone to sneeze with little (if any) nasal agitation.
senses.example: I feel sneezy.

senses.definition: Characterized by sneezes.
senses.example: I had a very sneezy cold.

senses.definition: Resembling a sneeze.
senses.example: There was a sneezy sound from behind the hedge.

core.definition: Tending to sneeze often, or characterized by frequent sneezing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SNEE-zee. The final -y is a long ee sound, like 'easy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a physical state, usually a cold or allergies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sneezy in casual talk about allergies or colds, as in 'I'm feeling sneezy today.' It is informal and not common in formal writing, where people usually say 'prone to sneezing' or describe the symptom directly.

distinctions.note: Allergic describes the medical cause, while sneezy describes the symptom you notice.
Stuffy refers to a blocked nose, while sneezy refers to frequent sneezing.

examples.everyday: I'm getting sneezy again, so the cat must be nearby.
examples.professional: Our office gets sneezy in spring, so facilities added air filters near the desks.
examples.analytical: A sneezy response to pollen is one sign of an immune system overreacting to harmless particles.

nuance.analogy: Being sneezy is like having a faulty doorbell that rings every time someone walks by: the body keeps signaling for no good reason.
nuance.etymology: Formed from sneeze with the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using sneezy to describe a single sneeze; say 'I sneezed' for one event.
Confusing sneezy with sneezing, which is a noun, not an adjective.

senses.definition: The sound made by exhaling or inhaling roughly through the nose.
senses.example: He let out a loud snort of laughter when he read the silly caption.

senses.definition: A dose of snuff or other drug to be snorted.
senses.example: The old man took a snort of snuff and sneezed twice.

senses.definition: A consumed portion of an alcoholic drink.
senses.example: Let me pour you a quick snort of bourbon before the funeral.

senses.definition: To make a snort; to exhale roughly through the nose.
senses.example: She snorted with laughter.

senses.definition: To express or force out by snorting.
senses.example: He snorted a derisory reply and turned on his heel.

senses.definition: To express contempt or disgust by (or as if by) a snorting sound.
senses.example: She snorted at his excuse and went right back to her spreadsheet.

senses.definition: To inhale (usually a drug) through the nose.
senses.example: to snort cocaine

senses.definition: To sail at periscope depth through the use of a snort or snorkel.
senses.example: The submarine snorted along at periscope depth to recharge its batteries overnight.

core.definition: To push air forcefully out through the nose, making a rough sound, often to show scorn, amusement, or disbelief.

pronunciation.tip: The r is strong and must be clearly pronounced in American speech. The vowel is the open "or" sound, close to the vowel in "sport" and "north".

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. A snort can show laughter, scorn, or impatience depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "snort" for a loud, rough nasal sound, often when laughing or reacting with disbelief, as in "He snorted at that idea." It can be playful among friends, but if you snort at someone's idea in a meeting, it sounds rude and dismissive. In casual talk, people also say "snort with laughter" to describe laughing so hard that air is forced through the nose.

distinctions.note: Sniff is a quiet inhalation; snort is louder and forceful, often with emotion or a reaction.
Snore happens during sleep; snort is an awake sound used for reaction, laughter, or contempt.

examples.everyday: When I told him the pizza place was closed, he just snorted and said, "Of course it was."
examples.professional: Some of the managers snorted at the proposal in the meeting, so I rewrote it with clearer numbers.
examples.analytical: Hume's critics often snorted at his skepticism rather than taking the argument seriously.

nuance.analogy: A snort is like a horse blowing hard through its nose to show it is not impressed.
nuance.etymology: Middle English snorten, probably imitative of the sound of forceful breathing.
common_mistakes: Using "snort" as a neutral word for breathing; it implies a rough, audible burst of air.
Using "snort at" politely in front of someone; it usually signals scorn.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, Job 39:20 describes the war horse whose majestic snorting is terrible, portraying the animal's power and fearlessness. Jeremiah 8:16 mentions the snorting of horses in the enemy's approach as a sign of coming judgment.

snort.etymology: From Middle English *snorten*, from earlier *fnorten*, from Old English **fnorettan*, related to, *fnoren*, from Old English *fnora*.

senses.definition: To make something soft or softer.
senses.example: Soften the butter before beating in the sugar.

senses.definition: To undermine the morale of someone (often soften up).
senses.example: Before the invasion, we softened up the enemy with the artillery.

senses.definition: To make less harsh.
senses.example: Having second thoughts, I softened my criticism.

senses.definition: To become soft or softer.
senses.example: The butter softened as it warmed up.

senses.definition: To become or make (a consonant) more lenis, to lenite.
senses.example: Over centuries, the medial /t/ softened into a voiced sound in many Celtic dialects.

senses.definition: To palatalize.
senses.example: In the history of Slavic languages, the velar consonant softened before front vowels.

core.definition: To make something less hard, harsh or intense, or to become gentler in texture, tone or effect.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the t is silent, so the word is SAH-fuhn, not SOFT-en. The second syllable is reduced to a weak vowel and nasal n.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or neutral, as in soften a tone or butter; it can be negative in soften up, which suggests manipulating someone into agreeing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use soften for butter, fabric, skin, criticism, a tone of voice or the impact of bad news. The phrasal form soften up often means to win someone over through flattery or pressure, as in 'The salesman tried to soften us up before the pitch.' The word is neutral enough for everyday speech, workplace feedback and writing.

distinctions.note: Tenderize specifically means making meat or food more tender; soften is the general word.
Mellow describes becoming calmer or less intense over time, often for a person, mood or sound; soften is more about reducing hardness or harshness.
Relent means to give in or become less strict about a decision or demand; soften can refer to physical, emotional or verbal change.

examples.everyday: Let the butter soften on the counter for about an hour before you bake the cookies.
examples.professional: Maybe soften your tone in the email, since the client already feels rushed about the timeline.
examples.analytical: The author softens her moral claim in the conclusion, which makes the argument harder to attack but also less clear.

nuance.analogy: Like warming a cold stick of butter until it spreads without tearing the bread.
nuance.etymology: From soft (Old English softe) plus the verb-forming suffix -en, meaning to make soft.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the t as in SOFT-en; the t is silent in standard American speech.
Using soften up only for physical softness; in American English it often means to win someone over, sometimes by pressure or flattery.

senses.definition: Dirty, defiled, stained.
Having a specific or particular type of soil.
senses.example: The vineyard's clay-soiled hillside drained poorly after every heavy spring rain.

senses.definition: That has been fed or nourished with green fodder.
senses.example: The herd was soiled on fresh alfalfa and clover throughout the summer.

senses.definition: Of a patient or child, stained or dirtied by defecation.
senses.example: The nurse changed the soiled sheets after the toddler had an accident overnight.

core.definition: Dirty or stained, especially from use, handling or spills.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable of the word. The final sound is a D after a voiced consonant, so say 'soyld' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that something is no longer clean and may need washing or replacing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use soiled for clothing, linens, carpets and diapers, and sometimes for a reputation. It is a neutral, practical word in service settings, such as hotels or hospitals, and in everyday talk about laundry. It is less strong than filthy or disgusting.

distinctions.note: Dirty is the most general word for not clean. Soiled suggests stains from use or contact, often on fabric or surfaces.
Stained refers to a specific mark that has penetrated a surface. Soiled is broader and describes an overall state of being dirtied.
Filthy is much stronger and implies extreme dirtiness. Soiled is milder and more neutral.

examples.everyday: I threw the soiled towels in the washing machine before we left for the beach.
examples.professional: Please bring any soiled linens to the laundry closet at the end of your shift.
examples.analytical: A soiled reputation is harder to restore than soiled cloth, because other people keep the memory long after the stain has been washed away.

nuance.analogy: Like a white shirt after one messy meal: it still looks like a shirt, but it no longer looks clean.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of soil, from Old French soiller, meaning to make dirty.
common_mistakes: Using soiled as a noun, as in 'the soiled', when a noun such as 'soiled items' or 'the dirty ones' is needed.
Saying 'soiled' for a serious health or hygiene problem where 'contaminated' or 'infected' is correct.

senses.definition: The Protestant Christian doctrine that the Bible is the supreme authority in all matters of doctrine and practice.
senses.example: Her seminary professor argued that sola scriptura makes the Bible the final authority for every believer's faith.

core.definition: A Latin phrase for the Reformation principle that Scripture alone is the final authority for Christian faith and practice.

pronunciation.tip: Say SOH-luh (not 'SOL-uh') and stress the TOOR in scriptura. Use American r in both scriptura's syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive among Protestants as a core principle; debated by Catholics and Orthodox, who see it as limiting.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theological discussions, usually with the other 'solas' of the Reformation. Many Protestants distinguish between sola scriptura (Scripture as the final authority) and nuda scriptura (Scripture without any tradition).

distinctions.note: Prima scriptura holds that Scripture is the highest authority, though tradition and reason have a role.
Solo scriptura rejects all creeds and tradition; many scholars say it is a distortion of sola scriptura.
Holy Tradition is the Church's handed-down teaching, which sola scriptura limits to a subordinate role.

examples.everyday: In our class we talked about why Protestants hold to sola scriptura.
examples.professional: The seminary's statement of faith affirms sola scriptura alongside the historic creeds.
examples.analytical: Sola scriptura does not reject tradition outright; it holds that tradition stands under Scripture's final judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a court with one supreme law, though other sources may advise.
nuance.etymology: Latin, 'by Scripture alone,' from sola (alone) and scriptura (writing, Scripture).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing sola as 'SOL-a.'
Saying 'sola scriptures' with an s.
Equating sola scriptura with rejecting all church teaching.
nuance.biblical_note: Advocates point to 2 Timothy 3:16-17, which says Scripture equips the believer for every good work, and Acts 17:11, where the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to test Paul's teaching. Catholic and Orthodox readers cite 2 Thessalonians 2:15, which urges holding to traditions taught by word or letter.

traditions.view: Rejects sola scriptura; Scripture is part of Holy Tradition and is rightly interpreted within the Church and the Fathers.
Rejects it; Scripture and Sacred Tradition together form one deposit of faith, interpreted by the Magisterium.
Affirms it as a principle of the Reformation, though Lutherans, Reformed and Anglicans give creeds and confessions a stronger role than many Baptists or Pentecostals do.

senses.definition: Fine black or dull brown particles of amorphous carbon and tar, produced by the incomplete combustion of coal, oil etc.
To cover or dress with soot.
senses.example: Years of cooking over the open fire had sooted the cabin's beams black.

core.definition: Fine black powder of carbon particles left in the air or on surfaces after wood, coal, oil or gas burns incompletely.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, like the oo in 'book' or 'put', not the long oo of 'boot'. Many learners say 'soot' with a long vowel, which makes it sound like 'suit' or 'soot' from a different word.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Soot suggests dirt, damage, pollution or a mess that is hard to clean.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use soot in everyday talk about chimneys, fireplaces, candles, car exhaust, and wildfire damage. In technical or environmental writing it appears as particulate matter or black carbon. It is usually uncountable, so say 'a lot of soot' rather than 'many soots'.

distinctions.note: Soot is fine black carbon that floats and settles on surfaces, while ash is the mineral residue left after something burns.
Smoke is the gas and particles that rise from a fire, and soot is the solid part that can settle out of that smoke.

examples.everyday: After we lit the fireplace, there was soot all over the mantel, so I had to wipe it down.
examples.professional: The facilities report flagged soot buildup in the boiler, so we need to schedule a cleaning before winter.
examples.analytical: Black carbon, or soot, is a climate concern because it absorbs sunlight and darkens snow and ice.

nuance.analogy: Soot is like the dark fingerprint a candle leaves on the ceiling, a sign that something burned and left a trace behind.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sot, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing soot with a long oo vowel, as in 'boot'.
Using soot for ash, when ash is the mineral residue that remains after burning.

soot.etymology: Middle English *soot,soote,sote,sot*, from Old English *sōt*, from Proto-Germanic **sōtą* (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European **sed-* (“to sit”).

senses.definition: In a sophomoric way.
senses.example: He sophomorically quoted philosophy at dinner, mistaking cleverness for wisdom.

core.definition: In an immature, overconfident way, showing half-learned knowledge and a lack of judgment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAH, the same as in sophomoric. The final -ly is a light lee sound, and the r in the middle stays clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes behavior or writing that is arrogantly immature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in conversation; it appears mostly in writing, reviews, or criticism. In speech, people usually say 'in a sophomoric way' or choose a simpler word like 'immaturely.'

distinctions.note: Immaturely is a plain word for childish behavior; sophomorically suggests arrogance based on shallow knowledge.

examples.professional: The vendor argued sophomorically that the migration would take a weekend, ignoring our legacy dependencies.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the problem sophomorically, offering a clever paradox without examining its premises.

nuance.analogy: Acting sophomorically is like a young pianist who plays fast and loud, certain of mastery, while missing the phrasing.
nuance.etymology: From sophomoric, with the adverbial -ally ending, from sophomore.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adverb with sophomore, the noun for a second-year student.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress falls on the third syllable, MAH.

senses.definition: Saying the caller dialed the wrong person.

core.definition: Something you say when you have reached the wrong person by phone, or when you dialed a number that is not the one you meant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAHR, RAWNG and NUM. The r in wrong is pronounced, and the ng is a clear nasal ending. Number is said with a flapped or soft t and a reduced final syllable, sounding like 'NUM-ber'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It is a brief apology that ends the call without awkwardness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when they dial a wrong number or answer a call intended for someone else; the caller might say 'Sorry, wrong number' too. Often you will hear it as a standalone line with a click of the call ending. You do not need to say more, though a friendly 'No problem' is a natural reply.

distinctions.vs: I'm sorry, I have the wrong number.
distinctions.note: The longer form is slightly more formal and clearer for someone who might be confused.

distinctions.vs: Sorry, you've got the wrong person.
distinctions.note: This is used when someone calls the right number but asks for someone who does not live there.

collocations: I think you have the wrong number

examples.everyday: Sorry, wrong number. Nobody named Mike lives here.
examples.professional: Sorry, wrong number; I was trying to reach the vendor support line, not your office.
examples.analytical: Sorry, wrong number, but the mistake was instructive: the dialing error reveals how little verification we build into routine calls.

nuance.analogy: Like knocking on the wrong door; you apologize and walk away.
common_mistakes: Saying 'You are wrong number' instead of 'Wrong number' or 'You have the wrong number'.
Pronouncing number with a full 'NUM-bur' vowel; American speech often reduces it to 'NUM-ber'.

conversation.text: "Is this Jenny?" "No, sorry, wrong number."
Sorry, wrong number. I was trying to call my dentist.

senses.definition: An autoencoder trained to represent activations with few active features; used to find interpretable features in models.
senses.example: We trained a sparse autoencoder on the layer activations to recover features humans can interpret.

core.definition: A neural network trained to rebuild its input using only a few active hidden features, which makes those features easier to interpret.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word on SPAHRS and the main stress of autoencoder on KOH. The first syllable of autoencoder is a secondary stress, and the final -er is reduced to a quick schwa-like sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a specialist term that carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Researchers in AI interpretability use this term in papers, talks and team meetings, usually abbreviated as SAE. Outside research, people would say a neural network or a model instead. When you mention it, it is normal to name the model and layer it was trained on.

distinctions.note: A plain autoencoder compresses and reconstructs data, while a sparse autoencoder adds a penalty that keeps only a few hidden units active.
A sparse model is any model that activates few parameters per input, while a sparse autoencoder is a specific kind of autoencoder used for finding features.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says she spends her days training sparse autoencoders to see what a language model is thinking.
examples.professional: We trained a sparse autoencoder on the residual stream of layer twelve, and the features look much more interpretable.
examples.analytical: A sparse autoencoder aims to decompose model activations into a dictionary of features, but whether those features reflect the model's own computation remains debated.

nuance.analogy: It is like a sorting machine that tries to explain each photo using only a handful of labeled tags.
nuance.etymology: Autoencoder comes from auto, meaning self, and encoder, meaning something that encodes; sparse comes from Latin sparsus.
common_mistakes: Stressing autoencoder on the first syllable instead of KOH.
Saying sparse auto-encoder with a hyphen in the middle when speaking; the word is one unit in the technical community.

conversation.text: A sparse autoencoder learns to rewrite model activations as a sparse combination of many, hopefully interpretable, features.
We trained a sparse autoencoder on one layer and found features for concepts like legal language and code errors.
A sparse autoencoder doesn't reconstruct activations perfectly, so some of the model's computation goes unexplained.

senses.definition: Clipping of specification.
senses.example: job spec

senses.definition: Clipping of speculation.
senses.example: Most of that coverage was just spec about what the board might decide next quarter.

senses.definition: Clipping of specialization.
senses.example: She chose data engineering as her spec in the master's program at the university.

senses.definition: Clipping of specialist.
senses.example: Our hospital's spec on rare cardiac conditions flew in to consult on the difficult case.

senses.definition: Clipping of spectrum.
senses.example: The lab's new sensor picks up the full spec of visible and infrared light.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of specifier.
senses.example: The architect's spec insisted on bamboo flooring throughout the entire building.

senses.definition: Clipping of specifier.
senses.example: The architect was the spec on the project, so every material choice went through her.

senses.definition: Clipping of spectacular mark, a type of catch in Australian rules football.
senses.example: The crowd roared when he took a spec over two defenders in the final quarter.

senses.definition: To specify, especially in a formal specification document.
senses.example: Please spec the materials and dimensions clearly in the contract before we sign it.

senses.definition: Clipping of special. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The restaurant ran a spec menu all weekend, with dishes that changed every few hours.

senses.definition: Clipping of specified.
senses.example: The spec amount must be wired to the account within thirty days of signing.

senses.definition: Clipping of speculative.
senses.example: His spec investments in the crypto market lost most of their value last year.

core.definition: A detailed written description of the requirements, dimensions, features, or performance a product, project, or software must meet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, pronounced with a short e as in 'bed', then a hard k. Do not add a vowel after the k, which is a common error for speakers who expect a longer word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it is a casual workplace shorthand, so in formal documents people write 'specification'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in engineering, software, construction, and product teams use 'spec' every day, as in 'send me the specs' or 'the spec changed.' In formal documents, emails to clients, or contracts, people write 'specification'. The plural 'specs' is common and means the set of details about a product, such as a computer's specs.

distinctions.note: Specification is the formal, complete term used in contracts and standards, while spec is the casual shorthand used in conversation and everyday work.
Spec usually refers to one document or one detail, while specs in the plural means the collection of technical details, as in 'the specs of this laptop.'

examples.everyday: Can you send me the specs for that new laptop before we decide?
examples.professional: The API spec has to be finalized before the frontend team starts building the client code.
examples.analytical: A formal spec sets out what a system must do, which makes it possible to test whether an implementation really satisfies the requirements.

nuance.analogy: A spec is like a recipe card for a product: it lists the exact ingredients and steps so that different cooks produce the same result.
nuance.etymology: Clipping of specification, from Latin specificare, to make specific.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'spec' with a long vowel or an added 'uh' sound, as in 'speck-uh'.
Using 'spec' in a formal letter or contract, where 'specification' is expected.
Using 'specs' for a single detail, when the singular 'spec' is correct.

senses.definition: The state of being speechless.

core.definition: The state of being unable to speak, usually from shock, anger, awe or another strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SPEECH. The middle '-less' is short, and the final '-ness' is a weak 'nuhs', not a long 'nes'. Keep the 'ch' as in 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to intense. It usually signals strong emotion, such as shock, awe or grief.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'I was speechless' rather than using the noun, which sounds more formal or written. You are most likely to hear the noun in writing, such as 'a moment of speechlessness' in a news story or novel. In conversation, it is best to use the adjective speechless.

distinctions.note: Silence is simply the absence of sound and can be chosen, while speechlessness describes being unable to speak, usually because of strong emotion.
Muteness is a lasting inability to speak, often medical, while speechlessness is usually temporary and caused by a feeling.
Shock is the emotional cause, while speechlessness is the resulting state of being unable to speak.

collocations: speechlessness in the face of tragedy

examples.everyday: After the bad news from the doctor, there was a long moment of speechlessness in the car.
examples.professional: The room fell into speechlessness when the CFO announced the layoffs, and nobody knew who should speak next.
examples.analytical: Theologians often read the speechlessness of Job before the whirlwind as a form of wisdom rather than a failure of faith.

nuance.analogy: Speechlessness is like a phone line that goes dead mid-sentence: the connection is still there, but nothing passes through.
nuance.etymology: From 'speech' (Old English 'spǣc'), the suffix '-less' (without) and the noun suffix '-ness'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am speechlessness' instead of 'I am speechless'.
Mispronouncing the final '-ness' as a full 'nes' sound instead of a weak 'nuhs'.

senses.definition: Splendid, having splendor.

core.definition: Full of splendor; brilliant, magnificent, or grand in appearance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the last two syllables light. The word has four syllables, not five, so do not add an extra vowel before the s.

nuance.connotation: Positive and poetic. It sounds elevated and can seem overwrought in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use splendorous mainly in poetry, fiction, or highly descriptive writing. In normal conversation they would say splendid, beautiful, or magnificent. Using it casually can sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Splendid is the everyday adjective; splendorous is more literary and emphasizes the quality of having splendor.
Magnificent stresses grandeur and impressiveness, while splendorous suggests shining brilliance.

examples.everyday: Those autumn leaves looked splendorous this year, so we took a long walk just to see them.
examples.professional: The product brochure used splendorous images, but the actual interface is much simpler.
examples.analytical: The poet describes the splendorous ruins to show how beauty and decay coexist.

nuance.analogy: Like a palace painted in gold, it draws the eye with light and richness.
nuance.etymology: Formed from splendor with the suffix -ous, meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Using splendorous in everyday conversation, where splendid or beautiful is more natural.
Confusing it with splendid in formal writing.

senses.definition: One who speaks as the voice of another person or a group of people.

core.definition: A person who speaks publicly on behalf of a group, company, government or another person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'man' is reduced to 'muhn', so do not give it a full 'man' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role without judgment, though it can imply the speaker is officially authorized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'spokesperson' or 'spokesman' depending on the setting, and many organizations now prefer the gender-neutral 'spokesperson.' In news reports, 'a spokesperson said' is standard. The word is common in business, government and media. In casual talk, people might say 'the person speaking for them.'

distinctions.note: 'Spokesperson' is gender-neutral and preferred in most current American institutions, while 'spokesman' is traditional and used for men.
A 'representative' acts for a group with authority, while a 'spokesman' only speaks publicly for them.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's brother is the spokesman for the local school district.
examples.professional: Our communications team will send a statement, and the company spokesperson will handle the press calls.
examples.analytical: Aaron functions as Moses' spokesman, carrying Moses' words to Pharaoh and the people.

nuance.analogy: A spokesman is like a microphone for a group: the words are theirs, but the voice is one person's.
nuance.etymology: From 'spoke', past of 'speak', plus 'man', one who speaks.
common_mistakes: Using 'spokesman' when the speaker is a woman, where 'spokeswoman' or 'spokesperson' is better.
Confusing 'spokesman' with 'speaker', which is a presiding officer or a loudspeaker.
nuance.biblical_note: In Exodus, Aaron is appointed to speak on behalf of Moses, who said he was slow of speech. The Hebrew idea centers on 'peh' (mouth), since Aaron serves as Moses' mouth. Exodus 4:16 describes Aaron speaking to the people for Moses, and Exodus 7:1 describes Moses as a god to Pharaoh while Aaron is his prophet who speaks for him.

senses.definition: A bar or pub themed around sports, typically with sporting memorabilia and sport events shown on television.
senses.example: We watched the playoff game at a crowded sports bar with TVs on every wall.

core.definition: A bar or pub decorated with sports memorabilia that shows games on several television screens.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BAR, with a lighter stress on sports. The final s of 'sports' often links into the next word's sound, and the r in both words is pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sports bar for a casual place to watch games with friends, eat wings, and drink beer, often in a loud, friendly crowd. Asking 'Want to go to a sports bar for the game?' is a very natural invitation. Americans rarely say 'sports pub' outside of British-influenced settings.

distinctions.note: A pub is a British term; in the US, people say bar, and a sports bar is specifically themed around games.
Tavern sounds old-fashioned and rustic, while sports bar is a modern, casual term.

collocations: watch the game at a sports bar

examples.everyday: Let's meet at the sports bar downtown, they have a big screen for the playoff game.
examples.professional: Our team celebrated the product launch at a sports bar near the office on Friday.
examples.analytical: The sports bar functions as a social space where strangers become temporary fans united by a shared outcome.

nuance.analogy: Like a living room with a giant TV and a crowd of cheering friends, it is built around the game.
nuance.etymology: Sports from Old French desport; bar from Old French barre, a barrier, later a counter.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sport bar' without the s, which is a common shortening that sounds slightly off.
Calling it a 'sports pub,' which Americans rarely use.

conversation.text: Let's watch the game at the sports bar downtown.
The sports bar was packed for the playoff game.
That sports bar has like thirty TVs.

senses.definition: A vernal equinox.
senses.example: The spring equinox falls on March 20 in most years, when day and night are nearly equal.

core.definition: The moment in March when day and night are roughly equal in length, marking the start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable of 'equinox,' EE, and the 'qui' is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'kwuh.' The final x is a 'ks' sound, and 'spring' carries only light stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise astronomical term with a seasonal, celebratory tone in popular use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'spring equinox' in everyday talk and news, while 'vernal equinox' is more formal and technical. The equinox falls around March 20 or 21 in the Northern Hemisphere, and it is not an exact date each year. In the Southern Hemisphere, the same event marks the start of autumn.

distinctions.note: Both refer to the same event; 'vernal' is more technical and Latin-based, while 'spring equinox' is the common everyday term in American English.
An equinox has roughly equal day and night, while a solstice marks the longest or shortest day of the year.

examples.everyday: Grandma says spring really starts on the equinox, so we're basically there already.
examples.professional: Our solar-panel output forecast resets after the spring equinox, when the sun's angle shifts.
examples.analytical: Many ancient calendars were aligned to the spring equinox, which made planting a matter of astronomy as well as tradition.

nuance.analogy: The spring equinox is like a seesaw balanced in the middle: day and night sit at the same height for a brief moment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'aequinoctium,' from 'aequus' (equal) and 'nox' (night), meaning equal night.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable of 'equinox,' as in 'ih-KWIH-nox.'
Writing 'spring equinox' with a capital letter when it is not part of a formal name.

senses.definition: Any person or thing that brings stability.
Any substance added to something in order to stabilize it, as for example a fuel additive that prolongs the shelf life of petrol.
senses.example: Adding a stabilizer to the gasoline keeps it fresh through the winter storage season.

senses.definition: An additional wheel on a bicycle to keep it upright to assist a learner.
senses.example: My daughter is learning to ride, so the stabilizers stay on her bike for now.

senses.definition: A gyroscopically controlled fin or similar device that prevents the excess rolling of a ship in rough seas.
senses.example: The ship's stabilizers kept the deck level as waves battered the bow.

senses.definition: An airfoil that stabilizes the flight of an aircraft or missile.
senses.example: The tail stabilizer keeps the missile on a steady path during its climb.

senses.definition: A piece of backing fabric used in embroidery.
senses.example: She backed the cross-stitch with a stabilizer so the thin cotton would not pucker.

senses.definition: A mechanical component that supports a large key on a keyboard (such as the space bar) and prevents it from wobbling or tilting.
senses.example: The keyboard's stabilizer keeps the space bar from wobbling when I type.

senses.definition: For a group operating on a set and an element x of the set, the set of all group elements fixing x.
senses.example: For the group action on the set, the stabilizer of x contains every element that fixes x.

core.definition: A person, thing or substance that makes something steady, such as a device on a bicycle or a chemical added to keep a product from breaking down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on STAY, and the final -er is a reduced American 'r' sound, not a full 'ur' vowel. Keep the 'lie' vowel long in the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a practical, descriptive word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'training wheels' for the extra bike wheels a child uses while learning, but a technical person may say 'stabilizers'. In food, cosmetics and fuel products, 'stabilizer' is a standard label term. In everyday conversation, 'something that keeps things steady' is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Training wheels is the everyday American term for the bike attachments; stabilizer is more formal or technical and can apply to many things.
An additive is any substance added for any purpose, while a stabilizer is added specifically to keep a mixture or product from changing.

examples.everyday: My daughter finally rode without the stabilizers, so we took the training wheels off.
examples.professional: Adding a stabilizer to the emulsion keeps the sauce from separating in the warehouse.
examples.analytical: Trust can act as a social stabilizer, absorbing shocks so that conflict does not spread through the community.

nuance.analogy: A stabilizer is like the keel of a sailboat: it keeps the boat from tipping over in the wind.
nuance.etymology: From stabilize plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'stabilizator' or other forms with extra suffixes.
Pronouncing the final -er as a full vowel instead of the American 'r' sound.

senses.definition: The state of being stagnant; an instance of this.
senses.example: Factors known to encourage the growth of harmful bacteria inside cooling systems include the stagnation of the water.

senses.definition: The state of lacking flow or motion, usually causing a lack of freshness or health; an instance of this.
senses.example: Factors known to encourage the growth of harmful bacteria inside cooling systems include the stagnation of the water.

senses.definition: The state of lacking activity, change or progress, or excitement in an unhealthy manner; inactivity, staleness; an instance of this.
senses.example: The general concern about industrial stagnation inspired an overhaul of the patent system.

senses.definition: The state of low or no growth in an economy; an instance of this.

core.definition: A state of no growth, movement, or progress, often causing stale or unhealthy conditions.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAY, the second syllable of the -ation ending. The final syllable is a reduced shun sound, not a full on.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes a serious lack of growth or movement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stagnation for economies, wages, cities, and personal growth. It is common in news, policy, and professional talk, but in casual speech people often say things are stuck or not moving. Calling a person's life in stagnation can sound heavy, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: A recession is a decline in economic output; stagnation is the absence of growth, not necessarily a fall.
Standstill is a more everyday word for a complete stop; stagnation suggests a longer, less visible lack of progress.

examples.everyday: Many people in our town feel a real sense of stagnation since the factory closed.
examples.professional: Wage stagnation has made it hard for our customers to afford the premium plan.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that intellectual stagnation follows when a community stops asking hard questions.

nuance.analogy: Like a lake with no river flowing out: it stays still, collects debris, and slowly grows stale.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stagnatio, from stagnare, to stand still.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as STAG-nation-style.
Using stagnation for a short pause; it implies a longer period of no progress.

stagnation.etymology: From *stagnate* + *-ation*, is derived, the stem of Latin *stagnāre*, the of *stāgnō* (“of waters: to cover the land as a lake, to become a pool, to stagnate”), from *stāgnum* (“body of standing water”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European **steh₂g-* (“to…

senses.definition: In a steady manner; with a steady progression.
senses.example: Enrollment grew steadily over the decade as the town attracted new families.

core.definition: In a continuous, even, and consistent way, without sudden changes or interruptions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a short reduced vowel, and the d between vowels is a flap, so it sounds close to 'STEH-dih-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes reliable, controlled progress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use steadily in business reports, news, and everyday talk about progress, growth, or health. It is neutral and widely used. In casual speech people sometimes say 'steady' as an adverb, but in writing use steadily.

distinctions.note: Constantly means all the time or repeatedly, often with irritation, while steadily describes an even, controlled rate.
Gradually emphasizes small changes over time, while steadily emphasizes consistency of pace.

examples.everyday: My grandfather is recovering steadily after his surgery.
examples.professional: Our signups have grown steadily for six straight months.
examples.analytical: The argument develops steadily, with each example building on the last until the conclusion feels inevitable.

nuance.analogy: Like a metronome keeping an even beat.
nuance.etymology: Formed from steady plus the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as a long 'ee' as in 'STEE-dee'.
Confusing steadily with steadfastly, which stresses loyalty or firm commitment.

senses.definition: To make steeper.
To become steeper.

core.definition: To make something steeper, or to become steeper, such as a slope, a hill, or the difference between interest rates.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the last syllable a quick, unstressed 'en'. Do not pronounce the final sound as a separate 'ayn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, and it describes a physical or measurable change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use steepen for hills, roads, learning curves, and financial graphs, such as the yield curve. In finance news, the verb often appears with 'the yield curve steepened'. In everyday talk, Americans are more likely to say 'the hill gets steeper'.

distinctions.note: Steepen describes a change in slope or angle, while increase only describes a general growth in amount.
Steep is the basic adjective; steepen is the verb meaning to make or become steeper.

examples.everyday: The trail steepens after the second creek, so take it slow.
examples.professional: The yield curve steepened after the announcement, so long-term rates rose faster than short-term ones.
examples.analytical: Adding the interaction term steepens the slope for high-income households, which changes the estimate considerably.

nuance.analogy: Steepen is like a ramp being raised at one end: the same surface becomes harder to climb.
nuance.etymology: From steep plus -en, meaning to make or become.
common_mistakes: Using steepen for a general increase, such as prices rising, where increase or rise is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: Not moving; calm.
senses.example: Sit there and stay still!

senses.definition: Not effervescing; not sparkling.
senses.example: still water; still wines

senses.definition: Uttering no sound; silent.
Having the same stated quality continuously from a past time.
Comparatively quiet or silent; soft; gentle; low.
Dormant.
senses.example: a still spore

senses.definition: Without motion.
senses.example: They stood still until the guard was out of sight.

senses.definition: Up to a time, as in the preceding time.
senses.example: Is it still raining? It was still raining five minutes ago.

senses.definition: To an even greater degree. Used to modify comparative adjectives or adverbs.
senses.example: Tom is tall; Dick is taller; Harry is still taller / Harry is taller still.

senses.definition: Nevertheless.
senses.example: I’m not hungry, but I’ll still manage to find room for dessert.

senses.definition: Even, yet.
senses.example: Some dogs howl; more yelp; still more bark.

senses.definition: A period of calm or silence.
senses.example: the still of the night

senses.definition: A photograph, as opposed to movie footage.
A single frame from a film.
A resident of the Falkland Islands.
A device for distilling liquids.
A large water boiler used to make tea and coffee.
The area in a restaurant used to make tea and coffee, separate from the main kitchen.
A building where liquors are distilled; a distillery.
To calm down, to quiet.
senses.example: to still the raging sea

senses.definition: To cause to fall by drops.
To expel spirit from by heat, or to evaporate and condense in a refrigeratory; to distill.

core.definition: Not moving; calm, without motion or noise.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short, relaxed i of 'sit', not the long 'ee' of 'steel'. Learners often stretch the vowel, which turns it into a different word.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, suggesting peace and calm; can be negative when it means inactive or unchanged.
nuance.usage_note: This is one of the most common words in American English, with several senses. As an adjective it means calm or motionless. As an adverb it often means 'continuing' ('Are you still coming?'). To ask someone not to move, Americans say 'Hold still' or 'Stay still.'

distinctions.note: Quiet describes sound; still describes motion or the absence of it, so a quiet room can still have people moving in it.
Silent means making no sound, while still means not moving; a silent person may be moving, and a still one may be talking.

examples.everyday: Hold still, there's a mosquito right on your arm.
examples.professional: Please keep the dataset still while we run the benchmark so we can compare results fairly.
examples.analytical: In Psalm 46:10 the call to be still is not only physical quiet but an act of trust that God is God.

nuance.analogy: Like a pond at dawn before the wind picks up, with no ripples on the surface.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stille, meaning motionless or quiet.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'steel' with a long vowel; the vowel is short.
Confusing the adverb still with yet in negatives: say 'I haven't finished yet', not 'I haven't still finished'.
nuance.biblical_note: Psalm 46:10 (RSV) tells the reader to be still and know that God is God. The Hebrew verb is rapha (רָפָה), meaning to let go, relax, or cease striving. Psalm 37:7 similarly tells believers to be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him. In both passages stillness means active trust in God's sovereignty rather than simple inactivity.

still.etymology: From Middle English *stille* (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English *stille* (“still, quiet”), from **stillī*, from Proto-Indo-European **telH-* (“to be silent; to be still”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to strategy.
senses.example: The general's decision to abandon the bridge was strategic, not cowardly.

senses.definition: Of or relating to military operations that are more large-scale or long-range than local or tactical ones.
senses.example: a strategic nuclear weapon

core.definition: Relating to a long-term plan designed to achieve an important goal, rather than to small or immediate steps.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the 'TI' syllable, not the first. The first vowel is a reduced schwa, and the 'g' sounds like the 'j' in 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests careful, forward-looking thinking, and it is used both to praise a choice and to describe a plan.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly in business, government, sports, and everyday discussion of big decisions, as in 'a strategic move'. In casual talk it can sound a little formal or corporate, so people often say 'smart' or 'a good play' instead. The word is standard; the variant 'strategical' is rare.

distinctions.note: Strategic concerns the overall, long-term goal; tactical concerns the specific methods used for immediate steps toward it.
Strategical means the same thing but is rare and sounds old-fashioned; Americans use strategic.

examples.everyday: Picking the checkout line was strategic: I chose the one with the fewest carts.
examples.professional: We need a strategic plan for cloud costs over the next three years, not just a quick fix.
examples.analytical: Clausewitz treats war as a strategic instrument of politics rather than an isolated military act.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess player thinking several moves ahead, rather than reacting to the last move.
nuance.etymology: From strategy plus -ic, from Greek strategia, 'generalship'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (STRAT-uh-jik) instead of the middle one.
Spelling it 'strategical' in ordinary writing; 'strategic' is the standard American form.

strategic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *στρατηγικός* (“of or for a general", also "a treatise on strategy”), from *στρατηγός* (“the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from *στρατός* (“army”) + *ἄγω* (“I lead, I conduct”).

senses.definition: The act of one who strays; deviation or sin, often sexual infidelity.
senses.example: His straying from the marriage cost him his friendships and his trust.

core.definition: The act of wandering away from a path, a group, or accepted behavior, often including sin or unfaithfulness.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on STRAY, and the final -ing is a short, light vowel, so say 'STRAY-ing' with the second syllable reduced. Keep the r clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative or serious. It often implies moral failure or sin, such as infidelity, though it can be neutral when describing a path or an animal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use straying as a noun mainly in religious, literary, or formal discussions. In everyday talk, people usually say cheating, wandering, or getting off track. Be careful, because straying can sound heavy or judgmental when applied to someone's personal life.

distinctions.note: Wandering often suggests aimless movement and can be neutral or romantic. Straying implies leaving a proper path or obligation, with a sense of fault.
Sin is a specific moral wrong in religious thought, while straying is a broader image of drifting from the right path.
Infidelity specifically means sexual unfaithfulness in a relationship. Straying can refer to this but also to any wandering from duty or faith.

examples.everyday: Nobody talks about their own straying at dinner, but we all know how easily a good habit can slip.
examples.professional: The team's straying from the project plan caused the delay, so we need tighter weekly checkpoints.
examples.analytical: For Augustine, straying from God is not merely a change of direction but a disordered love of lesser goods.

nuance.analogy: Straying is like a river that leaves its channel during a flood. The water still flows, but it no longer follows the course it was meant to keep.
nuance.etymology: From stray (Middle English strayen, from Old French estraier) with the noun ending -ing.
common_mistakes: Using straying as a casual word for a small mistake; it sounds heavy, so 'getting off track' is better in work talk.
Confusing it with straying in the sense of stray animals; the noun is usually about people's behavior or faith.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often describes sin as straying from God's way. The Hebrew shagah (to go astray, err) and the Greek planaō (to wander, go astray) carry this idea. Isaiah 53:6 says that all of us, like sheep, have gone astray. Matthew 18:12-13 describes a shepherd who searches for a sheep that has gone astray, showing God's concern for the one who wanders. Psalm 119:176 is a prayer that asks God to seek the psalmist, who has wandered like a lost sheep.

senses.definition: To pack up and leave.
To yield, give up, or surrender.
senses.example: Facing a losing vote, the senator finally struck the tent and conceded the fight.

core.definition: To take down a tent and pack up to leave a campsite or a place of gathering.

pronunciation.tip: The article the reduces to a weak thuh before the consonant t. The main stress falls on tent, which carries the short e vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes the practical act of packing up, but it has a traditional, stately tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use strike the tent in everyday speech; they would say pack up or break camp. The phrase appears in military writing, literary prose, historical accounts and sometimes in sermons about life as a journey. Using it in casual talk may sound deliberately old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Break camp is the common American phrase for leaving a campsite, while strike the tent is stately and somewhat literary.
Pack up is the everyday phrase and can refer to any belongings, while strike the tent focuses on taking down a tent.

collocations: strike the tent before the storm
strike the tent and move on

examples.everyday: Let's strike the tent before the storm rolls in.
examples.professional: The festival crew will strike the tent Monday, and the vendors will leave by noon.
examples.analytical: The phrase carries the image of a people who pitch and strike their dwellings with the seasons, a figure of human transience.

nuance.analogy: Striking the tent is like taking down a stage set after the last performance: the structure comes down, and only the memory of it remains.
nuance.etymology: Strike from Old English strīcan (to take down) plus tent from Latin tendere, to stretch.
common_mistakes: Confusing strike the tent with pitch the tent, which means setting it up.
Using the phrase in casual conversation, where break camp or pack up sounds more natural.

inflections: struck the tent, stricken the tent

senses.definition: Miscellaneous items or objects; (with possessive) personal effects.
senses.example: What is all that stuff on your bedroom floor?He didn't want his pockets to bulge so he was walking around with all his stuff in his hands.

senses.definition: Unspecified things or matters.
senses.example: I had to do some stuff.

senses.definition: The tangible substance that goes into the makeup of a physical object.
senses.example: What kind of stuff is this sofa cushion made of?

senses.definition: Abstract/figurative substance or character.
senses.example: She has the stuff of a great leader, calm under pressure and fair to everyone.

senses.definition: Used as placeholder, usually for material of unknown type or name.
senses.example: Can I have some of that stuff on my ice-cream sundae?

senses.definition: Narcotic drugs, especially heroin.
senses.example: Police found a bag of stuff hidden under the seat of the car.

senses.definition: Refuse or worthless matter; hence, also, foolish or irrational language.
senses.example: Don't give me any of that 'what-about' stuff!

senses.definition: Money.
senses.example: Do you have the stuff to pay for dinner tonight?

senses.definition: A melted mass of turpentine, tallow, etc. with which the masts, sides, and bottom of a ship are smeared for lubrication.
senses.example: The shipwright melted the stuff and smeared it along the hull below the waterline.

senses.definition: (dated) Pulp; paper stock ground ready for use. When partly ground, it is called half stuff.
senses.example: The mill ground the wood into stuff ready for the paper machines.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To fill by packing or crowding something into; to cram with something; to load to excess.
senses.example: I'm going to stuff this pillow with feathers.

senses.definition: To fill a space with (something) in a compressed manner.
senses.example: He stuffed his clothes into the closet and shut the door.

senses.definition: To fill with seasoning.
senses.example: She stuffed the turkey for Thanksgiving using her secret recipe.

senses.definition: To load goods into (a container) for transport.
senses.example: We stuffed the trunk with winter coats before driving north.

senses.definition: To sate.
senses.example: I’m stuffed after having eaten all that turkey, mashed potatoes and delicious stuffing.

senses.definition: To eat, especially in a hearty or greedy manner.
senses.example: She sits on the sofa all day, watching TV and stuffing herself with cream buns.

senses.definition: Used to contemptuously dismiss or reject something. See also stuff it.
senses.example: Stuff your stupid rules, I'll do what I like.

senses.definition: To heavily defeat or get the better of.
senses.example: Mudchester Rovers were stuffed 7–0 in the semi-final.

senses.definition: To cut off another competitor in a race by disturbing his projected and committed racing line (trajectory) by an abrupt maneuver.
senses.example: I got stuffed by that guy on the supermoto going into that turn, almost causing us to crash.

senses.definition: To preserve a dead bird or other animal by filling its skin.
senses.example: The museum hired an expert to stuff the old bison for the exhibit.

senses.definition: To obstruct, as any of the organs; to affect with some obstruction in the organs of sense or respiration.
senses.example: The allergy medicine did little to help, and my nose remained stuffed all week.

senses.definition: To form or fashion by packing with the necessary material.
senses.example: The chef stuffed the chicken with bread, herbs, and lemon before roasting it.

senses.definition: To compress (a file or files) in the StuffIt format, to be unstuffed later.
senses.example: Before emailing the photos, I stuffed the folder into a single archive file.

senses.definition: (dated) To crowd with facts; to cram the mind of; sometimes, to crowd or fill with false or idle tales or fancies.
senses.example: Their teacher stuffed the children's heads with facts about dates and kings.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Miscellaneous things or objects, especially personal belongings that you carry, own or leave somewhere.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short uh vowel, as in cup, not the long oo sound of stoof. The final f is clear and unvoiced, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In casual speech it is friendly and vague. In formal writing it can sound careless.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stuff constantly in conversation: 'Where's my stuff?' or 'Put your stuff away.' It is uncountable, so say a lot of stuff, not many stuffs. For formal contexts, use items, belongings, or materials instead.

distinctions.note: Things is countable and neutral. Stuff is uncountable and more casual, and it implies a mixed collection.
Belongings is more formal and refers to personal possessions. Stuff can be casual or even dismissive.

examples.everyday: Can you move your stuff off the couch so we can sit down?
examples.professional: Before the review, make sure all your stuff is in the shared folder so the team can find it.
examples.analytical: The essay leans on a lot of stuff about intuition that it never defines, so the argument is hard to test.

nuance.analogy: Stuff is like the junk drawer in a kitchen: it holds a little of everything, and you rarely name each item.
nuance.etymology: From Old French estoffe, meaning material or equipment.
common_mistakes: Using stuffs as a plural noun, as in 'many stuffs'; say 'a lot of stuff' instead.
Using stuff for a formal report or email where items or materials is more precise.

stuff.etymology: From Middle English *stuf*, *stuffe*, from Anglo-Latin *stuffa* and its etymon Old French *estofe*, *estoffe*, *estuf*, *estuffe*, *stoffe*, from *estoffer*, *estofer* (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”), borrowed from Old High German *stoffōn*,…

senses.definition: A daring or dangerous feat, often involving the display of gymnastic skills.
senses.example: The skateboarder landed a daring stunt off the rooftop ramp, to the crowd's cheers.

senses.definition: An act or activity viewed as the outcome of a plan or scheme, often malicious or nefarious.
senses.example: His stunt to get the manager fired was a scheme no one saw coming.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of publicity stunt.
A special means of rushing the quarterback done to confuse the opposing team's offensive line.
senses.example: The defensive coordinator called a stunt that sent two linemen crossing in front of the quarterback.

senses.definition: A check in growth.
senses.example: Doctors worried about the stunt in her son's growth after his illness.

senses.definition: That which has been checked in growth; a stunted animal or thing.
senses.example: The farmer culled the stunt from the litter because it would never grow properly.

senses.definition: A two-year-old whale, which, having been weaned, is lean and yields little blubber.
senses.example: Whalers preferred the mature animals, leaving the lean stunt in the water.

senses.definition: To perform a stunt.
senses.example: He stunted the motorcycle jump himself, refusing any double for the dangerous ramp.

senses.definition: To show off; to posture; to flaunt valuables.
senses.example: He stunted in front of the girls, flashing his new watch and expensive sneakers.

senses.definition: To check or hinder the growth or development of.
senses.example: Some have said smoking stunts your growth.

core.definition: A daring or showy act done to impress people or attract attention, or a trick that is dangerous or unusual.

pronunciation.tip: Stunt is one syllable with the short vowel of cup. Clearly pronounce the final nt; do not drop the t or add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: a stunt can be impressive, but it often suggests showing off, a publicity grab, or something foolish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stunt for many everyday acts, from a skateboarder's jump to a silly prank: 'He pulled a stunt in the meeting.' The phrase publicity stunt is common in news and marketing talk. Calling someone's act a stunt can sound critical, so it fits better among friends than in a formal complaint.

distinctions.note: Trick can mean a skill, a magic effect or a deception; stunt is usually a bold, visible act meant to impress.
Gimmick refers to a repeated device used to sell a product or idea; stunt is usually a single, eye-catching event.

examples.everyday: My brother pulled a stunt on his bike and ended up in the neighbor's hedge.
examples.professional: The launch event was a clever publicity stunt, but customers will need real product data before they buy.
examples.analytical: The senator's walkout was less a principled stand than a political stunt designed for the evening news.

nuance.analogy: A stunt is like a fireworks show: loud, brief and designed to be seen by the largest possible crowd.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the sense of a daring feat dates from the nineteenth century.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun stunt with stun, which has a different meaning and no -t sound at the end.
Saying 'a stunt man' in a general sense; stuntman is the usual spelling for film performers.

senses.definition: Synonym of sublimate.

To heat (a substance) in a container so as to convert it into a gas which then condenses in solid form on cooler parts of the container; to change (a solid substance) into a gas without breaking down or passing through the liquid state by heating it gently.
To raise (someone or an intangible thing) to a state of (especially moral or spiritual) excellence; to exalt.
To cause (someone or something) to ascend; to raise (someone or something) to a high position.
To cause (juice or sap) to rise in a plant.
Especially of the sun: to heat (something) and cause vapors, etc. to rise from it.
To purify (someone) from a bad influence or from sin.
To raise (someone) to a high office or status; to dignify, to exalt.
To raise (a physical thing) to a state of excellence; to improve.
Of a substance: to change from a solid into a gas without passing through the liquid state, with or without being heated.
Of a substance: to change from a gas into a solid without passing through the liquid state.
To become higher in quality or status; to improve.
Of an aspect of art or nature: causing awe or deep respect due to its beauty or magnificence; awe-inspiring, impressive.
senses.example: sublime scenery

senses.definition: Of flight: ascending, soaring.
Of an idea or other thing: requiring great intellectual effort to appreciate or understand; very elevated, refined, or subtle.
Of language, style, or writing: expressing opinions in a grand way.
Of a person or their actions or qualities: intellectually, morally, or spiritually superior.
senses.example: a sublime deed

senses.definition: Of an office or status: very high; exalted; also, used as an honorific (often capitalized as Sublime) to refer to someone of high office or status, especially the Ottoman sultan; or to things associated with such a person.
senses.example: the Sublime Porte

senses.definition: Of a thing: consummate, perfect; excellent, marvellous, wonderful.
Complete, downright, utter.
senses.example: He is behaving like a sublime idiot.

senses.definition: Elevated by joy; elated.
Of a substance: purified, refined; hence, of the highest quality.
Of breathing: very labored.
Of a muscle (especially the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle of the forearm which lies above the flexor digitorum profundus muscle): positioned above another muscle; superficial.
(poetic) Of arms: lifted up, raised.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: Something which is sublime; a sublimity.
In the form the sublime of: the highest degree; the acme, the height.
Chiefly preceded by the.
An aspect of art or nature which causes awe or deep respect due to its beauty or magnificence; hence, the great beauty or magnificence of a place, a thing, etc.
A style of language or writing which expresses opinions in a grand way.
That which is intellectually, morally, or spiritually superior in human life or human nature.

core.definition: Awe-inspiring in beauty or greatness, so impressive that it seems to lift the spirit beyond ordinary experience.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, BLYME, which rhymes with time. The first syllable is a reduced uh, not sub.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as extraordinary, though it can sound exaggerated in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sublime mostly in writing, art criticism, and formal speech. In everyday conversation, they would more often say amazing, stunning, or perfect. Saying sublime about a sandwich would sound playful or ironic, so keep it for landscapes, music, and deep experiences.

distinctions.note: Beautiful describes pleasing qualities, while sublime suggests greatness so vast that it inspires awe or even fear.
Amazing is an everyday word for surprising or impressive things, while sublime is more elevated and literary.

examples.everyday: That sunset over the lake was sublime, honestly one of the best views I've seen all year.
examples.professional: The product demo was sublime, but the onboarding process still needs simpler steps.
examples.analytical: Kant distinguishes the beautiful from the sublime, locating the sublime in experiences that overwhelm the imagination yet reveal the mind's power.

nuance.analogy: Like standing at the edge of a canyon, where the scale humbles you and lifts your sense of what is possible.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sublimis, lofty, from sub- up and limen, threshold, or from a phrase meaning up to the lintel.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as sub, as in SUB-lime; the first syllable is weak.
Using sublime for everyday good food or minor pleasures, which sounds overblown in American speech.

senses.definition: To sign; to mark with one's signature as a token of consent or attestation.
senses.example: Parties subscribe a covenant or contract; a man subscribes a bond.

senses.definition: To sign up to have copies of a publication, such as a newspaper or a magazine, delivered for a period of time.
senses.example: Would you like to subscribe or subscribe a friend to our new magazine, Lexicography Illustrated?

senses.definition: To pay for the provision of a service, such as Internet access, a cell phone plan, or a streaming service.
senses.example: I subscribed to this streaming service years ago.

senses.definition: To believe or agree with a theory or an idea [with to].
senses.example: I don’t subscribe to that theory.

senses.definition: To pay money to be a member of an organization.
senses.example: To get the discount, he had to subscribe to the club for a full year.

senses.definition: To contribute or promise to contribute money to a common fund.
senses.example: Every family on the street agreed to subscribe to the fund for new playground equipment.

senses.definition: To promise to give, by writing one's name with the amount.
senses.example: Each man subscribed ten dollars.

senses.definition: To agree to buy shares in a company.
senses.example: Investors could subscribe to the new shares before the public offering closed.

senses.definition: To indicate interest in the communications made by a person or organization.
senses.example: Please like this video, and subscribe to my YouTube channel.

senses.definition: To register for notifications about an event or similar.
senses.example: If you subscribe to the MouseClick event, your application can react to the user clicking the mouse.

core.definition: To sign up to receive a magazine, newspaper, or service regularly, usually by paying for it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SCRIBE. The first syllable is a reduced /səb/, not 'sub' as in 'submarine'. Pronounce the b at the end clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a normal, polite everyday verb.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'subscribe to' a newspaper, magazine, streaming service, podcast or YouTube channel, and they use it in everyday talk about buying access. On websites the button often says 'Subscribe' or 'Sign up'. Replying 'Sure, I'll subscribe' or 'I already subscribe' is natural. The same verb also means to agree with a document or opinion, but that sense is formal and rare in daily use.

distinctions.note: Sign up is broader and casual, and it can mean joining a website or an event; subscribe usually implies ongoing payment or regular delivery.
Join means becoming a member of a group or organization; subscribe means signing up for a regular publication or service.

examples.everyday: I subscribe to the local paper so I can read it with my coffee every morning.
examples.professional: Please subscribe to the team channel so you get the release updates as soon as they go out.
examples.analytical: Readers who subscribe to a journal commit themselves to a steady stream of ideas that gradually shapes how they see the field.

nuance.analogy: Like paying a monthly toll to keep a road open: you keep getting access as long as you keep paying.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subscribere, 'to write under', from sub- (under) plus scribere (to write).
common_mistakes: Using 'subscribe' with a wrong preposition. Say 'subscribe to' the magazine, not 'subscribe the magazine'.
Mispronouncing the first syllable as 'sub' with a full vowel, as in 'SUB-scribe'.

subscribe.etymology: From Middle English *subscriben*, *subskryben*, from Latin *subscrībō* (“write beneath”).

senses.definition: To sink or fall to the bottom; to settle, as lees.
To fall downward; to become lower; to descend; to sink.
To fall into a state of calm; to be calm again; to settle down; to become tranquil.
senses.example: The sea subsides.

senses.definition: To cease talking.

core.definition: To become less intense, less loud or less severe; to settle down or calm down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SIDE. The first syllable is a reduced uh, and the final d is pronounced like a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Positive, describing a return to calm or an easing of trouble.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subside in writing and in calm speech about weather, pain, anger, floods, crowds or fear. It is more formal than 'calm down' or 'die down' and is common in news reports, such as 'the storm subsided.' In casual talk, people often say 'it's dying down' or 'it's letting up' instead.

distinctions.note: Calm down is more casual and often said to a person, while subside is typically used for things like storms, pain or emotions.
Abate is more formal and literary and often used for legal or moral matters, while subside is common in everyday news and speech.

collocations: wait for the anger to subside

examples.everyday: Once the rain subsided, we finally went outside to walk the dog.
examples.professional: The outage should subside once the servers finish restarting, so let's monitor the dashboard for another ten minutes.
examples.analytical: Hume suggests that passions subside over time, though the reflective mind may decide when such a calm truly lasts.

nuance.analogy: Subside is like a wave that rolls onto the beach and gradually loses its height until the water is flat and still.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subsidere, to sink down or settle, from sub- plus sedere, to sit.
common_mistakes: Using subside with an object, as in 'subside the pain'; it is intransitive, so write 'the pain subsided.'
Confusing subside with subsidize, which means to pay money to support something.

senses.definition: Clockwise.
senses.example: Villagers danced sunwise around the stone circle at midsummer, following the path of the sun.

senses.definition: Clockwise.
senses.example: Villagers danced sunwise around the stone circle at midsummer, following the path of the sun.

core.definition: In the direction the sun appears to move, from left to right across the sky; clockwise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUN, and let the second part be a light, unstressed-sounding 'wise' with a long i. Do not say 'sun-WISE' or confuse it with 'sunrise.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a descriptive term with no emotional charge, mostly found in old texts, folklore, and ritual description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'sunwise' in ordinary speech. Today they say 'clockwise' for the same direction, as in 'turn the knob clockwise.' You will meet 'sunwise' in older books, historical accounts, some folk traditions, and descriptions of ancient monuments or ritual processions.
word_family: wise (suffix meaning in the manner of)

distinctions.note: 'Clockwise' is the everyday American word; 'sunwise' is archaic and tied to the sun's apparent motion rather than a clock face.
'Widdershins' means counterclockwise or against the sun, and is also an old and rare word, so the two are opposites in folklore contexts.

examples.professional: In the museum guide, the docent explained that the carved stones were arranged so visitors would walk sunwise around the central altar.
examples.analytical: Early medieval texts describe the procession as moving sunwise, a detail that scholars read as a symbolic alignment with the heavens.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock's hands seen from before the clock was invented, when people measured turning by the sun instead.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sunne (sun) and -wise (in the manner of), so 'in the manner of the sun.'
common_mistakes: Using 'sunwise' in modern American conversation, where 'clockwise' is expected.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'sun-WISE.'

related: wise (suffix meaning in the manner of)

senses.definition: Lying on its back.
