Of the hand, forearm or foot, turned facing toward the body or upward: with the thumb outward (palm up), or with the big toe raised relative to the little toe. A foot in the prone, normal, and supine positions.
senses.example: when one is washing one’s face, the hand is in the supine position; and then the forearm is also in the supine position; when the foot is resting on the outer side of the sole, it is in the supine position

senses.definition: Reluctant to take action due to indifference or moral weakness; apathetic or passive towards something.
senses.example: Such corruption is commonplace in a world of supine civil servants and underfunded ministries.

senses.definition: (rare, poetic) Inclining or leaning backward; inclined, sloping.
senses.example: The supine trunk of the ancient oak leaned back over the hillside.
senses.label: rare, poetic

senses.definition: In Latin and other languages: a type of verbal noun used in the ablative and accusative cases, which shares the same stem as the passive participle.
senses.example: Students learning Latin must memorize the supine alongside the infinitive and the participle.

senses.definition: In Swedish, Faroese, Icelandic and Old Norse: a verb form that combines with an inflection of ha/hafa/hava to form the present perfect and pluperfect tenses.
senses.example: In Icelandic, the supine form combines with hafa to build the present perfect tense.

core.definition: Lying flat on your back with your face and stomach facing upward.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PINE, which rhymes with 'spine' and 'line'. Do not pronounce the first syllable as 'SOO'; it is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the physical sense. The word becomes negative when used of a passive, apathetic person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use supine mainly in medical, anatomical and formal writing, such as 'position the patient supine'. In everyday speech they say 'on your back' or 'face up'. The adjective also means passive or apathetic, which is a separate, more literary sense; avoid using it casually for a person who simply lies on a couch. Its opposite is prone, meaning face down.

distinctions.note: Prone means lying face down; supine means lying face up.
Recumbent is a general word for any reclining posture; supine specifically means face-up on the back.

examples.everyday: She fell asleep supine on the couch, with her arms over her head.
examples.professional: Position the patient supine before starting the ultrasound so the abdomen is fully exposed.
examples.analytical: Anatomists describe the body as supine when lying face up, a convention that makes the curvature of the spine easier to compare across figures.

nuance.analogy: Like a beetle flipped on its back, face up to the sky.
nuance.etymology: From Latin supinus, 'lying on the back, face upward'.
common_mistakes: Confusing supine with prone; they are opposites.
Pronouncing it 'SOO-pine'. The stress falls on the second syllable.

senses.definition: Entreating with humility; supplicant.
senses.example: The suppliant villagers knelt before the king, begging for mercy after the harvest failed.

senses.definition: Supplying; auxiliary.
senses.example: The suppliant pumps kept the reservoir filled when the main system failed.

senses.definition: One who pleads or requests earnestly.
senses.example: He was a suppliant at the mayor's office, pleading for funds to repair the bridge.

core.definition: Humbly asking for something earnestly, like a person pleading for mercy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ia is pronounced as one syllable, lee, and the final -ant is weak, not a full ant vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It implies humility, sometimes servility, and sounds dignified in writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use suppliant in speech. It appears in literature, poetry, religious writing, and formal essays. In everyday English, say pleading, begging, or asking humbly. Use suppliant in writing when you want a dignified, old-fashioned tone.

distinctions.note: Supplicant is mainly a noun for the person who pleads, while suppliant is mostly an adjective describing a humble, pleading manner.
Imploring is more urgent and emotional, while suppliant emphasizes a humble posture of asking.

examples.everyday: He gave me a sort of suppliant smile when he asked if he could borrow my charger.
examples.professional: The vendor sent a suppliant email asking for one more week before the contract expires.
examples.analytical: The psalms of lament are often read as suppliant prayers, moving from distress to a plea for mercy.

nuance.analogy: Like a person kneeling before a judge with folded hands, asking for mercy instead of demanding justice.
nuance.etymology: From Latin supplicans, present participle of supplicare, 'to beg on one's knees'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it SUP-plee-ant with the i and a as two separate syllables; it is SUP-lee-uhnt.
Using suppliant for a casual request, where it sounds overly dramatic.

senses.definition: One who supplies; a provider.
Someone who assists (sets up) a goal.
senses.example: The midfielder was named supplier of the season after setting up twelve goals.

core.definition: A company or person that provides goods or materials to a business or customer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PLY, as in supply. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so do not pronounce it as ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and business-like. It is positive when the supplier is reliable and negative when deliveries fail.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, supplier is the standard word for a company that provides parts, materials, or services to another company. In everyday talk people say the place or the company that sells something. Outside business, calling someone a supplier can sound slangy or suspicious, so use vendor or provider in casual talk.

distinctions.note: A vendor usually means a seller in a commercial or contract relationship, while supplier focuses on providing goods or materials for production or resale.
Provider is broader and often used for services, such as a health care provider, while supplier is typically used for goods.
A distributor moves products to retailers, while a supplier makes or sources the product.

examples.everyday: My uncle runs a small restaurant, and he's always complaining about his produce supplier.
examples.professional: Our main supplier missed two deliveries, so we need to qualify a backup vendor this month.
examples.analytical: Porter's analysis of competitive forces treats the bargaining power of the supplier as a key factor shaping an industry's profitability.

nuance.analogy: Like a farm that delivers fresh vegetables to a restaurant kitchen every morning.
nuance.etymology: From supply, from Latin supplere, 'to fill up', with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SUP-plier; the main stress is on PLY.
Expecting supplier to mean a retail store, when it refers to the business that provides goods to the store.

senses.definition: One who or that which suspends.
senses.example: The engineer inspected each suspender cable holding up the footbridge.

senses.definition: An item of apparel consisting of a strap worn over the shoulder and used to hold up trousers.

core.definition: A strap worn over the shoulders and clipped to trousers to hold them up; usually used in the plural.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPEN. The final -er is a rhotic American r-colored vowel, and the d is clearly voiced, not a t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly old-fashioned; it can suggest a traditional or workwear style.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, suspenders are the straps that go over the shoulders and hold up pants. Most Americans use the plural form for the pair. In Britain, braces is the usual word, and suspenders there means garters for stockings, which can cause confusion when traveling.

distinctions.note: A belt wraps around the waist to hold up pants, while suspenders go over the shoulders and attach to the trousers.
Braces is the British word for the same item, so Americans would say suspenders, not braces.
Garters are bands that hold up socks or stockings, while suspenders hold up trousers.

examples.everyday: My grandfather wears suspenders with his jeans and a flannel shirt, even in July.
examples.professional: We need to add two more colors of suspenders to the spring menswear line before the buyers meet.
examples.analytical: The return of suspenders in fashion reflects a nostalgic taste for workwear and older forms of masculine style.

nuance.analogy: Suspenders hold up pants from the top, the way a clothesline holds laundry up by its hanging points.
nuance.etymology: From the verb suspend, from Latin suspendere 'to hang up', plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using the British meaning of suspenders (garters) when talking about trousers in the United States.
Saying 'a suspender' for a single item; Americans usually say 'a pair of suspenders' or just 'suspenders'.

senses.definition: The quality of being synchronous or simultaneous.
The study of a language as a complete system at a single point in time for the purpose of typological analysis, without considering its historical development or language family.
senses.example: In her synchrony analysis, the linguist described Swahili noun classes as they operate today.

core.definition: The state of occurring at the same time or moving in step; the coordination of events or movements in time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SING. The final -ny is a short 'ee' sound, not 'ay', and the middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say it quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes timing without praise or blame, and it is a technical term in science and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'synchrony' in casual speech. You will hear it in neuroscience, engineering, music, or linguistics, for example when researchers describe neurons firing in synchrony. In everyday talk, people say 'at the same time' or 'in sync', and the adjective 'synchronous' is more common.

distinctions.note: Synchronicity is the more everyday noun for things happening together and also Jung's term for meaningful coincidence; synchrony is more technical and neutral.
Simultaneity stresses two things happening at the exact same moment, while synchrony stresses coordinated timing or rhythm over time.

examples.everyday: The two kids were dancing in perfect synchrony, and their mom couldn't stop laughing.
examples.professional: Before we merge the sensor data, the model checks whether the streams show real synchrony.
examples.analytical: Many accounts of ritual argue that bodily synchrony within a congregation binds individuals into a shared community.

nuance.analogy: Like a choir singing on the same beat, synchrony means many parts moving together in time.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synchronia, 'at the same time', from syn- 'together' and chronos 'time'.
common_mistakes: Using 'synchrony' in casual talk where 'synchronicity' or 'in sync' is more natural.
Pronouncing the 'ch' with an English 'ch' sound; in the root it is a hard /k/ sound.

senses.definition: Synergy.
senses.example: The team's synergism produced results none of the individual researchers could have reached alone.

senses.definition: The theological doctrine that salvation is brought about by a combination of human will and divine grace.

core.definition: In theology, the view that salvation involves cooperation between human will and divine grace.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The middle 'er' is a weak American r-colored vowel, and the final syllable is a light 'um'. Don't pronounce it SIN-urr-jizz-em.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theological discussion; it can be contested because Protestant traditions often reject it as a doctrine of salvation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use synergism mostly in theology and religious studies. In general conversation, the word means cooperation or combined effort, but this sense is rare. Among Protestant theologians it often signals a contrast with monergism, the view that God alone works salvation.

distinctions.note: Synergy is the everyday and business term for combined effect; synergism in theology names a specific doctrine about human cooperation with grace.
Monergism holds that God alone effects salvation; synergism holds that human cooperation with grace is involved.

examples.everyday: My friend in Bible study asked whether we can cooperate with God or whether he does everything, and that question is about synergism.
examples.professional: In the seminary course, we contrasted Orthodox synergism with the Reformed view of monergism.
examples.analytical: The author argues that synergism does not diminish grace, because the human will is itself enabled by God's initiative.

nuance.analogy: Like a team effort where the coach provides the plan and the players still have to run.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synergos, working together, from syn- (together) and ergon (work).
common_mistakes: Using synergism to mean any teamwork; in theology it is a precise doctrine.
Confusing synergism with synergy, which is the general term.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word synergos means fellow worker, and Paul uses it to describe believers who work alongside God and with his servants. 1 Corinthians 3:9 says Christians are God's fellow workers. Philippians 2:12-13 tells believers to work out their salvation while affirming that God works in them. 2 Corinthians 6:1 speaks of working together with God, which theologians cite for the synergistic view.

traditions.view: Salvation involves synergy, a cooperation in which the human will freely responds to God's grace, which always comes first. Human effort is real but is enabled by grace.
Justification involves cooperation between God's grace and human free will, and the Council of Trent taught that the human will assents to and cooperates with grace.

Lutheran and Reformed theologians differ: Lutherans have often accepted a qualified synergism in the Formula of Concord, while Reformed theologians generally reject synergism in favor of monergism, the view that God alone effects regeneration.

senses.definition: Any synergistic agent.
One who holds the religious doctrine of synergism.
senses.example: The seminary professor was known as a synergist who insisted that God and human will cooperate in salvation.

senses.definition: A chemical compound that increases the chemical activity of another compound when used with it.
senses.example: Adding a synergist to the pesticide mixture greatly boosted its effect on the aphids.

core.definition: An agent or substance that works together with another to produce a combined effect greater than either would produce alone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SIN, and reduce the middle syllable to a quick 'er'. Do not say 'sin-ER-jist'; the stress stays on the first syllable as in 'synergy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes a functional role and carries no praise or blame, though in a theological setting it can be a contested label.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in chemistry, pharmacology, agriculture, and theology. In a pesticide label or pharmaceutical text, a synergist such as piperonyl butoxide boosts the effect of an active ingredient. In theology it names a person who holds the doctrine of synergism, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed, while a synergist is an agent whose main role is to increase the combined effect of another substance or force.
Enhancer is a general, everyday word for anything that improves something, while synergist is technical and implies a combined effect beyond the sum of parts.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says adding a little lemon juice is a synergist for the garlic in her sauce, because the two flavors make each other stronger.
examples.professional: The formulation team tested a new synergist to see whether it would boost the efficacy of the active ingredient at a lower dose.
examples.analytical: Some theologians describe grace and human effort as synergists in salvation, though others argue that grace alone is the decisive cause.

nuance.analogy: Think of a synergist as a good dance partner: each makes the other look better than either would alone.
nuance.etymology: From Greek synergos, 'working together', from syn- 'together' and ergon 'work'.
common_mistakes: Confusing synergist (the agent) with synergy (the effect), as in 'the two drugs are a synergist' when 'synergy' or 'a synergist' is meant depending on the sentence.
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'sin-ER-jist'.

traditions.view: Human cooperation with divine grace is affirmed, often called synergy; the human will freely responds to God's grace without earning salvation, a view shaped by Gregory Palamas and later Orthodox theology.
Grace comes first and makes free cooperation possible; human acts done in grace have real merit, and the Council of Trent taught that the sinner cooperates with grace in justification.

Lutheran and Reformed Christians disagree. Reformed theology teaches monergism, that God alone effects regeneration, while the Formula of Concord rejected the Synergistic position of Philippists who gave human will a role in conversion.

senses.definition: The act of systematizing.
A systematic organization.

core.definition: The process of arranging things into a fixed, orderly system or method, or the organized structure that results.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'ZAY', so 'shun' is a reduced ending, not a separate strong syllable. The vowels before the stress are all reduced to a schwa, so each 'uh' should be very light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process of organizing, which is usually seen as positive, but it can sound bureaucratic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in academic, legal and business writing about turning scattered material into a coherent scheme. It is heavier than everyday words like 'organizing' or 'sorting,' so in casual talk people would say 'getting everything in order.' It appears more in philosophy, law and research than in workplace chatter.

distinctions.note: Standardization makes things conform to a common norm or size; systematization builds an organized, interconnected structure.
Categorization sorts items into classes; systematization creates the whole scheme that shows how the classes relate.

examples.everyday: She spent all Sunday on the systematization of her recipe box, sorting everything by season and then by cuisine.
examples.professional: The systematization of our onboarding documents cut the number of new-hire questions in half.
examples.analytical: Hegel's project was the systematization of all knowledge into a single, self-developing philosophical system.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of scattered tools that finally gets a labeled pegboard, with each tool in a place that shows how it fits with the others.
nuance.etymology: From 'systematize' (from 'system,' Greek systēma, 'organized whole') plus the suffix '-ation'.
common_mistakes: Using it for ordinary tidying up, where 'organizing' is more natural.
Spelling it 'systematisation', which is the British form.
Stressing the wrong syllable, like 'sis-tuh-MAT-uh-ZAY-shun'.

senses.definition: To request or accept a rain check (an agreement from a merchant to honor a special offer, temporarily unavailable, after the expiration date).
senses.example: I'll take a rain check on the sale, since the tablets are sold out.

senses.definition: In social interactions, to request a deferred invitation, as a polite way to turn down an engagement, usually with the implication that one is simply postponing it and another time might be acceptable.
senses.example: I can't go with you to the museum this Saturday, but can I take a rain check?

core.definition: To postpone an invitation politely, saying you will accept it at another time instead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on CHEK, and the r in rain is strongly pronounced in American speech. Keep the ch sound clear, as in check.

nuance.connotation: Polite and friendly. It declines without rejecting the person.
nuance.usage_note: The phrase comes from ticket stubs for rained-out games that let you attend later, and Americans now use it for declining social plans. Say 'Can I take a rain check?' or 'Let's take a rain check on dinner.' A natural reply is 'Sure, just let me know when you're free.'

distinctions.note: Decline is a final refusal; take a rain check suggests you still hope to do it later.
Postpone is more formal and used for scheduled events; take a rain check is casual and used for social invitations.

collocations: take a rain check on dinner

examples.everyday: Thanks for the invite, but I'm wiped out tonight, so can I take a rain check?
examples.professional: I can't join the Thursday review, so let's take a rain check and find a time next week.
examples.analytical: The idiom preserves a commercial origin, since a rain check kept a claim on a canceled event for a later date, which signals hope rather than refusal.

nuance.analogy: Like a claim ticket for a coat you cannot pick up today but can collect later.
nuance.etymology: American English, from the ticket stubs issued for rained-out baseball games that allowed a later attendance.
common_mistakes: Using rain check as a noun to mean a refusal, when it implies a postponed acceptance.
Saying take the rain check, with the article, which is less natural than a rain check or just take a rain check.

conversation.text: Can I take a rain check on drinks? I'm exhausted.
I'll have to take a rain check on lunch today; something came up.
She took a rain check on the movie because her kid was sick.

senses.definition: Synonym of take control, especially in situations involving informal command over a group of people.
senses.example: When the manager left, Rosa quickly took charge of the nervous new hires.

core.definition: To assume control of a situation or group and direct what happens next.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on CHARGE, which rhymes with 'large' and has a clear American r. Learners often say 'CHARJ' with a short vowel, but American speech uses an open 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes confidence, initiative, and leadership, especially in a crisis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in workplaces, families, and emergencies when someone steps forward to lead. It is often used in praise, as in 'She really took charge.' A natural reply to 'Someone needs to take charge' is 'I can do it.'

distinctions.note: Be in charge describes a state of authority; take charge describes the action of assuming it.
Take control is broader and can describe taking control of a machine or a situation; take charge emphasizes leading people.
Lead focuses on guiding and inspiring others; take charge focuses on stepping in to direct things, often in a crisis.

examples.everyday: When the power went out, my dad took charge and found the flashlights.
examples.professional: Since our tech lead left, Priya has taken charge of the migration project.
examples.analytical: Weber's account of charismatic authority describes leaders who take charge in moments of crisis and win followers through their perceived gifts.

nuance.analogy: Like grabbing the steering wheel when the driver freezes.
nuance.etymology: Charge comes from Old French charger 'to load', from Latin carricare 'to load a wagon'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'take the charge' when the idiom is normally 'take charge' without an article.
Using 'take charge to' instead of 'take charge of' when an object follows.
Mispronouncing charge with a soft 'j' sound and a short vowel.

senses.definition: A cafe or restaurant that serves tea, usually with light food.
A public lavatory.
senses.example: The old park teahouse was the only public restroom within half a mile.

senses.definition: A meeting place for gay men.
senses.example: In the 1950s, the teahouse was a quiet meeting place for gay men in the city.

core.definition: A cafe or restaurant where tea is the main drink, usually also serving light food or snacks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say 'house' with the normal American 'ow' diphthong, ending with a /s/ sound. The noun 'houses' is pronounced with a /z/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; a teahouse suggests a calm, relaxed place to talk or rest.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'teahouse' usually refers to a tea shop that serves Chinese, Japanese or other Asian-style teas, or a cafe focused on loose-leaf tea. Americans may also use 'tearoom' for a more formal place with afternoon tea. Older dictionary senses such as a public lavatory or a meeting place for gay men are archaic or slang and should not be used.

distinctions.note: A tearoom usually serves formal afternoon tea with sandwiches and scones; a teahouse is more casual and focused on the tea itself.
A cafe is usually coffee-focused; a teahouse is centered on tea, often with a menu of many loose-leaf varieties.

examples.everyday: Let's meet at that teahouse on Main Street; their jasmine tea is great and the seating is quiet.
examples.professional: We hold our client check-ins at a teahouse near the office, which makes the conversation feel more relaxed.
examples.analytical: The traditional Japanese teahouse, with its deliberate simplicity, embodies aesthetic ideals of restraint and attention to the present moment.

nuance.analogy: A teahouse is like a living room that is open to the public, where people sit, talk and take their time.
nuance.etymology: Formed from tea and house.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words 'tea house' in formal writing; the standard form is one word.
Using 'teahouse' for a formal afternoon tea in a hotel, which Americans would call a tearoom.

senses.definition: A person who can function effectively with others in a group, sharing information and striving towards a common goal.
senses.example: She is a real team player, always sharing her notes and helping the group hit deadlines.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see team,‎ player.

core.definition: A person who works well with others, sharing information and credit and supporting a shared goal.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, 'team' carries the main stress and 'player' is lighter. The final syllable is a reduced 'er', not 'ur' as in 'bird'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a compliment at work and in sports, but it can sound like a cliché in job interviews if used without an example.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase to praise someone who puts the group first, often in performance reviews, job descriptions and coaching talk. You will hear 'She's a real team player' or 'We need a team player for this role.' A natural reply is 'Yes, I like working with people who share credit.'

distinctions.note: A team player works well within a group; a team leader directs the group and is responsible for its results.
A self-starter works independently and needs little direction; a team player focuses on collaboration with others.

collocations: show that you're a team player

examples.everyday: My brother is a real team player, so he always helps when the neighborhood cleans up.
examples.professional: We need a team player for this project, someone who shares credit and asks for help early.
examples.analytical: The ideal of the team player can mask a demand for conformity, rewarding agreement over honest dissent.

nuance.analogy: A team player is like a good sous chef: the dish succeeds because they make everyone else's job easier, not because they take the spotlight.
nuance.etymology: A compound of team (from Old English tēam) and player (from play, Old English plega).
common_mistakes: Omitting the article: saying 'He is team player' instead of 'He is a team player'.
Using 'team player' as a verb or as the name of an action; it is only a noun phrase.

senses.definition: A paint in which the pigments are suspended in a water-soluble emulsion, such as of egg yolk or gelatine, which hardens and becomes insoluble on exposure to air.
senses.example: She mixed egg yolk with powdered pigment to make tempera for her icon panels.

senses.definition: The artistic technique of painting in this medium.
senses.example: Her art history seminar focused on tempera, comparing it with oil painting from the fifteenth century.

senses.definition: A painting done in this medium.
senses.example: The gallery's tempera by Duccio glowed with gold leaf and deep blue.

core.definition: A paint made by mixing pigment with egg yolk or another water-based binder, used especially in painting and art.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'ruh', not 'rah', and do not stress the ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term used in art, art history and conservation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tempera' mainly in art classes, museums and art history, while most people just say 'paint' or 'acrylic' in everyday speech. When talking about a painting, you would say 'It's done in egg tempera' or 'a tempera painting'. The word can name the paint, the technique or the finished work, so context tells you which.

distinctions.note: Acrylic is a modern synthetic paint that dries quickly and is plastic-based, while tempera is older, water-based and bound with egg or a similar emulsion.
Oil paint uses drying oil as its binder and dries slowly, while tempera dries fast and gives a thin, matte finish.

examples.everyday: My daughter's art class uses tempera paint, so the kitchen table is covered in it.
examples.professional: The conservator said the panel was painted in egg tempera, so we need to avoid solvents when cleaning it.
examples.analytical: Early Italian panel paintings show how the layered transparency of egg tempera gave artists their luminous flesh tones.

nuance.analogy: Like a smooth emulsion in a salad dressing, the pigment is held in the egg yolk so it spreads evenly and dries in a thin, matte layer.
nuance.etymology: From Italian tempera, from Latin temperare, 'to mix in proper proportion'.
common_mistakes: Calling all water-based paint 'tempera'; the term means paint bound with egg or a similar emulsion.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being tenacious, or persistence of purpose; tenaciousness.
senses.example: Her tenacity in chasing grant funding eventually kept the lab's doors open.

senses.definition: The quality of bodies which keeps them from parting without considerable force, as distinguished from brittleness, fragility, mobility, etc.
senses.example: Materials scientists measured the tenacity of the polymer to see how much force it needed to break apart.

senses.definition: The effect of this attraction, cohesiveness.
senses.example: The tenacity of the water droplets kept them clinging to the leaf despite the wind.

senses.definition: The quality of bodies which makes them adhere to other bodies; adhesiveness, viscosity.
senses.example: Engineers tested the tenacity of the glue on wet surfaces before approving it for construction.

senses.definition: The greatest longitudinal stress a substance can bear without tearing asunder, usually expressed with reference to a unit area of the cross section of the substance, as the number of pounds per square inch, or kilograms per square centimeter, necessary to produce rupture.
senses.example: The tenacity of the cable, measured in newtons per square millimeter, exceeded the design specifications.

core.definition: Determination and persistence in holding onto a goal, opinion, or effort, even when it is difficult.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'NAS', and the second syllable is reduced to a schwa. The final syllable is a light 'tee', and the 'a' in the middle is short, as in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises determination, though it can sound like obstinacy in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tenacity in workplace praise, sports, and personal achievement, such as 'It took tenacity to finish the marathon.' It is a formal word for everyday talk. Casual speakers often say 'grit' or 'determination'.

distinctions.note: Persistence is continued effort over time; tenacity adds a sense of strong grip and resistance to giving up.
Grit is informal and emphasizes courage and endurance; tenacity is more formal and focuses on holding firm.
Stubbornness is refusal to change, often negative; tenacity is usually positive.

collocations: tenacity in the face of adversity

examples.everyday: Your tenacity with that puzzle is impressive; I would have given up an hour ago.
examples.professional: Her tenacity in following up on the data quality issue is why the project is finally on schedule.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's account of faith displays a kind of tenacity in holding a paradox that reason alone cannot resolve.

nuance.analogy: Tenacity is like a root that keeps a tree standing through storms: it holds on whatever the weather does.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tenacitas, 'holding fast', from tenax, from tenere 'to hold'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as 'te-NAS-i-ty'.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'tie' rather than 'tee'.
Using tenacity for physical grip only, when it mostly describes mental or moral persistence.

senses.definition: A projecting member left by cutting away the wood around it, and made to insert into a mortise, and in this way secure together the parts of a frame.
senses.example: The carpenter cut a tenon on the end of each rail so it would fit snugly into the mortise.

senses.definition: To make into a tenon.
senses.example: First we'll tenon this part, then we'll make a mortise that will fit it on that part.

senses.definition: To fit with tenons.
senses.example: Before gluing the table frame, he tenoned each leg into the apron for extra strength.

core.definition: A wooden projection cut to fit into a matching hole, called a mortise, to join two pieces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'un', not 'ohn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in woodworking and carpentry.
nuance.usage_note: Woodworkers and carpenters use 'tenon' every day, usually paired with 'mortise' as in 'mortise and tenon joint'. Ordinary people rarely use it, and they would say 'joint' or 'connection' instead. Americans who work with furniture or timber frames will know the word right away.

distinctions.note: A mortise is the hole cut into wood; a tenon is the matching projection that fits into it.
A dowel is a separate wooden pin used for joining; a tenon is cut from the same piece of wood.

examples.everyday: The chair legs were held together with a tenon, so it doesn't wobble.
examples.professional: The timber framer cut each tenon by hand to fit the mortise in the post.
examples.analytical: The strength of the frame depends on the precision of the tenon, since the joint must bear load without glue alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a puzzle piece cut to slide into its matching slot, the tenon locks two pieces of wood together.
nuance.etymology: From Old French tenon, from tenir 'to hold'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'tenon' with 'tennon' or 'tenant' (a renter).
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ohn'.

tenon.etymology: From Middle English *tenoun*, *tenown*, *tenon*, from Anglo-Norman *tenoun*, from Old French *tenon*.

senses.definition: A block of the Earth's crust that differs from the surrounding material, and is separated from it by faults.

core.definition: A large block of Earth's crust with its own geological history, separated from neighboring rock by faults.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and say it exactly like 'terrain.' Geologists use the same pronunciation for both words, though their meanings differ.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in geology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'terrane' in geology, tectonics, and earth science, especially when discussing mountain belts or the western United States. It is not used in everyday conversation. In a general sense you would say 'a block of rock' or 'a rock formation' for non-specialists.

distinctions.note: A terrain is the visible surface of land, while a terrane is a deep block of crust defined by its geological history and its boundaries.
A tectonic plate is a whole large slab of lithosphere, while a terrane is a smaller fragment that was often accreted onto a larger landmass.

examples.everyday: On the hike, the ranger said the rock on this ridge is a different terrane from the valley below.
examples.professional: The geologic map marks three terranes, each with a different fault boundary and a separate depositional history.
examples.analytical: The accreted terrane shows how the coastline grew through the collision of oceanic blocks over millions of years.

nuance.analogy: Like puzzle pieces of crust that were pushed together over time, each with its own history and seam.
nuance.etymology: Shares its origin with terrain, from Latin terrenum 'earth, ground.'
common_mistakes: Using 'terrane' to mean the visible surface of land, which is the meaning of 'terrain.'
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: (historical) Of or related to a tetrarchy, particularly the era of Diocletian and his three coemperors in Late Antiquity.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Relating to a tetrarchy, a government in which four people share power, especially Diocletian's system in the Roman Empire.

pronunciation.tip: The stress shifts from the first syllable of the noun 'TET-rahr-kee' to the second syllable of the adjective, 'teh-TRAHR-kik'. The 'ar' is r-colored in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tetrarchic almost only in classical history, ancient studies and biblical history. Most people would not use it in everyday talk. When you discuss the Roman Empire, say 'the tetrarchic system' or 'the rule of four emperors'.

distinctions.note: Monarchic describes rule by one person; tetrarchic describes shared rule by four people.
Triumviral describes rule by three people, as in the Roman triumvirates; tetrarchic describes rule by four.

examples.everyday: My history podcast explained how Diocletian's tetrarchic arrangement shared power among four rulers.
examples.professional: The museum exhibit on late Roman coins includes several tetrarchic portraits of the emperors.
examples.analytical: Diocletian's tetrarchic settlement tried to solve succession and frontier defense at once, though its unity faded soon after his retirement.

nuance.analogy: A tetrarchic government is like four co-owners running one company, each responsible for a different division.
nuance.etymology: From tetrarchy, with the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Using tetrarchic for tetrahedral, which is a shape term.
Stressing the first syllable (TET-rar-kick) rather than the second.
nuance.biblical_note: The New Testament calls Herod Antipas a tetrarch, Greek tetrarchēs, meaning a ruler of a fourth part of a region. Matthew 14:1 describes Herod the tetrarch hearing about Jesus. Luke 3:1 names Herod as tetrarch of Galilee. Luke 9:7 reports that Herod the tetrarch heard all that was done.

senses.definition: The land ruled by such a government, either together or separately.
senses.example: The tetrarchy covered Galilee and Perea, lands that were divided among several minor rulers.

senses.definition: (historical) A government where power is shared by four people, especially the Herodian tetrarchy established in Judea after the death of Herod and the Tetrarchy of Diocletian which ruled the Roman Empire in the years 293-313.
senses.example: Historians debate whether the tetrarchy of Diocletian truly stabilized the Roman Empire.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A government in which power is shared among four rulers, or the territory such a ruler governs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The 'ar' is r-colored, and the final '-chy' is pronounced 'kee', not 'chee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a specialized historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tetrarchy mainly in history classes, scholarship on ancient Rome and studies of the New Testament. It is rare in everyday speech. Use it to describe Diocletian's system or the divided rule of Herod's territories.

distinctions.note: A monarchy is rule by one person; a tetrarchy is rule by four people sharing power.
A triumvirate is rule by three people; a tetrarchy is rule by four.

examples.everyday: We watched a documentary about Rome, and the narrator said the empire had a tetrarchy for a while.
examples.professional: The conference paper compares the Roman tetrarchy with modern power-sharing agreements among four regional governments.
examples.analytical: Diocletian's tetrarchy was an ingenious attempt at power-sharing, yet its reliance on personal loyalty undermined its stability.

nuance.analogy: A tetrarchy is like a four-person leadership team in which each leader holds a region and the team must cooperate to keep the whole company together.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tetrarkhia, 'rule of a fourth part', from tetra- 'four' and arkhein 'to rule'.
common_mistakes: Confusing tetrarchy with monarchy, which means rule by one person.
Pronouncing the final '-chy' as /tʃi/ instead of /ki/.
nuance.biblical_note: The New Testament refers to Herod Antipas as tetrarch, Greek tetrarchēs, meaning ruler of a fourth part, and his territory of Galilee and Perea was a tetrarchy. Matthew 14:1 and Luke 3:1 describe Herod in this role. Luke 9:7 reports Herod hearing of Jesus's deeds.

tetrarchy.etymology: From Latin *tetrarchia*, from Ancient Greek *τετραρχία*, from *τετρα-* (“four”) + *-αρχία* (“-archy: rule”), equivalent to *tetra-* + *-archy*.

senses.definition: Introduces something you just remembered.

core.definition: Used to introduce something you just remembered while talking, often to change topics or add a related thought.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MINDZ, and 'me' reduces to a quick 'mih'. In fast speech the d in 'reminds' is often dropped, so it sounds closer to 'ree-MINES'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is friendly and casual, with no emotional charge, and it signals that you are shifting to a related thought.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this constantly mid-conversation, as in 'Oh, that reminds me, did you send the invoice?' It is fine with colleagues in informal talk, but in a formal presentation say 'I also need to mention'. A natural reply is 'Oh right, thanks for the reminder.'

distinctions.note: Reminisce means talking fondly about past experiences, while this phrase simply shifts to a new related thought.
Add 'of' plus a noun when something resembles or recalls another thing: 'That reminds me of my trip to Maine.'

collocations: that reminds me, by the way

examples.everyday: Oh, that reminds me, do you still have my phone charger?
examples.professional: Thanks for the dashboard update. That reminds me, can we add the latency metric to Thursday's review?
examples.analytical: That reminds me that Anselm's ontological argument rests on a contested assumption about whether existence can be treated as a predicate.

nuance.analogy: Like a browser tab that pops up when you remember you left it open.
nuance.etymology: Remind comes from re- (again) plus mind, meaning to bring something back to mind.
common_mistakes: Placing 'me' incorrectly, as in 'That reminds to me'; the correct order is 'That reminds me to'.
Saying 'That reminds me of' without a noun after 'of'; 'of' needs an object such as 'a trip' or 'my mother'.

conversation.text: That reminds me, I still owe you twenty bucks.
"We went to the zoo yesterday." "Oh, that reminds me, the kids want to go too."
That reminds me, did you ever finish that book?

senses.definition: Having little thickness or extent from one surface to its opposite.
senses.example: thin plate of metal; thin paper; thin board; thin covering

senses.definition: Very narrow in all diameters; having a cross section that is small in all directions.
senses.example: thin wire; thin string

senses.definition: Having little body fat or flesh; slim; slender; lean; gaunt.
senses.example: thin person

senses.definition: Of low viscosity or low specific gravity.
senses.example: Water is thinner than honey.

senses.definition: Scarce; not close, crowded, or numerous; not filling the space.
senses.example: The trees of a forest are thin; the corn or grass is thin.

senses.definition: Describing a poorly played golf shot where the ball is struck by the bottom part of the club head. See fat, shank, toe.
senses.example: He hit a thin iron that skipped along the grass and ended in the water.

senses.definition: Lacking body or volume; small; feeble; not full.
senses.example: a thin, tight-lipped smile

senses.definition: Slight; small; slender; flimsy; superficial; inadequate; not sufficient for a covering.
senses.example: a thin disguise

senses.definition: Of a route: relatively little used.
senses.example: We took a thin road through the hills that few tourists ever bother to find.

senses.definition: Poor; scanty; without money or success.
senses.example: Their thin savings barely covered rent, so they skipped every dinner out.

senses.definition: A loss or tearing of paper from the back of a stamp, although not sufficient to create a complete hole.
senses.example: The collector rejected the stamp because it had a thin along its back.

senses.definition: Any food produced or served in thin slices.
senses.example: chocolate mint thins

senses.definition: To make thin or thinner.
senses.example: Winter rain thinned the crowds along the beach until only a few joggers remained.

senses.definition: To become thin or thinner.
senses.example: The crowds thinned after the procession had passed: there was nothing more to see.

senses.definition: To dilute.
senses.example: She thinned the paint with turpentine before brushing on the first coat.

senses.definition: To remove some plants or parts of plants in order to improve the growth of what remains.
senses.example: In late spring, the gardener thinned the carrots so each one had room to grow.

senses.definition: Not thickly or closely; in a scattered state.
senses.example: seed sown thin

core.definition: Having little distance between two opposite surfaces, or having little body fat; slim, narrow, or not dense.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short vowel, as in 'sit,' and keep the final n clear. Do not add a vowel after it, and do not confuse it with 'thing' (ending in ng).

nuance.connotation: Neutral for objects and food, and positive or neutral for people, since 'thin' can suggest fitness. It becomes negative when it suggests weakness or sickness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'thin' for both physical objects and people, but for a person they often prefer 'slim' or 'slender' as more polite. Calling someone 'too thin' can imply illness or eating problems, so be careful. For paper and food, 'thin' is perfectly natural, as in 'thin crust pizza.'

distinctions.note: 'Slim' is a positive word for a person's body; 'thin' is more neutral and can sound like a criticism if said of someone's health.
'Narrow' refers to width from side to side; 'thin' refers to the smallest dimension between two surfaces.
'Dilute' is the verb for making a liquid weaker by adding water; 'thin' describes a liquid that flows easily or has been made less dense.

examples.everyday: Could you cut the onions thin? I like them almost see-through on my burger.
examples.professional: The new panel is thin enough to fit behind the display, but it still meets the stiffness requirement.
examples.analytical: A thin reading of the parable misses its social critique, since the text is not only about individual virtue but about the community's obligations.

nuance.analogy: A thin layer of frosting covers a cake without weighing it down; it is noticeable, but it adds little bulk.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'thynne,' meaning not thick or dense, from a Germanic root.
common_mistakes: Using 'thin' for a person's body in polite conversation without care; 'slim' or 'slender' is more appropriate.
Confusing 'thin' with 'thing' by dropping the t or ending the word in ng.

thin.etymology: From Middle English *thinne*, *thenne*, *thünne*, from Old English *þynne*, from **þunnī*, from Proto-Germanic **þunnuz* (“thin”) – compare **þanjaną* (“to stretch, spread out”) – from Proto-Indo-European **ténh₂us* (“thin”), from **ten-* (“to…

senses.definition: Doubting Thomas: a person who refuses to believe something without proof.

core.definition: Thomas the Apostle, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus, called Didymus, known in John's Gospel for doubting the Resurrection until he sees Jesus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'TAH-mus', not 'tah-MAS'. The th is voiceless as in 'think'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; as a common name it is neutral, but 'doubting Thomas' is a mildly negative phrase for someone who refuses to believe without proof.
nuance.usage_note: Thomas is a common English first name in the United States. In church and Bible study it refers to the apostle, and people commonly speak of 'doubting Thomas' as an idiom for a skeptic who needs evidence.

distinctions.note: A different Thomas, a 13th-century theologian, not one of the Twelve.

examples.everyday: My friend Thomas is a bit of a doubting Thomas, so he wants to see the proof before he believes a rumor.
examples.professional: In the leadership training, we used the story of Thomas to talk about asking for evidence before committing to a plan.
examples.analytical: John 20:24-29 presents Thomas as the disciple who demands physical evidence, and his confession 'My Lord and my God' is one of the strongest christological statements in the Gospel.

nuance.analogy: Like a skeptical auditor who insists on seeing the books before signing off.
nuance.etymology: From Aramaic te'oma, meaning 'twin', which is also the sense of Greek Didymos.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'tom-AS'.
Pronouncing th as a d, as in 'Tomas'.
nuance.biblical_note: Thomas is one of the Twelve apostles, named Didymus (the Twin) in John's Gospel. He appears in John 11:16 (willing to go to Jerusalem with Jesus), John 14:5 (asking how they can know the way), and John 20:24-29 (doubting until he sees the risen Jesus, then confessing 'My Lord and my God'). Thomas is also listed among the Twelve in Acts 1:13.

thomas.etymology: Middle English *Thomas*, from Latin *Thōmās*, from Ancient Greek *Θωμᾶς*, the Biblical Greek transcription of Aramaic *תאומא* or *תאמא* (“twin”), the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles.

senses.definition: An act of turning around a car, involving one forward turn and two backward turns (or vice-versa).
senses.example: I practiced a three-point turn in the empty parking lot before my driving test.

core.definition: A maneuver for reversing a car in a narrow space by turning forward and backward in three moves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TURN, with secondary stress on three and point. The r in turn is strong in American English, so do not drop it and do not say tuhn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a practical driving term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use three-point turn in driving instruction, road talk, and everyday conversation about cars. It is a common term in driver's education, and people also say do a three-point turn when a road is too narrow for a U-turn. It is not a metaphor in everyday use, though it can be used that way in writing.

distinctions.note: A U-turn is one continuous turn in the road, while a three-point turn uses forward and backward moves in a narrow space.

examples.everyday: I had to make a three-point turn on that narrow road to get back to the house.
examples.professional: The fleet manager told the drivers to practice a three-point turn in the lot before taking the trucks onto public roads.
examples.analytical: The three-point turn is a useful image for reversing course without a full stop, though it still requires forward and backward moves.

nuance.analogy: Like folding a fitted sheet: you move the car back and forth in small steps until the whole car faces the other way.
nuance.etymology: English compound of three, point and turn, referring to the three movements used in the maneuver.
common_mistakes: Calling the maneuver a U-turn, which is a different movement on a road.
Dropping the r in turn, which makes the word sound like tun or tuhn in American speech.

senses.definition: To hit (someone or something) hard, especially with a flat implement or a stick; to thrash, to whack.
To drive or force (someone or something) by, or as if by, beating or hitting; to knock.
senses.example: The wind thwacked the loose shutters against the siding until the nails gave way.

senses.definition: To pack (people or things) closely together; to cram.
senses.example: The organizers thwacked two hundred guests into a room meant for eighty.

senses.definition: To decisively defeat (someone) in a contest; to beat, to thrash.
senses.example: Our underdog team thwacked the defending champions three to nothing in the final.

senses.definition: To fall down hard with a thump.
senses.example: He slipped on the icy steps and thwacked onto the sidewalk with a groan.

senses.definition: An act of hitting hard, especially with a flat implement or a stick; a whack; also, a powerful stroke involved in such hitting; a blow, a strike.
senses.example: A sharp thwack on the back of the head sent the toddler running for the couch.

senses.definition: A dull or heavy slapping sound.
senses.example: Over the fence came the thwack of a tennis ball against a wooden racket.

senses.definition: Used to represent the dull or heavy sound of someone or something being hit or slapped.
senses.example: She swatted the screen door, and it went thwack against the frame.

core.definition: To hit something or someone hard, usually with a flat object or stick, making a sharp, dull sound; to whack.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a voiceless th followed by a clear w. Do not drop the w and say tak; start with a quick th-w sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it suggests a forceful, noisy blow, sometimes playful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thwack for a hard, sharp hit, often in casual or storytelling contexts, such as 'He thwacked the ball with his bat.' As a noun it describes the sound. It sounds vivid and informal, so use hit or strike in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Whack is more common and casual and can also mean a share; thwack emphasizes the sharp sound of the blow.
Smack often suggests a slap or a quick hit with an open hand, while thwack suggests a heavier blow with an object.

examples.everyday: My brother thwacked a tennis ball over the fence, and the neighbors all laughed.
examples.professional: The technician thwacked the stuck valve with a rubber mallet during the site walk.
examples.analytical: Each ball in a Newton's cradle makes a thwack as it strikes the next, which illustrates conservation of momentum.

nuance.analogy: A thwack is like a bat meeting a baseball squarely: the sound is sharp and the contact is solid.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of the sound of a blow.
common_mistakes: Dropping the w and saying tak instead of thwak
Using thwack in formal writing where hit or strike is more appropriate

senses.definition: A period of time where one is not required to work.
senses.example: I've got some time off next week, so maybe we could meet up then?

core.definition: A period when you are not required to work, such as a vacation, a day off or a sick day.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on off, which has the vowel of 'saw' or 'cot,' since many American speakers merge these vowels. Keep the final f clearly voiceless and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive. The phrase suggests rest, relief and something pleasant, although requesting it can sometimes feel stressful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use time off in everyday talk and at work to mean any period away from the job, such as vacation, personal days or sick leave. People often say take time off, and many companies offer paid time off, called PTO. A natural reply is 'Enjoy it!' or 'Have a great trip!'

distinctions.note: A vacation is a trip or planned holiday, while time off is any period of not working, including sick days or personal days.
Leave is more formal and official, used for specific types of absence such as medical leave or family leave.
A break is usually shorter, such as a lunch break, while time off covers longer periods away from work.

examples.everyday: I'm taking some time off next week to visit my parents in Ohio.
examples.professional: Please submit your time-off request in the HR portal at least two weeks before the trip.
examples.analytical: The ethics of time off turns on whether rest is treated as a right that workers hold or a privilege that employers grant.

nuance.analogy: Time off is like a pause button for the work week, letting you step away so the rest of your life can continue.
nuance.etymology: From time and off, from Old English of, meaning away from.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make time off' or 'do a time off'; the usual verb is take.
Pluralizing it as 'time offs'; the noun is normally uncountable, as in 'some time off.'

senses.definition: Agent noun of tinker; one who tinkers with things.
senses.example: My grandfather was a tinkerer who rebuilt clocks, radios, and old lawnmowers in his garage.

senses.definition: A meddler.
senses.example: Our manager is a tinkerer who keeps changing the schedule after we've already finalized it.

core.definition: A person who enjoys experimenting with and improving machines, gadgets or ideas, often by hand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The last two syllables are both reduced, so the word ends in a soft r-colored sound, not 'ear' or 'air'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It admires someone who builds, fixes or experiments with things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often call hobbyists tinkerers, especially people who build or repair things in a garage or workshop. It is a warm, admiring word. In technical circles, hacker can mean something similar, but tinkerer is more everyday.

distinctions.note: An inventor creates a new device or process, often with a patent; a tinkerer experiments with and improves existing things.
An engineer uses formal training and systematic methods; a tinkerer works by hands-on trial and error.
A meddler interferes in other people's affairs; a tinkerer meddles with objects, which is usually positive.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a tinkerer who fixes every old radio he finds at a yard sale.
examples.professional: We need a couple of tinkerers on the team to prototype the idea before we commit to a design.
examples.analytical: The philosopher was a tinkerer of concepts, testing definitions until they worked in practice.

nuance.analogy: A tinkerer is like a home cook who keeps adjusting the recipe until it tastes right.
nuance.etymology: Agent noun formed from the verb tinker and the suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'ear' instead of a soft r-colored sound
Using tinkerer for a formally trained engineer, which may sound unintentionally dismissive

senses.definition: Relevant or pertinent; succinct; specific. (The article "the" may be replaced by a possessive form denoting whose point is being acknowledged.)
senses.example: His letter was short and to the point.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see to,‎ point.
senses.example: confident to the point of imperiousness

core.definition: Relevant and direct, with no unnecessary words, detours or irrelevant details.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'point', with a diphthong that starts with an open o, sounding like 'poyn-t'. The final t is lightly released, and 'to the' reduces quickly in speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises clear, efficient communication.
nuance.usage_note: Americans praise an email, speech or answer as 'to the point' when it is brief and clear. 'Let's get to the point' is a common way to start a meeting or move a rambling conversation forward. Saying 'Get to the point!' can sound impatient, so a softer form is 'Let me get to the point.'

distinctions.note: 'Concise' describes brevity alone; 'to the point' also means relevant to the topic at hand.
'Blunt' suggests harshness of tone; 'to the point' is neutral to positive and need not be rude.

examples.everyday: Your text was short and to the point, which I really appreciate.
examples.professional: Her status update was to the point: the release is delayed two days because a key test failed.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's definitions are to the point, stripping away rhetorical ornament to isolate the essential features of a thing.

nuance.analogy: Like an arrow flying straight to the target rather than curving around the field.
nuance.etymology: 'Point' comes from Latin punctum, 'a prick, a dot', via Old French; the phrase means reaching the central matter.
common_mistakes: Thinking 'to the point' means rude or sharp; it is usually positive, though 'get to the point' can sound impatient.
Dropping the article as in 'to point'; the standard phrase is 'to the point'.

senses.definition: An establishment, such as a shop or display, where tourists are encouraged to spend money on goods or services not necessarily of good value.
senses.example: The shop by the pier was a tourist trap, charging twelve dollars for ordinary seashell keychains.

core.definition: A place or shop that charges tourists high prices for goods or services of poor value.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word TRAP most strongly, and say the first word as a reduced TOOR-ist with a clear r. The middle syllable of tourist is often reduced to a quick schwa sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies overpriced or low-quality places designed to exploit visitors.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in everyday travel conversation to warn friends about overpriced places near famous landmarks. It is casual and common in guidebooks and reviews. Saying a place is a tourist trap is a mild criticism, so it fits casual talk well but may sound rude if used about a friend's favorite spot.

distinctions.note: A tourist attraction is a popular sight that is often worth visiting, while a tourist trap is overpriced or poor value.
A scam is deliberate fraud, whereas a tourist trap is usually legal but overpriced or disappointing.

collocations: a tourist trap near the pier

examples.everyday: Skip that restaurant by the pier; it's a tourist trap with frozen food and huge prices.
examples.professional: Our travel team warns clients to avoid tourist traps when planning corporate retreats.
examples.analytical: The author argues that tourist traps reveal how commerce can hollow out the authenticity of a place.

nuance.analogy: Like a bait shop that sells you the same lure at triple price, a tourist trap relies on visitors not knowing better.
nuance.etymology: Tourist from tour, plus trap, from an Old English word for a snare.
common_mistakes: Writing "tourists trap" with an extra s on tourist.
Using the phrase for any popular attraction; it specifically implies poor value.

conversation.text: That restaurant is a total tourist trap; the food's overpriced.
Skip the gift shop by the pier; it's a tourist trap.
Times Square is kind of a tourist trap, but you have to see it once.

senses.definition: To change or convert one thing to another, or from one state or form to another.
senses.example: The alchemists tried to transmute base metals to gold.

core.definition: To change one thing into another substance, form, or state, especially in a dramatic or transforming way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MYOOT, which sounds like the word mute with a y sound before the oo. Keep the first syllable short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a transformation of substance or essence, often with an element of wonder.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transmute in academic, literary, and historical writing, such as about alchemy or the change of ideas or values. In daily speech they would normally say change, turn into, or convert. Using transmute in casual conversation can sound overly fancy.

distinctions.note: Transform is broad and common; transmute often suggests a change at the level of substance or essence.
Convert usually refers to a practical change in form or use; transmute is more literary and suggests a change of nature.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor likes to say that a little bit of baking can transmute a bad day into a good one.
examples.professional: The workshop will show how to transmute raw sales notes into a clear, structured report.
examples.analytical: In the poem, suffering is transmuted into a form of spiritual insight rather than mere despair.

nuance.analogy: Like an alchemist turning lead into gold, transmute describes a change that alters the basic nature of something.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transmutare, to change across, from trans- (across) and mutare (to change).
common_mistakes: Using transmute for a simple change of appearance; use change or transform for everyday contexts.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: That has been trimmed.
senses.example: The lawn looked neat, with its trimmed hedges and freshly edged walkways.

senses.definition: Furnished with trimmings.
senses.example: The bride wore a gown trimmed with lace and tiny pearls.

core.definition: Having had extra or unwanted parts cut off, so it looks neater, smaller, or more efficient.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i, and the final d is clear. Do not add a vowel between the m and the d, even in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. A trimmed hedge or a trimmed budget sounds tidy and controlled, though a trimmed budget can also mean cuts that hurt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trimmed for hair, beards, hedges, nails, and budgets. A trimmed-down version is a smaller or simpler version of something. Use cut for a complete haircut, since trimmed suggests small removals.

distinctions.note: Cut is the general word for separating something. Trimmed suggests removing small excess parts to improve shape.
Shaved implies removing a thin surface layer, usually hair, very close to the skin.
Pruned is specific to plants and branches, usually for health or shape.

examples.everyday: I got my beard trimmed at the barbershop on Saturday.
examples.professional: The team presented a trimmed version of the model with fewer features.
examples.analytical: The argument is a trimmed form of Aquinas's claim, stripped of its metaphysical premises.

nuance.analogy: Like a hedge clipped back to its shape, trimmed means the excess has been cut away.
nuance.etymology: From Old English trymman, 'to make firm or strong', later 'to put in order' and 'to cut'.
common_mistakes: Using trimmed for a complete haircut; say cut when much of the hair is removed.
Pronouncing trimmed as two syllables (TRIM-id) instead of one.

senses.definition: An expression consisting of three terms.
Consisting of three names or parts or terms.
senses.example: The mathematics student factored the trinomial x squared plus five x plus six.

core.definition: In algebra, an expression made up of three terms joined by addition or subtraction, such as x² + 2x + 1.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NOH, the second syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced uh-l sound. Many learners stress the first syllable, so keep the main stress in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trinomial mainly in algebra classes and in mathematical writing. It is paired with binomial and monomial, which describe expressions with one or two terms. As an adjective it describes a three-part name in biology, but that use is specialized.

distinctions.note: A binomial has two terms, while a trinomial has three. Both are algebraic expressions.
A polynomial is the general term for any sum of terms with variables and whole-number exponents. A trinomial is one specific type of polynomial with three terms.

examples.everyday: My daughter said she had to factor a trinomial for her algebra quiz, and I could not remember how.
examples.professional: The optimization library handles polynomial inputs, but it requires us to expand any trinomial before passing it to the solver.
examples.analytical: A quadratic trinomial of the form ax² + bx + c can be factored over the integers only when its discriminant is a perfect square.

nuance.analogy: A trinomial is like a three-course meal: three distinct parts combined into one whole.
nuance.etymology: Coined by analogy with binomial, from Latin tri- (three) and nomen (name or term).
common_mistakes: Confusing trinomial with triple nominal, which is not a term in mathematics.
Saying trinomial with stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: Made up of three related elements, often matching.
senses.example: The triple markings on this vase are quite unique.

senses.definition: Of three times the quantity; treble.
senses.example: Give me a triple serving of mashed potatoes.

senses.definition: Designed for three users.
senses.example: a triple room

senses.definition: Folded in three; composed of three layers.
senses.example: She folded the paper triple, creasing each edge so it sat flat in her pocket.

senses.definition: Having three aspects.
senses.example: a triple meaning

senses.definition: Of time, three times as fast as very fast.
senses.example: The drummer kicked the song into triple time, racing through the chorus.

senses.definition: Three times or thrice the number, amount, size, etc.
senses.example: Sales this quarter reached a triple of last year's, which surprised the whole team.

senses.definition: A drink with three portions of alcohol.
senses.example: I've had a hard day; make that a triple.

senses.definition: A hamburger with three patties.
senses.example: I'd like a triple with cheese.

senses.definition: A three-point field goal.
senses.example: He hit a triple from the corner with two seconds left in the game.

senses.definition: A takeout shot in which three stones are removed from play.
senses.example: Her triple knocked two stones out of the house and left her stone sitting in the center.

senses.definition: A sequence of three elements or 3-tuple.
senses.example: The function returns a triple containing the name, age, and email address.

senses.definition: Short for triple combination engine.
senses.example: The engineers tested the triple on the test stand before the rocket's first flight.

senses.definition: Three runs.
senses.example: The home team's score in the seventh inning was a triple, giving them the lead.

senses.definition: A three-base hit.
senses.example: The shortstop hit a triple to lead off the ninth.

senses.definition: To multiply by three.
senses.example: The company tripled their earnings per share over last quarter.

senses.definition: To become three times as large.
senses.example: Our earnings have tripled in the last year.

senses.definition: To serve or operate as (something), in addition to two other functions.
senses.example: The old barn triples as a workshop and as a storage shed for the farm.

senses.definition: To get a three-base hit.
senses.example: The batter tripled into the gap.

core.definition: Three times as great or as many, or made up of three parts or three of the same kind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a syllabic l, so do not add a full uh vowel before it: TRIP-l, not TRIP-ul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes multiplication or strength, as in a triple threat or triple-check.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use triple for things like triple the price, triple-check, or a triple-decker sandwich. In baseball, a triple is a three-base hit, which many Americans know as a sports term. Treble is more often heard in British English, while Americans usually say triple.

distinctions.note: A triplet is one of three children born together, or a group of three notes in music, not the number three times something.
Treble means the same as triple, but Americans use triple far more often in everyday speech.
Threefold is more formal and often used in literary or abstract contexts.

examples.everyday: Let's get a triple-decker club sandwich; I'm starving.
examples.professional: If we triple the batch size, the training time will be about three times longer.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a triple structure of premise, qualification, and reversal, each depending on the one before.

nuance.analogy: Like a three-layer cake where each layer is the same, so the whole is three times as tall.
nuance.etymology: From Latin triplus, 'threefold', from Greek triplous.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (trip-ULL) instead of the first (TRIP-l).
Confusing triple, which means three times, with triplet, which means one of a set of three.

senses.definition: (rare) Sad; sorrowful; gloomy.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Sad, sorrowful, or gloomy in mood. A rare literary word borrowed from French.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, lax i as in 'list', not the long French vowel of 'triste' in Paris. The word is one syllable and rhymes with 'mist'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a quiet, gentle melancholy and sounds deliberately old-fashioned or poetic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use triste in speech. You will meet it in older poetry, literary criticism, or deliberately elegant prose. In everyday American English, say 'sad', 'gloomy', or 'melancholy' instead.

distinctions.note: Sad is the everyday word for unhappiness of any kind, while triste is rare and carries a literary, elegant tone.
Gloomy often describes weather, rooms, or a dark outlook, while triste is more about a person's inner mood.
Melancholy suggests a thoughtful, lingering sadness, and it is more common in both speech and writing than triste.

examples.professional: The team's triste mood after the quarter showed in every email, even though the numbers were improving.
examples.analytical: Several Romantic poets wrote in a triste register, where grief becomes a kind of quiet consolation rather than a crisis.

nuance.analogy: Triste is like a dim room rather than a dark one: the light is still there, but it has faded into a soft, low gloom.
nuance.etymology: From French triste, from Latin tristis, meaning sad.
common_mistakes: Using triste in ordinary conversation, where 'sad' sounds more natural and less affected.
Giving it the long French vowel, instead of a short English i as in 'list'.
Confusing triste (adjective) with tristesse (noun), which is the literary word for the feeling itself.

triste.etymology: Middle English *trist*, *triste*, borrowed from Old French *trist*, *triste*, from Latin *trīstis* (“sad, sorrowful”).

senses.definition: A tramp, i.e. a long and tiring walk.
senses.example: After the long trudge from the trailhead, we were grateful for the cold lake.

senses.definition: To walk wearily with heavy, slow steps.
To trudge along or over a route etc.
senses.example: The hikers trudged along the muddy ridge trail in silence for hours.

core.definition: To walk slowly and wearily with heavy steps, usually because of exhaustion, difficult ground, or a long distance.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short u in cut, and the dge ending is the j sound. Make the d and j blend into one quick sound, and keep the r clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It suggests tiredness, effort, and lack of energy, though it can describe determined perseverance too.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trudge in everyday descriptions of walking through snow, mud, or up a hill after a long day. It is a vivid, informal verb that sounds natural in storytelling and in conversation about travel or bad weather. It is less common as a formal term, where walk or make one's way is more typical.

distinctions.note: Plod stresses heavy, steady, and sometimes dull movement, while trudge stresses fatigue and a difficult journey.
Trek is a long, often deliberate journey, usually on foot, while trudge focuses on the slow, tired manner of walking.
Stomp describes heavy, forceful steps, often in anger, while trudge describes weary, slow movement.

examples.everyday: After the long shift, we had to trudge through the snow to reach the bus stop.
examples.professional: The team had to trudge through a backlog of tickets before the release could go out this week.
examples.analytical: The narrator's account of the journey shows how a single image of walking slowly can express exhaustion and loss.

nuance.analogy: Trudging is like walking with ankle weights on, where each step is a real effort and the body moves slowly forward.
common_mistakes: Using trudge for brisk or happy walking, which contradicts its meaning of weary effort.
Pronouncing the vowel like the u in rude instead of the short u in cut.
Forgetting the j sound at the end and saying trudj or trudg.

senses.definition: To cease paying attention.
senses.example: As soon as I turned my back, he started writing on the wall.

senses.definition: To forsake, to abandon; to ignore. [with on]
senses.example: He got off to a strong start, only to turn his back on the project two months later.

senses.definition: To turn away, as when fleeing or in contempt.
senses.example: When the scandal broke, the senator turned his back on his former allies.

core.definition: To ignore, reject or abandon someone or something, often by refusing to help or support them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on back. One's is reduced and sounds like 'wunz', with a final z. Keep the r in turn and say the phrase as one flowing unit: 'turn-wunz-BACK'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies rejection, betrayal or deliberate disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom when someone deliberately rejects a friend, a cause or a principle: 'Don't turn your back on your family.' It appears in everyday talk, news and sermons. A natural reply is a question such as 'Why did you give up on it?' Use on with the thing or person you reject: turn your back on, not turn back to.

distinctions.note: Abandon is direct and often literal, such as leaving a place or person; turn one's back is idiomatic and implies a deliberate turning away.
Ignore is neutral and general; turn one's back suggests a stronger, more visible rejection.
Desert is formal and often legal or military; turn one's back is everyday and can be emotional rather than legal.

collocations: turn your back on your friends
turn your back on the past
turn your back on the job
turn your back on the deal

examples.everyday: When my friend needed help moving, the others turned their backs on him and went home.
